living. I hardly know how Mr. Collins was first introduced to her
notice, but he certainly has not known her long.
question: What does Elizabeth tell Wickham about Mr. Collins's connection to Lady Catherine?
answer: She says Lady Catherine recently gave Mr. Collins a living, though he has not known her long.
evidence: Lady Catherine de Bourgh has very lately given him a living.

quote_text:
You know of course that Lady Catherine de Bourgh and Lady Anne Darcy
were sisters; consequently that she is aunt to the present Mr. Darcy.
question: What family connection does Wickham reveal to explain Lady Catherine's importance?
answer: Lady Catherine and Lady Anne Darcy were sisters, making Lady Catherine the present Darcy's aunt.
evidence: Lady Catherine de Bourgh and Lady Anne Darcy were sisters; consequently that she is aunt to the present Mr. Darcy.

quote_text:
No, indeed, I did not.--I knew nothing at all of Lady Catherine's
connections. I never heard of her existence till the day before
yesterday.
question: How much did Elizabeth know about Lady Catherine's family connections before Wickham told her?
answer: She knew nothing and had never heard of Lady Catherine until two days earlier.
evidence: I never heard of her existence till the day before yesterday.

quote_text:
Her daughter, Miss de Bourgh, will have a very large fortune, and it is
believed that she and her cousin will unite the two estates.
question: What does Wickham say about Miss de Bourgh's future according to common belief?
answer: She will have a large fortune, and it is believed she and her cousin Darcy will unite the two estates.
evidence: Her daughter, Miss de Bourgh, will have a very large fortune, and it is believed that she and her cousin will unite the two estates.

quote_text:
Mr. Collins, speaks highly both of Lady Catherine and her
daughter; but from some particulars that he has related of her ladyship,
I suspect his gratitude misleads him, and that in spite of her being his
patroness, she is an arrogant, conceited woman.
question: Why does Elizabeth doubt Mr. Collins's praise of Lady Catherine?
answer: From his anecdotes she suspects gratitude misleads him and that Lady Catherine is arrogant and conceited.
evidence: I suspect his gratitude misleads him, and that in spite of her being his patroness, she is an arrogant, conceited woman.

quote_text:
I believe her to be both in a great degree, I have
not seen her for many years, but I very well remember that I never liked
her, and that her manners were dictatorial and insolent. She has the
reputation of being remarkably sensible and clever; but I rather believe
she derives part of her abilities from her rank and fortune, part from
her authoritative manner, and the rest from the pride of her nephew, who
chuses that every one connected with him should have an understanding of
the first class.
question: How does Wickham confirm Elizabeth's suspicion about Lady Catherine?
answer: He says she is both arrogant and conceited and remembers her manners as dictatorial and insolent.
evidence: her manners were dictatorial and insolent

quote_text:
They have both, been deceived, I dare say, in some way or
other, of which we can form no idea. Interested people have perhaps
misrepresented each to the other. It is, in short, impossible for us to
conjecture the causes or circumstances which may have alienated them,
without actual blame on either side.
question: How does Jane try to explain the conflict between Darcy and Wickham?
answer: She suggests both were deceived by interested people who misrepresented each to the other, without blame on either side.
evidence: Interested people have perhaps misrepresented each to the other.

quote_text:
Very true, indeed;--and now, my dear Jane, what have you got to say in
behalf of the interested people who have probably been concerned in the
business?--Do clear _them_ too, or we shall be obliged to think ill of
somebody.
question: What does Elizabeth challenge Jane to do after Jane blames meddling outsiders?
answer: She asks Jane to clear the interested people too, or else they must think ill of somebody.
evidence: Do clear them too, or we shall be obliged to think ill of somebody.

quote_text:
Laugh as much as you chuse, but you will not laugh me out of my
opinion. My dearest Lizzy, do but consider in what a disgraceful light
it places Mr. Darcy, to be treating his father's favourite in such a
manner,--one, whom his father had promised to provide for.--It is
impossible. No man of common humanity, no man who had any value for his
character, could be capable of it. Can his most intimate friends be so
excessively deceived in him? oh! no.
question: What is Jane's stance about Darcy's treatment of Wickham despite Elizabeth's teasing?
answer: She insists it is impossible that a man of common humanity could treat his father's favorite so disgracefully.
evidence: No man of common humanity, no man who had any value for his character, could be capable of it.

quote_text:
I can much more easily believe Mr. Bingley's being imposed on, than
that Mr. Wickham should invent such a history of himself as he gave me
last night; names, facts, every thing mentioned without ceremony.--If it
be not so, let Mr. Darcy contradict it. Besides, there was truth in his
looks.
question: Why does Elizabeth find Wickham's story more credible than Jane does?
answer: She thinks his detailed account with names and facts is hard to invent and says there was truth in his looks.
evidence: names, facts, every thing mentioned without ceremony

quote_text:
It is difficult indeed--it is distressing.--One does not know what to
think.
question: How does Jane react to Elizabeth's certainty about Wickham and Darcy?
answer: She is distressed and uncertain, unable to decide what to think.
evidence: One does not know what to think.

quote_text: I beg your pardon;--one knows exactly what to think.
question: What does Elizabeth mean by correcting Jane's uncertainty?
answer: She means she herself has no doubt and thinks the matter clear against Darcy.
evidence: one knows exactly what to think.

quote_text:
While I can have my mornings to myself, it is enough.--I
think it no sacrifice to join occasionally in evening engagements.
Society has claims on us all; and I profess myself one of those who
consider intervals of recreation and amusement as desirable for every
body.
question: How does Mary justify joining the Netherfield ball excitement?
answer: She says she values her mornings alone and considers occasional evening engagements a reasonable social duty.
evidence: I think it no sacrifice to join occasionally in evening engagements.

quote_text:
I am by no means of opinion, I assure you, that a ball of
this kind, given by a young man of character, to respectable people, can
have any evil tendency; and I am so far from objecting to dancing myself
that I shall hope to be honoured with the hands of all my fair cousins
in the course of the evening, and I take this opportunity of soliciting
yours, Miss Elizabeth, for the two first dances especially,--a
preference which I trust my cousin Jane will attribute to the right
cause, and not to any disrespect for her.
question: Why does Mr. Collins accept the ball and ask Elizabeth for the first dances?
answer: He sees no evil in a respectable ball and wants to dance with all his cousins, especially Elizabeth first.
evidence: I shall hope to be honoured with the hands of all my fair cousins

quote_text:
I do not imagine his business would have called him away just now, if
he had not wished to avoid a certain gentleman here.
question: What does Denny imply about the reason for Wickham's absence from the Netherfield ball?
answer: He suggests Wickham stayed away to avoid a certain gentleman, evidently Mr. Darcy.
evidence: if he had not wished to avoid a certain gentleman here.

quote_text: I dare say you will find him very agreeable.
question: Why does Charlotte offer this prediction after Elizabeth reluctantly agrees to dance with Darcy?
answer: She wants Elizabeth not to let her fancy for Wickham make her appear unpleasant to a man of Darcy's consequence.
evidence: not to be a simpleton and allow her fancy for Wickham to make her appear unpleasant

quote_text:
Heaven forbid!--_That_ would be the greatest misfortune of all!--To
find a man agreeable whom one is determined to hate!--Do not wish me
such an evil.
question: Why does Elizabeth reject Charlotte's suggestion that she may find Darcy agreeable?
answer: Because she is determined to hate him and thinks finding him agreeable would be the worst misfortune.
evidence: To find a man agreeable whom one is determined to hate!

quote_text:
It is _your_ turn to say something now, Mr. Darcy.--_I_ talked about
the dance, and _you_ ought to make some kind of remark on the size of
the room, or the number of couples.
question: Why does Elizabeth prompt Darcy to make conversation during their dance?
answer: She is trying to break their awkward silence by ironically instructing him in the usual ballroom small talk.
evidence: It is your turn to say something now, Mr. Darcy.

quote_text:
Very well.--That reply will do for the present.--Perhaps by and bye I
may observe that private balls are much pleasanter than public
ones.--But _now_ we may be silent.
question: How does Elizabeth treat Darcy's compliant reply about what to say?
answer: She accepts it as sufficient for the moment, then suggests they may be silent again.
evidence: That reply will do for the present.

quote_text: Do you talk by rule then, while you are dancing?
question: What does Darcy want to know about Elizabeth's remark on conversation while dancing?
answer: He asks whether she follows a set rule for talking during a dance.
evidence: Do you talk by rule then, while you are dancing?

quote_text:
Sometimes. One must speak a little, you know. It would look odd to be
entirely silent for half an hour together, and yet for the advantage of
_some_, conversation ought to be so arranged as that they may have the
trouble of saying as little as possible.
question: What is Elizabeth's view of conversation during a dance?
answer: She thinks a little talk is socially necessary, but it could be arranged to spare people trouble.
evidence: One must speak a little, you know.

quote_text:
Are you consulting your own feelings in the present case, or do you
imagine that you are gratifying mine?
question: Why does Darcy question Elizabeth's motive for arranging conversation?
answer: He suspects she is teasing him and asks whether she is considering her own feelings or his.
evidence: Are you consulting your own feelings in the present case, or do you imagine that you are gratifying mine?

quote_text:
Both, for I have always seen a great
similarity in the turn of our minds.--We are each of an unsocial,
taciturn disposition, unwilling to speak, unless we expect to say
something that will amaze the whole room, and be handed down to
posterity with all the eclat of a proverb.
question: Why does Elizabeth answer that she is consulting both her own and Darcy's feelings?
answer: She claims they share an unsocial, taciturn disposition, so minimizing conversation suits them both.
evidence: I have always seen a great similarity in the turn of our minds.

quote_text:
This is no very striking resemblance of your own character, I am sure, How near it may be to _mine_, I cannot pretend to say.--_You_
think it a faithful portrait undoubtedly.
question: What is Darcy challenging in Elizabeth's comparison of their characters?
answer: He says her description of an unsocial disposition does not resemble her own character.
evidence: This is no very striking resemblance of your own character, I am sure.

quote_text: I must not decide on my own performance.
question: Why does Elizabeth refuse to judge her own portrait?
answer: She playfully declines to assess her own performance in their banter about character.
evidence: I must not decide on my own performance.

quote_text:
When you met us there the other day, we had just
been forming a new acquaintance.
question: Why does Elizabeth mention that they had just been forming a new acquaintance when Darcy met them?
answer: She deliberately brings up Wickham to probe Darcy's reaction to him.
evidence: we had just been forming a new acquaintance.

quote_text:
Mr. Wickham is blessed with such happy manners as may ensure his
_making_ friends--whether he may be equally capable of _retaining_ them,
is less certain.
question: What is Darcy implying about Wickham's ability to keep friends?
answer: Wickham may charm people into friendship, but Darcy doubts he can retain it.
evidence: whether he may be equally capable of retaining them, is less certain.

quote_text:
He has been so unlucky as to lose _your_ friendship, and in a manner which he is likely to suffer from all
his life.
question: Why does Elizabeth say Wickham has been unlucky to lose Darcy's friendship?
answer: She accuses Darcy of cutting Wickham in a way that will harm him for life.
evidence: in a manner which he is likely to suffer from all his life.

quote_text:
I have been most highly gratified indeed, my dear Sir. Such very
superior dancing is not often seen. It is evident that you belong to the
first circles. Allow me to say, however, that your fair partner does not
disgrace you, and that I must hope to have this pleasure often repeated,
especially when a certain desirable event, my dear Miss Eliza, (glancing
at her sister and Bingley,) shall take place. What congratulations will
then flow in! I appeal to Mr. Darcy:--but let me not interrupt you,
Sir.--You will not thank me for detaining you from the bewitching
converse of that young lady, whose bright eyes are also upbraiding me.
question: Why does Sir William compliment Darcy on his dancing and partner?
answer: He is trying to be gallant and alludes to the hoped-for marriage between Jane and Bingley.
evidence: Such very superior dancing is not often seen.

quote_text: Sir William's interruption has made me forget what we were talking of.
question: Why does Darcy say he has forgotten their conversation?
answer: Sir William's interruption gives him an awkward excuse to restart or avoid their former subject.
evidence: Sir William's interruption has made me forget what we were talking of.

quote_text:
I do not think we were speaking at all. Sir William could not have
interrupted any two people in the room who had less to say for
themselves.--We have tried two or three subjects already without
success, and what we are to talk of next I cannot imagine.
question: What does Elizabeth's remark reveal about their dance so far?
answer: They had been almost silent, so Sir William interrupted no real conversation.
evidence: We have tried two or three subjects already without success.

quote_text: What think you of books?
question: Why does Darcy propose books as a topic?
answer: He is trying to find a subject they can discuss after their earlier attempts failed.
evidence: What think you of books?

quote_text:
Books--Oh! no.--I am sure we never read the same, or not with the same
feelings.
question: What does Elizabeth mean by saying they never read the same or with the same feelings?
answer: She doubts they share tastes or responses, so books will not help their conversation.
evidence: I am sure we never read the same, or not with the same feelings.

quote_text:
I am sorry you think so; but if that be the case, there can at least be
no want of subject.--We may compare our different opinions.
question: How does Darcy respond to Elizabeth's claim that they read differently?
answer: He says differing opinions still give them something to discuss.
evidence: We may compare our different opinions.

quote_text:
No--I cannot talk of books in a ball-room; my head is always full of
something else.
question: Why does Elizabeth refuse to talk of books in the ballroom?
answer: She says her mind is occupied by something else in that setting.
evidence: I cannot talk of books in a ball-room; my head is always full of something else.

quote_text: The _present_ always occupies you in such scenes--does it?
question: Why does Darcy doubt Elizabeth's claim that her head is full of something else?
answer: He suspects she is absorbed by the present scene and asks her about it with doubt.
evidence: with a look of doubt.

quote_text: Yes, always,
question: Why does Elizabeth answer Darcy mechanically?
answer: Her thoughts have wandered away from the conversation, so she answers without full attention.
evidence: her thoughts had wandered far from the subject.

quote_text:
I remember hearing you once say, Mr. Darcy,
that you hardly ever forgave, that your resentment once created was
unappeasable. You are very cautious, I suppose, as to its _being
created_.
question: Why does Elizabeth bring up Darcy's boast about unforgiving resentment?
answer: She is testing his character and linking his unforgiving temper to his treatment of Wickham.
evidence: your resentment once created was unappeasable.

quote_text: I am,
question: What is Darcy agreeing to when he says I am?
answer: He admits he is cautious about creating a resentment he cannot appease.
evidence: I am, said he, with a firm voice.

quote_text: And never allow yourself to be blinded by prejudice?
question: What is Elizabeth probing with her question about prejudice?
answer: She asks whether Darcy's fixed judgments might be blinded by prejudice.
evidence: And never allow yourself to be blinded by prejudice?

quote_text: I hope not.
question: What does Darcy's I hope not concede?
answer: He hopes he is not blinded by prejudice, without claiming certainty.
evidence: I hope not.

quote_text:
It is particularly incumbent on those who never change their opinion,
to be secure of judging properly at first.
question: What warning does Elizabeth give Darcy about never changing his opinions?
answer: She implies that people who never change their minds must be especially sure their first judgment is right.
evidence: to be secure of judging properly at first.

quote_text: May I ask to what these questions tend?
question: Why does Darcy ask where Elizabeth's questions are tending?
answer: He is uncomfortable with her probing questions about his resentment and prejudice.
evidence: your resentment once created was unappeasable.

quote_text: Merely to the illustration of _your_ character, I am trying to make it out.
question: What does Elizabeth claim is her purpose in questioning Darcy?
answer: She says she is trying to illustrate and understand his character.
evidence: I am trying to make it out.

quote_text: And what is your success?
question: Why does Darcy ask about Elizabeth's success?
answer: He wants to know whether her attempt to make out his character has succeeded.
evidence: I am trying to make it out.

quote_text:
I do not get on at all. I hear such different
accounts of you as puzzle me exceedingly.
question: Why is Elizabeth unable to get on in understanding Darcy?
answer: She has heard such conflicting reports of him that she is puzzled.
evidence: I hear such different accounts of you as puzzle me exceedingly.

quote_text:
I can readily believe, that report may vary
greatly with respect to me; and I could wish, Miss Bennet, that you were
not to sketch my character at the present moment, as there is reason to
fear that the performance would reflect no credit on either.
question: Why does Darcy ask Elizabeth not to sketch his character at that moment?
answer: He fears her portrait would be unflattering and embarrassing to both of them.
evidence: the performance would reflect no credit on either.

quote_text:
But if I do not take your likeness now, I may never have another
opportunity.
question: What does Elizabeth imply by saying she may never have another opportunity?
answer: She means to keep teasing him by sketching his character now, as if their chance may pass.
evidence: I may never have another opportunity.

quote_text: I would by no means suspend any pleasure of yours,
question: How does Darcy respond to Elizabeth's determination to sketch him?
answer: He coldly says he will not stop her pleasure, and they part dissatisfied.
evidence: he coldly replied.

quote_text:
So, Miss Eliza, I hear you are quite delighted with George
Wickham!--Your sister has been talking to me about him, and asking me a
thousand questions; and I find that the young man forgot to tell you,
among his other communications, that he was the son of old Wickham, the
late Mr. Darcy's steward. Let me recommend you, however, as a friend,
not to give implicit confidence to all his assertions; for as to Mr.
Darcy's using him ill, it is perfectly false; for, on the contrary, he
has been always remarkably kind to him, though George Wickham has
treated Mr. Darcy in a most infamous manner. I do not know the
particulars, but I know very well that Mr. Darcy is not in the least to
blame, that he cannot bear to hear George Wickham mentioned, and that
though my brother thought he could not well avoid including him in his
invitation to the officers, he was excessively glad to find that he had
taken himself out of the way. His coming into the country at all, is a
most insolent thing indeed, and I wonder how he could presume to do it.
I pity you, Miss Eliza, for this discovery of your favourite's guilt;
but really considering his descent, one could not expect much better.
question: Why does Miss Bingley tell Elizabeth about Wickham's descent and Darcy's supposed kindness?
answer: She wants to discredit Wickham and undermine Elizabeth's admiration while defending Darcy.
evidence: as to Mr. Darcy's using him ill, it is perfectly false.

quote_text:
His guilt and his descent appear by your account to be the same, for I have heard you accuse him of nothing worse
than of being the son of Mr. Darcy's steward, and of _that_, I can
assure you, he informed me himself.
question: What point is Elizabeth making about Miss Bingley's accusation of Wickham?
answer: She says Miss Bingley treats Wickham's low birth as his guilt and offers no real charge beyond that.
evidence: I have heard you accuse him of nothing worse than of being the son of Mr. Darcy's steward.

quote_text: I beg your pardon, Excuse my interference.--It was kindly meant.
question: How does Miss Bingley react when Elizabeth defends Wickham?
answer: She turns away with a sneer and makes a sarcastic apology for her interference.
evidence: turning away with a sneer.

quote_text:
Insolent girl! You are much mistaken if
you expect to influence me by such a paltry attack as this. I see
nothing in it but your own wilful ignorance and the malice of Mr.
Darcy.
question: What does Elizabeth conclude about Miss Bingley's attack on Wickham?
answer: She sees it as a paltry, malicious effort rooted in Miss Bingley's ignorance and Darcy's influence.
evidence: I see nothing in it but your own wilful ignorance and the malice of Mr. Darcy.

quote_text:
I want to know, what you have learnt about Mr. Wickham. But perhaps you have
been too pleasantly engaged to think of any third person; in which case
you may be sure of my pardon.
question: Why does Elizabeth want to know what Jane learned about Wickham?
answer: She wants Bingley's account after Miss Bingley's accusations, and teases Jane about being with Bingley.
evidence: who had undertaken to make inquiries on the same subject of Bingley.

quote_text:
No, I have not forgotten him; but I have nothing
satisfactory to tell you. Mr. Bingley does not know the whole of his
history, and is quite ignorant of the circumstances which have
principally offended Mr. Darcy; but he will vouch for the good conduct,
the probity and honour of his friend, and is perfectly convinced that
Mr. Wickham has deserved much less attention from Mr. Darcy than he has
received; and I am sorry to say that by his account as well as his
sister's, Mr. Wickham is by no means a respectable young man. I am
afraid he has been very imprudent, and has deserved to lose Mr. Darcy's
regard.
question: What does Jane report about Bingley's view of Wickham?
answer: Bingley does not know the full history but defends Darcy and believes Wickham is not respectable.
evidence: Mr. Wickham is by no means a respectable young man.

quote_text: Mr. Bingley does not know Mr. Wickham himself?
question: Why does Elizabeth ask whether Bingley knows Wickham personally?
answer: She suspects Bingley's account comes from Darcy rather than personal knowledge.
evidence: Mr. Bingley does not know Mr. Wickham himself?

quote_text: No; he never saw him till the other morning at Meryton.
question: What does Jane's answer show about Bingley's knowledge of Wickham?
answer: Bingley has barely met Wickham, so his opinion is based on what Darcy told him.
evidence: he never saw him till the other morning at Meryton.

quote_text:
This account then is what he has received from Mr. Darcy. I am
perfectly satisfied. But what does he say of the living?
question: Why does Elizabeth conclude that Mr. Bingley's account of Wickham must be secondhand?
answer: Because Jane has just said Bingley never met Wickham, so his information could only have come from his friend Darcy.
evidence: he never saw him till the other morning at Meryton

quote_text:
He does not exactly recollect the circumstances, though he has heard
them from Mr. Darcy more than once, but he believes that it was left to
him _conditionally_ only.
question: What does Jane report about how much Bingley actually knows concerning the living?
answer: He does not recall the details but believes, on Darcy's word, that it was left to Wickham only conditionally.
evidence: he believes that it was left to him conditionally only

quote_text:
I have not a doubt of Mr. Bingley's sincerity, but you must excuse my not being convinced by assurances only. Mr.
Bingley's defence of his friend was a very able one I dare say, but
since he is unacquainted with several parts of the story, and has learnt
the rest from that friend himself, I shall venture still to think of
both gentlemen as I did before.
question: Why does Elizabeth remain unconvinced by Bingley's defence of Darcy?
answer: Because Bingley is ignorant of parts of the story and learned the rest from Darcy himself, so his assurances prove nothing.
evidence: since he is unacquainted with several parts of the story, and has learnt the rest from that friend himself

quote_text:
I have found out, by a singular accident, that there is now
in the room a near relation of my patroness. I happened to overhear the
gentleman himself mentioning to the young lady who does the honours of
this house the names of his cousin Miss de Bourgh, and of her mother
Lady Catherine. How wonderfully these sort of things occur! Who would
have thought of my meeting with--perhaps--a nephew of Lady Catherine de
Bourgh in this assembly!--I am most thankful that the discovery is made
in time for me to pay my respects to him, which I am now going to do,
and trust he will excuse my not having done it before. My total
ignorance of the connection must plead my apology.
question: How does Mr. Collins discover that a near relation of Lady Catherine is present at the ball?
answer: He overhears the gentleman mentioning Miss de Bourgh and Lady Catherine to the lady of the house.
evidence: I happened to overhear the gentleman himself mentioning to the young lady who does the honours of this house the names of his cousin Miss de Bourgh

quote_text: You are not going to introduce yourself to Mr. Darcy?
question: Why is Elizabeth so alarmed by Collins's intention to approach Mr. Darcy?
answer: She fears Darcy will regard an address without introduction as impertinent presumption rather than a compliment to his aunt.
evidence: Mr. Darcy would consider his addressing him without introduction as an impertinent freedom

quote_text:
Indeed I am. I shall intreat his pardon for not having done it earlier.
I believe him to be Lady Catherine's _nephew_. It will be in my power to
assure him that her ladyship was quite well yesterday se'night.
question: Why does Collins disregard Elizabeth's objections and insist on introducing himself to Darcy?
answer: He believes the clerical office equals the highest rank in dignity and that paying respect to his patroness's nephew is a point of duty.
evidence: I consider the clerical office as equal in point of dignity with the highest rank in the kingdom

quote_text:
My dear Miss Elizabeth, I have the highest opinion in the world of your
excellent judgment in all matters within the scope of your
understanding, but permit me to say that there must be a wide difference
between the established forms of ceremony amongst the laity, and those
which regulate the clergy; for give me leave to observe that I consider
the clerical office as equal in point of dignity with the highest rank
in the kingdom--provided that a proper humility of behaviour is at the
same time maintained. You must therefore allow me to follow the dictates
of my conscience on this occasion, which leads me to perform what I look
on as a point of duty. Pardon me for neglecting to profit by your
advice, which on every other subject shall be my constant guide, though
in the case before us I consider myself more fitted by education and
habitual study to decide on what is right than a young lady like
yourself.
question: Why does Collins refuse to be guided by Elizabeth's judgment on this matter?
answer: He claims his education and habitual study make him better fitted to judge what is right than a young lady like herself.
evidence: I consider myself more fitted by education and habitual study to decide on what is right

quote_text:
I have no reason, I assure you, to be dissatisfied with my
reception. Mr. Darcy seemed much pleased with the attention. He answered
me with the utmost civility, and even paid me the compliment of saying,
that he was so well convinced of Lady Catherine's discernment as to be
certain she could never bestow a favour unworthily. It was really a very
handsome thought. Upon the whole, I am much pleased with him.
question: How does Collins interpret Mr. Darcy's cold and slighting reception?
answer: He takes Darcy's distant bow as great civility and a compliment to Lady Catherine's discernment, and is much pleased with him.
evidence: Mr. Darcy seemed much pleased with the attention. He answered me with the utmost civility

quote_text:
What is Mr. Darcy to me, pray, that I should be afraid of him? I am
sure we owe him no such particular civility as to be obliged to say
nothing _he_ may not like to hear.
question: Why does Mrs. Bennet refuse to lower her voice while boasting of Jane's match?
answer: She feels no obligation to show Darcy particular civility and does not care whether he overhears what she says.
evidence: we owe him no such particular civility as to be obliged to say nothing he may not like to hear

quote_text:
For heaven's sake, madam, speak lower.--What advantage can it be to you
to offend Mr. Darcy?--You will never recommend yourself to his friend by
so doing.
question: What does Elizabeth fear will come of her mother's loud, indiscreet talk about Jane and Bingley?
answer: She fears offending Darcy will only harm the family and bring her shame, since it can do no good.
evidence: What advantage can it be to you to offend Mr. Darcy?

quote_text:
That will do extremely well, child. You have delighted us long enough.
Let the other young ladies have time to exhibit.
question: Why does Mr. Bennet intervene to stop Mary from singing another song?
answer: Mary's weak voice and affected manner were painful to the company, and Elizabeth's silent entreaties moved him to put an end to it.
evidence: Her voice was weak, and her manner affected.--Elizabeth was in agonies

quote_text:
If I, were so fortunate as to be able to sing, I
should have great pleasure, I am sure, in obliging the company with an
air; for I consider music as a very innocent diversion, and perfectly
compatible with the profession of a clergyman.--I do not mean however to
assert that we can be justified in devoting too much of our time to
music, for there are certainly other things to be attended to. The
rector of a parish has much to do.--In the first place, he must make
such an agreement for tythes as may be beneficial to himself and not
offensive to his patron. He must write his own sermons; and the time
that remains will not be too much for his parish duties, and the care
and improvement of his dwelling, which he cannot be excused from making
as comfortable as possible. And I do not think it of light importance
that he should have attentive and conciliatory manners towards every
body, especially towards those to whom he owes his preferment. I cannot
acquit him of that duty; nor could I think well of the man who should
omit an occasion of testifying his respect towards any body connected
with the family.
question: What does Collins's long speech about music reveal about how he regards his clerical position?
answer: He treats his profession with pompous self-importance, listing his duties and ending with a flattering bow to Darcy, his patroness's nephew.
evidence: I consider music as a very innocent diversion, and perfectly compatible with the profession of a clergyman

quote_text:
Lord,
how tired I am!
question: What does Lydia's tired exclamation reveal about the Longbourn party's departure from Netherfield?
answer: They are kept waiting a quarter of an hour after everyone else has gone, while their hostesses plainly wish them away.
evidence: they had to wait for their carriages a quarter of an hour after every body else was gone

quote_text:
May I hope, Madam, for your interest with your fair daughter Elizabeth,
when I solicit for the honour of a private audience with her in the
course of this morning?
question: Why does Collins approach Mrs. Bennet before speaking to Elizabeth alone?
answer: He is proceeding in an orderly, formal manner, seeking the mother's permission for a private audience as part of a regular proposal.
evidence: he set about it in a very orderly manner, with all the observances which he supposed a regular part of the business

quote_text:
Oh dear!--Yes--certainly.--I am sure Lizzy will be very happy--I am
sure she can have no objection.--Come, Kitty, I want you up stairs.
question: How does Mrs. Bennet react to Collins's request for a private audience with Elizabeth?
answer: She joyfully assumes Elizabeth will accept and hurries Kitty away to leave them alone together.
evidence: I am sure Lizzy will be very happy--I am sure she can have no objection

quote_text:
Dear Ma'am, do not go.--I beg you will not go.--Mr. Collins must excuse
me.--He can have nothing to say to me that any body need not hear. I am
going away myself.
question: Why does Elizabeth beg her mother not to leave the room?
answer: She dreads being alone with Collins and insists that he can have nothing to say that anyone need not hear.
evidence: He can have nothing to say to me that any body need not hear. I am going away myself

quote_text:
No, no, nonsense, Lizzy.--I desire you will stay where you are. Lizzy, I _insist_ upon your staying and hearing
Mr. Collins.
question: What does Mrs. Bennet's insistence show about her feelings on the match?
answer: She is determined that Elizabeth hear the proposal and accept it, ignoring her daughter's evident distress and embarrassment.
evidence: upon Elizabeth's seeming really, with vexed and embarrassed looks, about to escape

quote_text:
Believe me, my dear Miss Elizabeth, that your modesty, so far from
doing you any disservice, rather adds to your other perfections. You
would have been less amiable in my eyes had there _not_ been this little
unwillingness; but allow me to assure you that I have your respected
mother's permission for this address. You can hardly doubt the purport
of my discourse, however your natural delicacy may lead you to
dissemble; my attentions have been too marked to be mistaken. Almost as
soon as I entered the house I singled you out as the companion of my
future life. But before I am run away with by my feelings on this
subject, perhaps it will be advisable for me to state my reasons for
marrying--and moreover for coming into Hertfordshire with the design of
selecting a wife, as I certainly did.
question: How does Collins interpret Elizabeth's evident reluctance to hear him?
answer: He reads it as charming modesty that adds to her perfections, and takes it as encouragement rather than a rebuff.
evidence: your modesty, so far from doing you any disservice, rather adds to your other perfections

quote_text:
"My reasons for marrying are, first, that I think it a right thing for
every clergyman in easy circumstances (like myself) to set the example
of matrimony in his parish. Secondly, that I am convinced it will add
very greatly to my happiness; and thirdly--which perhaps I ought to have
mentioned earlier, that it is the particular advice and recommendation
of the very noble lady whom I have the honour of calling patroness.
Twice has she condescended to give me her opinion (unasked too!) on this
subject; and it was but the very Saturday night before I left
Hunsford--between our pools at quadrille, while Mrs. Jenkinson was
arranging Miss de Bourgh's foot-stool, that she said, Allow me, by the
way, to observe, my fair cousin, that I do not reckon the notice and
kindness of Lady Catherine de Bourgh as among the least of the
advantages in my power to offer. You will find her manners beyond any
thing I can describe; and your wit and vivacity I think must be
acceptable to her, especially when tempered with the silence and respect
which her rank will inevitably excite. Thus much for my general
intention in favour of matrimony; it remains to be told why my views
were directed to Longbourn instead of my own neighbourhood, where I
assure you there are many amiable young women. But the fact is, that
being, as I am, to inherit this estate after the death of your honoured
father, (who, however, may live many years longer,) I could not satisfy
myself without resolving to chuse a wife from among his daughters, that
the loss to them might be as little as possible, when the melancholy
event takes place--which, however, as I have already said, may not be
for several years. This has been my motive, my fair cousin, and I
flatter myself it will not sink me in your esteem. And now nothing
remains for me but to assure you in the most animated language of the
violence of my affection. To fortune I am perfectly indifferent, and
shall make no demand of that nature on your father, since I am well
aware that it could not be complied with; and that one thousand pounds
in the 4 per cents. which will not be yours till after your mother's
decease, is all that you may ever be entitled to. On that head,
therefore, I shall be uniformly silent; and you may assure yourself that
no ungenerous reproach shall ever pass my lips when we are married."
question: What reasons does Collins give for wishing to marry?
answer: He thinks a clergyman should set an example of matrimony, that it will add to his happiness, and that Lady Catherine has advised it.
evidence: first, that I think it a right thing for every clergyman in easy circumstances (like myself) to set the example of matrimony in his parish

quote_text:
You are too hasty, Sir, You forget that I have made no
answer. Let me do it without farther loss of time. Accept my thanks for
the compliment you are paying me. I am very sensible of the honour of
your proposals, but it is impossible for me to do otherwise than decline
them.
question: How does Elizabeth cut short Collins's lengthy proposal?
answer: She interrupts to thank him for the compliment but tells him plainly that it is impossible for her to accept.
evidence: it is impossible for me to do otherwise than decline them

quote_text:
I am not now to learn, that it is usual with young ladies to reject the addresses of the
man whom they secretly mean to accept, when he first applies for their
favour; and that sometimes the refusal is repeated a second or even a
third time. I am therefore by no means discouraged by what you have just
said, and shall hope to lead you to the altar ere long.
question: Why is Collins not discouraged by Elizabeth's flat refusal?
answer: He believes it is the usual custom of young ladies to reject a suitor they secretly mean to accept, and expects to be asked again.
evidence: it is usual with young ladies to reject the addresses of the man whom they secretly mean to accept

quote_text:
Upon my word, Sir, your hope is rather an
extraordinary one after my declaration. I do assure you that I am not
one of those young ladies (if such young ladies there are) who are so
daring as to risk their happiness on the chance of being asked a second
time. I am perfectly serious in my refusal.--You could not make _me_
happy, and I am convinced that I am the last woman in the world who
would make _you_ so.--Nay, were your friend Lady Catherine to know me, I
am persuaded she would find me in every respect ill qualified for the
situation.
question: What does Elizabeth insist about her rejection of Collins?
answer: That she is perfectly serious and would never risk her happiness by hoping to be asked a second time.
evidence: I am perfectly serious in my refusal

quote_text:
Were it certain that Lady Catherine would think so, but I cannot imagine that her ladyship would at all
disapprove of you. And you may be certain that when I have the honour of
seeing her again I shall speak in the highest terms of your modesty,
economy, and other amiable qualifications.
question: What does Collins say he will do the next time he sees Lady Catherine?
answer: He will speak in the highest terms of Elizabeth's modesty, economy, and other amiable qualifications.
evidence: I shall speak in the highest terms of your modesty, economy, and other amiable qualifications

quote_text:
Indeed, Mr. Collins, all praise of me will be unnecessary. You must
give me leave to judge for myself, and pay me the compliment of
believing what I say. I wish you very happy and very rich, and by
refusing your hand, do all in my power to prevent your being otherwise.
In making me the offer, you must have satisfied the delicacy of your
feelings with regard to my family, and may take possession of Longbourn
estate whenever it falls, without any self-reproach. This matter may be
considered, therefore, as finally settled.
question: How does Elizabeth try to close the matter for good?
answer: She asks him to judge for himself and believe her, and declares the affair finally settled so he may take Longbourn without self-reproach.
evidence: This matter may be considered, therefore, as finally settled

quote_text:
When I do myself the honour of speaking to you next on this subject I
shall hope to receive a more favourable answer than you have now given
me; though I am far from accusing you of cruelty at present, because I
know it to be the established custom of your sex to reject a man on the
first application, and perhaps you have even now said as much to
encourage my suit as would be consistent with the true delicacy of the
female character.
question: How does Collins explain away Elizabeth's continued refusal?
answer: He calls it the established custom of her sex to reject a man on the first application, and even takes it as encouragement.
evidence: I know it to be the established custom of your sex to reject a man on the first application

quote_text:
Really, Mr. Collins, you puzzle me
exceedingly. If what I have hitherto said can appear to you in the form
of encouragement, I know not how to express my refusal in such a way as
may convince you of its being one.
question: Why is Elizabeth so exasperated at this point in the interview?
answer: Her plainest refusals keep being read as encouragement, so she cannot find words that will convince him she means no.
evidence: If what I have hitherto said can appear to you in the form of encouragement, I know not how to express my refusal

quote_text:
You must give me leave to flatter myself, my dear cousin, that your
refusal of my addresses is merely words of course. My reasons for
believing it are briefly these:--It does not appear to me that my hand
is unworthy your acceptance, or that the establishment I can offer would
be any other than highly desirable. My situation in life, my connections
with the family of De Bourgh, and my relationship to your own, are
circumstances highly in my favour; and you should take it into farther
consideration that in spite of your manifold attractions, it is by no
means certain that another offer of marriage may ever be made you. Your
portion is unhappily so small that it will in all likelihood undo the
effects of your loveliness and amiable qualifications. As I must
therefore conclude that you are not serious in your rejection of me, I
shall chuse to attribute it to your wish of increasing my love by
suspense, according to the usual practice of elegant females.
question: What arguments does Collins offer for treating Elizabeth's refusal as mere form?
answer: He cites his situation, his connection with the De Bourghs, and her small portion, which makes another offer unlikely.
evidence: Your portion is unhappily so small that it will in all likelihood undo the effects of your loveliness

quote_text:
I do assure you, Sir, that I have no pretension whatever to that kind
of elegance which consists in tormenting a respectable man. I would
rather be paid the compliment of being believed sincere. I thank you
again and again for the honour you have done me in your proposals, but
to accept them is absolutely impossible. My feelings in every respect
forbid it. Can I speak plainer? Do not consider me now as an elegant
female intending to plague you, but as a rational creature speaking the
truth from her heart.
question: What does Elizabeth ask Collins to see her as, instead of an elegant female playing games?
answer: As a rational creature speaking the truth from her heart, who means her refusal sincerely.
evidence: Do not consider me now as an elegant female intending to plague you, but as a rational creature speaking the truth from her heart

quote_text:
You are uniformly charming! and I am persuaded that when sanctioned by the express
authority of both your excellent parents, my proposals will not fail of
being acceptable.
question: How does Collins respond to Elizabeth's third, most emphatic refusal?
answer: He remains convinced that with her parents' authority behind him his proposals will still be accepted.
evidence: when sanctioned by the express authority of both your excellent parents, my proposals will not fail of being acceptable

quote_text:
But depend upon it, Mr. Collins, that Lizzy shall be
brought to reason. I will speak to her about it myself directly. She is
a very headstrong foolish girl, and does not know her own interest; but
I will _make_ her know it.
question: What does Mrs. Bennet promise to do about Elizabeth's rejection of Collins?
answer: She vows to bring Lizzy to reason and make her see her own interest, calling her headstrong and foolish.
evidence: I will speak to her about it myself directly. She is a very headstrong foolish girl

quote_text:
Pardon me for interrupting you, Madam, but if she
is really headstrong and foolish, I know not whether she would
altogether be a very desirable wife to a man in my situation, who
naturally looks for happiness in the marriage state. If therefore she
actually persists in rejecting my suit, perhaps it were better not to
force her into accepting me, because if liable to such defects of
temper, she could not contribute much to my felicity.
question: Why does Collins suddenly hesitate about forcing Elizabeth to accept him?
answer: He fears that a genuinely headstrong, foolish wife would not contribute much to his happiness.
evidence: if liable to such defects of temper, she could not contribute much to my felicity

quote_text:
Sir, you quite misunderstand me, Lizzy is
only headstrong in such matters as these. In every thing else she is as
good natured a girl as ever lived. I will go directly to Mr. Bennet, and
we shall very soon settle it with her, I am sure.
question: How does Mrs. Bennet try to repair the damage her words have done?
answer: She backtracks, saying Lizzy is headstrong only in such matters and otherwise good-natured, and hurries off to Mr. Bennet.
evidence: Lizzy is only headstrong in such matters as these. In every thing else she is as good natured a girl as ever lived

quote_text:
Oh! Mr. Bennet, you are wanted immediately; we are all in an uproar.
You must come and make Lizzy marry Mr. Collins, for she vows she will
not have him, and if you do not make haste he will change his mind and
not have _her_.
question: What does Mrs. Bennet demand that her husband do?
answer: She insists he come at once and make Lizzy marry Collins before Collins changes his mind and refuses her.
evidence: You must come and make Lizzy marry Mr. Collins, for she vows she will not have him

quote_text: I have not the pleasure of understanding you, Of what are you talking?
question: How does Mr. Bennet receive his wife's breathless account of the crisis?
answer: With calm unconcern, raising his eyes from his book and professing not to understand what she is talking about.
evidence: with a calm unconcern which was not in the least altered by her communication

quote_text:
Of Mr. Collins and Lizzy. Lizzy declares she will not have Mr. Collins,
and Mr. Collins begins to say that he will not have Lizzy.
question: What is the state of affairs Mrs. Bennet urgently describes?
answer: Elizabeth refuses Collins, and Collins now threatens to refuse her, so the match may slip away entirely.
evidence: Lizzy declares she will not have Mr. Collins, and Mr. Collins begins to say that he will not have Lizzy

quote_text: And what am I to do on the occasion?--It seems an hopeless business.
question: What is Mr. Bennet's attitude towards the quarrel between Elizabeth and Collins?
answer: He is detached and unruffled, treating the whole business as hopeless and beyond his interference.
evidence: Mr. Bennet raised his eyes from his book as she entered, and fixed them on her face

quote_text:
Speak to Lizzy about it yourself. Tell her that you insist upon her
marrying him.
question: What does Mrs. Bennet instruct her husband to tell Elizabeth?
answer: That he insists upon her marrying Mr. Collins.
evidence: Tell her that you insist upon her marrying him

quote_text: Let her be called down. She shall hear my opinion.
question: What does Mr. Bennet decide to do about the dispute?
answer: He has Elizabeth summoned so that she may hear his opinion on the proposal.
evidence: Mrs. Bennet rang the bell, and Miss Elizabeth was summoned to the library

quote_text:
Come here, child, I have sent for
you on an affair of importance. I understand that Mr. Collins has made
you an offer of marriage. Is it true?
question: What does Elizabeth feel as she follows her father into the library?
answer: She is curious, suspecting that what he has to say concerns Mr. Collins's proposal to her.
evidence: She followed him thither; and her curiosity to know what he had to tell her, was heightened

quote_text: Very well--and this offer of marriage you have refused?
question: How does Mr. Bennet go about settling the matter with Elizabeth?
answer: He calmly confirms the facts one by one, first the offer of marriage and then her refusal, before giving his own verdict.
evidence: I understand that Mr. Collins has made you an offer of marriage. Is it true?

quote_text: I have, Sir.
question: What does Elizabeth confirm to her father about Mr. Collins's proposal?
answer: She confirms that she has refused his offer of marriage.
evidence: this offer of marriage you have refused?

quote_text:
Very well. We now come to the point. Your mother insists upon your
accepting it. Is not it so, Mrs. Bennet?
question: How does Mr. Bennet frame the conflict over Elizabeth's refusal?
answer: He says Elizabeth's mother insists she accept Mr. Collins and asks Mrs. Bennet to confirm it.
evidence: Your mother insists upon your accepting it. Is not it so, Mrs. Bennet?

quote_text: Yes, or I will never see her again.
question: How does Mrs. Bennet react when asked whether she insists on the marriage?
answer: She fiercely confirms it, threatening never to see Elizabeth again if she refuses.
evidence: Yes, or I will never see her again.

quote_text:
An unhappy alternative is before you, Elizabeth. From this day you must
be a stranger to one of your parents.--Your mother will never see you
again if you do _not_ marry Mr. Collins, and I will never see you again
if you _do_.
question: What dilemma does Mr. Bennet present to Elizabeth regarding her parents' demands?
answer: She must lose one parent's society: her mother will disown her if she refuses Collins, her father if she accepts.
evidence: Your mother will never see you again if you do _not_ marry Mr. Collins

quote_text:
What do you mean, Mr. Bennet, by talking in this way? You promised me
to _insist_ upon her marrying him.
question: Why is Mrs. Bennet angry with Mr. Bennet's response to Elizabeth?
answer: She thinks he promised to insist that Elizabeth marry Mr. Collins but instead gave her a way out.
evidence: You promised me to _insist_ upon her marrying him.

quote_text:
My dear, I have two small favours to request.
First, that you will allow me the free use of my understanding on the
present occasion; and secondly, of my room. I shall be glad to have the
library to myself as soon as may be.
question: What does Mr. Bennet request from his wife after the argument over Elizabeth?
answer: He asks to use his own judgment and to be left alone in his library.
evidence: allow me the free use of my understanding on the present occasion; and secondly, of my room.

quote_text:
I am glad you are come, for there is such
fun here!--What do you think has happened this morning?--Mr. Collins has
made an offer to Lizzy, and she will not have him.
question: Why is Lydia excited when Charlotte arrives at Longbourn?
answer: She wants to share the news that Mr. Collins proposed to Elizabeth and was refused.
evidence: Mr. Collins has made an offer to Lizzy, and she will not have him.

quote_text:
Pray do, my dear Miss Lucas, for nobody is on my side, nobody takes part with me, I am cruelly used,
nobody feels for my poor nerves.
question: What does Mrs. Bennet want Charlotte to do about Elizabeth's refusal?
answer: She begs Charlotte to persuade Elizabeth to comply with the family's wishes.
evidence: entreating her to persuade her friend Lizzy to comply with the wishes of all her family.

quote_text:
Aye, there she comes, looking as unconcerned
as may be, and caring no more for us than if we were at York, provided
she can have her own way.--But I tell you what, Miss Lizzy, if you take
it into your head to go on refusing every offer of marriage in this way,
you will never get a husband at all--and I am sure I do not know who is
to maintain you when your father is dead.--_I_ shall not be able to keep
you--and so I warn you.--I have done with you from this very day.--I
told you in the library, you know, that I should never speak to you
again, and you will find me as good as my word. I have no pleasure in
talking to undutiful children.--Not that I have much pleasure indeed in
talking to any body. People who suffer as I do from nervous complaints
can have no great inclination for talking. Nobody can tell what I
suffer!--But it is always so. Those who do not complain are never
pitied.
question: How does Mrs. Bennet describe Elizabeth's attitude as Elizabeth enters?
answer: She complains that Elizabeth looks unconcerned and selfishly determined to have her own way.
evidence: looking as unconcerned as may be, and caring no more for us than if we were at York

quote_text:
Now, I do insist upon it, that you, all of you, hold your tongues, and
let Mr. Collins and me have a little conversation together.
question: What does Mrs. Bennet demand of the young women still in the room?
answer: She orders them to be quiet so she can speak privately with Mr. Collins.
evidence: let Mr. Collins and me have a little conversation together.

quote_text: Oh! Mr. Collins!
question: What is Mrs. Bennet about to do when she addresses Mr. Collins dolefully?
answer: She is beginning a private conversation with him, hoping to arrange the match with Elizabeth.
evidence: In a doleful voice Mrs. Bennet thus began the projected conversation.

quote_text:
My dear Madam, let us be for ever silent on this point.
Far be it from me,
question: How does Mr. Collins respond to Mrs. Bennet's lament about Elizabeth?
answer: He asks that the subject be dropped forever and then apologizes for withdrawing his suit.
evidence: let us be for ever silent on this point.

quote_text:
to resent the behaviour of your daughter. Resignation to
inevitable evils is the duty of us all; the peculiar duty of a young man
who has been so fortunate as I have been in early preferment; and I
trust I am resigned. Perhaps not the less so from feeling a doubt of my
positive happiness had my fair cousin honoured me with her hand; for I
have often observed that resignation is never so perfect as when the
blessing denied begins to lose somewhat of its value in our estimation.
You will not, I hope, consider me as shewing any disrespect to your
family, my dear Madam, by thus withdrawing my pretensions to your
daughter's favour, without having paid yourself and Mr. Bennet the
compliment of requesting you to interpose your authority in my behalf.
My conduct may I fear be objectionable in having accepted my dismission
from your daughter's lips instead of your own. But we are all liable to
error. I have certainly meant well through the whole affair. My object
has been to secure an amiable companion for myself, with due
consideration for the advantage of all your family, and if my _manner_
has been at all reprehensible, I here beg leave to apologise.
question: Why does Mr. Collins claim resignation is his duty after Elizabeth's rejection?
answer: He says he will not resent her behavior and that a fortunate young man like him should accept inevitable evils.
evidence: the peculiar duty of a young man who has been so fortunate as I have been

quote_text:
I found, as the time drew near, that I had better not meet
Mr. Darcy;--that to be in the same room, the same party with him for so
many hours together, might be more than I could bear, and that scenes
might arise unpleasant to more than myself.
question: Why does Wickham explain he stayed away from the Netherfield ball?
answer: He says he thought it better not to meet Mr. Darcy, fearing unpleasant scenes from being together so long.
evidence: I had better not meet Mr. Darcy;--that to be in the same room, the same party with him

quote_text:
This is from Caroline Bingley; what it contains, has surprised me a
good deal. The whole party have left Netherfield by this time, and are
on their way to town; and without any intention of coming back again.
You shall hear what she says.
question: What news in Caroline's letter upsets Jane?
answer: The whole Netherfield party has left for town and does not intend to return.
evidence: The whole party have left Netherfield by this time, and are on their way to town; and without any intention of coming back again.

quote_text:
It is unlucky, that you should not be
able to see your friends before they leave the country. But may we not
hope that the period of future happiness to which Miss Bingley looks
forward, may arrive earlier than she is aware, and that the delightful
intercourse you have known as friends, will be renewed with yet greater
satisfaction as sisters?--Mr. Bingley will not be detained in London by
them.
question: How does Elizabeth try to comfort Jane about the Bingleys' departure?
answer: She suggests Mr. Bingley will not be kept in London by his sisters and that Jane may soon be his sister.
evidence: Mr. Bingley will not be detained in London by them.

quote_text:
Caroline decidedly says that none of the party will return into
Hertfordshire this winter. I will read it to you--
question: What does Jane point out in Caroline's letter that makes her doubt Mr. Bingley's return?
answer: Caroline says none of the party will return to Hertfordshire that winter.
evidence: Caroline decidedly says that none of the party will return into Hertfordshire this winter.

quote_text:
It is evident by this, that he comes back no more this
winter.
question: What conclusion does Jane draw from Caroline's letter about Mr. Bingley's coming back?
answer: She concludes he will not return that winter.
evidence: he comes back no more this winter.

quote_text: It is only evident that Miss Bingley does not mean he _should_.
question: How does Elizabeth reinterpret Caroline's claim about the party not returning?
answer: She says it only shows Caroline does not mean Mr. Bingley to return, not that he will not.
evidence: It is only evident that Miss Bingley does not mean he should.

quote_text:
Why will you think so? It must be his own doing.--He is his own master.
But you do not know _all_. I _will_ read you the passage which
particularly hurts me. I will have no reserves from _you_.
question: Why does Jane insist on reading Elizabeth the passage that hurts her?
answer: She wants no reserves between them and is hurt by Caroline's hint about Miss Darcy.
evidence: I will read you the passage which particularly hurts me. I will have no reserves from you.

quote_text:
What think you of _this_ sentence, my dear Lizzy? Is it not clear enough?--Does it not expressly declare
that Caroline neither expects nor wishes me to be her sister; that she
is perfectly convinced of her brother's indifference, and that if she
suspects the nature of my feelings for him, she means (most kindly!) to
put me on my guard? Can there be any other opinion on the subject?
question: What does Jane ask Elizabeth to judge in Caroline's sentence about Miss Darcy?
answer: She asks whether it clearly declares Caroline neither expects nor wishes Jane to be her sister.
evidence: Caroline neither expects nor wishes me to be her sister

quote_text: Yes, there can; for mine is totally different.--Will you hear it?
question: How does Elizabeth respond when Jane asks if there can be another opinion of Caroline's sentence?
answer: She says yes, her own opinion is totally different, and offers to explain it.
evidence: for mine is totally different.--Will you hear it?

quote_text: Most willingly.
question: How does Jane react to Elizabeth's offer to explain her different interpretation?
answer: She eagerly agrees to hear it.
evidence: Most willingly.

quote_text:
You shall have it in few words. Miss Bingley sees that her brother is
in love with you, and wants him to marry Miss Darcy. She follows him to
town in the hope of keeping him there, and tries to persuade you that he
does not care about you.
question: What does Elizabeth think Miss Bingley is trying to achieve by going to town?
answer: She thinks Miss Bingley wants Mr. Bingley to marry Miss Darcy and is trying to keep him from Jane.
evidence: Miss Bingley sees that her brother is in love with you, and wants him to marry Miss Darcy.

quote_text:
Indeed, Jane, you ought to believe me.--No one who has ever seen you
together, can doubt his affection. Miss Bingley I am sure cannot. She is
not such a simpleton. Could she have seen half as much love in Mr. Darcy
for herself, she would have ordered her wedding clothes. But the case is
this. We are not rich enough, or grand enough for them; and she is the
more anxious to get Miss Darcy for her brother, from the notion that
when there has been _one_ intermarriage, she may have less trouble in
achieving a second; in which there is certainly some ingenuity, and I
dare say it would succeed, if Miss de Bourgh were out of the way. But,
my dearest Jane, you cannot seriously imagine that because Miss Bingley
tells you her brother greatly admires Miss Darcy, he is in the smallest
degree less sensible of _your_ merit than when he took leave of you on
Tuesday, or that it will be in her power to persuade him that instead of
being in love with you, he is very much in love with her friend.
question: Why does Elizabeth believe the Bingley sisters oppose a match between Jane and their brother?
answer: She says the Bennets are not rich or grand enough, and Miss Bingley hopes for an alliance with Miss Darcy.
evidence: We are not rich enough, or grand enough for them

quote_text:
If we thought alike of Miss Bingley, your
representation of all this, might make me quite easy. But I know the
foundation is unjust. Caroline is incapable of wilfully deceiving any
one; and all that I can hope in this case is, that she is deceived
herself.
question: Why can Jane not accept Elizabeth's theory that Miss Bingley is deliberately deceiving her?
answer: Jane believes Caroline is incapable of willful deception and may be deceived herself.
evidence: Caroline is incapable of wilfully deceiving any one

quote_text:
That is right.--You could not have started a more happy idea, since you
will not take comfort in mine. Believe her to be deceived by all means.
You have now done your duty by her, and must fret no longer.
question: What does Elizabeth advise Jane to do since Jane will not accept her view of Miss Bingley?
answer: She tells Jane to believe Caroline is deceived and stop fretting.
evidence: Believe her to be deceived by all means. You have now done your duty by her, and must fret no longer.

quote_text:
But, my dear sister, can I be happy, even supposing the best, in
accepting a man whose sisters and friends are all wishing him to marry
elsewhere?
question: What worry does Jane raise about marrying Bingley even if he returns her feelings?
answer: She worries she cannot be happy if his sisters and friends wish him to marry elsewhere.
evidence: accepting a man whose sisters and friends are all wishing him to marry elsewhere

quote_text:
You must decide for yourself, and if upon mature
deliberation, you find that the misery of disobliging his two sisters is
more than equivalent to the happiness of being his wife, I advise you by
all means to refuse him.
question: What does Elizabeth tell Jane to do if the disapproval of Bingley's sisters outweighs the happiness of marrying him?
answer: She advises Jane to refuse him.
evidence: I advise you by all means to refuse him.

quote_text:
How can you talk so? You must know that
though I should be exceedingly grieved at their disapprobation, I could
not hesitate.
question: How does Jane respond to Elizabeth's suggestion that she might refuse Bingley over his sisters' disapproval?
answer: She says she would be grieved but could not hesitate to accept him.
evidence: though I should be exceedingly grieved at their disapprobation, I could not hesitate.

quote_text:
I did not think you would;--and that being the case, I cannot consider
your situation with much compassion.
question: How does Elizabeth react to Jane's admission that she would not hesitate to marry Bingley?
answer: She says she expected that and therefore cannot pity Jane's situation much.
evidence: I cannot consider your situation with much compassion.

quote_text:
But if he returns no more this winter, my choice will never be
required. A thousand things may arise in six months!
question: What hope does Jane cling to when she thinks Bingley may not return this winter?
answer: She notes her choice will never be required and that many things may change in six months.
evidence: A thousand things may arise in six months!

quote_text:
It keeps him in good
humour, and I am more obliged to you than I can express.
question: Why is Elizabeth grateful to Charlotte during Mr. Collins's visit?
answer: Charlotte's attention keeps Mr. Collins in good humor and relieves Elizabeth.
evidence: It keeps him in good humour

quote_text:
My dear Madam, this invitation is particularly
gratifying, because it is what I have been hoping to receive; and you
may be very certain that I shall avail myself of it as soon as
possible.
question: How does Mr. Collins respond to Mrs. Bennet's invitation to visit Longbourn again?
answer: He says it is gratifying and he will accept as soon as possible.
evidence: this invitation is particularly gratifying, because it is what I have been hoping to receive

quote_text:
But is there not danger of Lady Catherine's disapprobation here, my
good sir?--You had better neglect your relations, than run the risk of
offending your patroness.
question: Why does Mr. Bennet warn Mr. Collins about returning to Longbourn?
answer: He ironically suggests Lady Catherine might disapprove and that offending his patroness is riskier than neglecting relations.
evidence: But is there not danger of Lady Catherine's disapprobation here, my good sir?

quote_text:
My dear sir, I am particularly obliged to you
for this friendly caution, and you may depend upon my not taking so
material a step without her ladyship's concurrence.
question: How does Mr. Collins take Mr. Bennet's caution about Lady Catherine?
answer: He thanks him and promises not to act without Lady Catherine's concurrence.
evidence: you may depend upon my not taking so material a step without her ladyship's concurrence.

quote_text:
You cannot be too much on your guard. Risk any thing rather than her
displeasure; and if you find it likely to be raised by your coming to us
again, which I should think exceedingly probable, stay quietly at home,
and be satisfied that _we_ shall take no offence.
question: What does Mr. Bennet urge Mr. Collins to do rather than risk Lady Catherine's displeasure by visiting?
answer: He tells him to stay quietly at home and not worry about offending the Bennets.
evidence: stay quietly at home, and be satisfied that we shall take no offence.

quote_text:
Believe me, my dear sir, my gratitude is warmly excited by such
affectionate attention; and depend upon it, you will speedily receive
from me a letter of thanks for this, as well as for every other mark of
your regard during my stay in Hertfordshire. As for my fair cousins,
though my absence may not be long enough to render it necessary, I shall
now take the liberty of wishing them health and happiness, not excepting
my cousin Elizabeth.
question: How does Mr. Collins close his farewell to the Bennet family?
answer: He thanks Mr. Bennet, promises a letter of thanks, and wishes all his cousins health and happiness, including Elizabeth.
evidence: I shall now take the liberty of wishing them health and happiness, not excepting my cousin Elizabeth.

quote_text: Engaged to Mr. Collins! my dear Charlotte,--impossible!
question: How does Elizabeth react when Charlotte tells her she is engaged to Mr. Collins?
answer: She is so shocked that she cries out that it is impossible.
evidence: Engaged to Mr. Collins! my dear Charlotte,--impossible!

quote_text:
Why should you be surprised, my dear Eliza?--Do you think it incredible
that Mr. Collins should be able to procure any woman's good opinion,
because he was not so happy as to succeed with you?
question: How does Charlotte defend her engagement after Elizabeth's shocked reaction?
answer: She asks why it is incredible that Mr. Collins could win a woman's good opinion just because he failed with Elizabeth.
evidence: Do you think it incredible that Mr. Collins should be able to procure any woman's good opinion

quote_text:
I see what you are feeling, you must be
surprised, very much surprised,--so lately as Mr. Collins was wishing to
marry you. But when you have had time to think it all over, I hope you
will be satisfied with what I have done. I am not romantic you know. I
never was. I ask only a comfortable home; and considering Mr. Collins's
character, connections, and situation in life, I am convinced that my
chance of happiness with him is as fair, as most people can boast on
entering the marriage state.
question: Why does Charlotte tell Elizabeth that she understands her surprise at the engagement?
answer: She knows Elizabeth is astonished that Charlotte accepted Mr. Collins so soon after he proposed to Elizabeth, and she defends the match as a practical choice rather than a romantic one.
evidence: I am not romantic you know. I never was. I ask only a comfortable home

quote_text: Undoubtedly;
question: What does Elizabeth's response to Charlotte's explanation reveal about her feelings?
answer: She gives only a quiet, noncommittal agreement, and the awkward pause shows she is not yet reconciled to the match.
evidence: and after an awkward pause, they returned to the rest of the family

quote_text:
Good Lord! Sir William, how can you tell such a story?--Do not you know
that Mr. Collins wants to marry Lizzy?
question: Why does Lydia accuse Sir William of telling a false story about Charlotte?
answer: She thinks Mr. Collins is supposed to marry Elizabeth, so she cannot believe he has engaged himself to Charlotte.
evidence: Do not you know that Mr. Collins wants to marry Lizzy?

quote_text:
Indeed, Mr. Bennet, it is very hard to think that Charlotte
Lucas should ever be mistress of this house, that I should be forced to
make way for _her_, and live to see her take my place in it!
question: What future prospect makes Mrs. Bennet complain to her husband?
answer: She dreads Charlotte Lucas becoming mistress of Longbourn and displacing her after Mr. Bennet's death.
evidence: Charlotte Lucas should ever be mistress of this house

quote_text:
My dear, do not give way to such gloomy thoughts. Let us hope for
better things. Let us flatter ourselves that _I_ may be the survivor.
question: How does Mr. Bennet try to console his wife about Charlotte inheriting Longbourn?
answer: He ironically suggests they hope he will survive her, so she need not see Charlotte take her place.
evidence: Let us flatter ourselves that _I_ may be the survivor.

quote_text:
I cannot bear to think that they should have all this estate. If it was
not for the entail I should not mind it.
question: What does Mrs. Bennet say is the real source of her distress about the Collinses?
answer: She says the entail is what she cannot bear; without it she would not mind their having the estate.
evidence: If it was not for the entail I should not mind it.

quote_text: What should not you mind?
question: What is Mr. Bennet teasing his wife about with this question?
answer: He is pressing her on her claim that only the entail troubles her, turning her complaint into an absurdity.
evidence: If it was not for the entail I should not mind it.

quote_text: I should not mind any thing at all.
question: How does Mrs. Bennet answer her husband's probing question, and why is it comic?
answer: She says she would not mind anything at all, a sweeping claim that exposes her illogic and gives Mr. Bennet another opening.
evidence: I should not mind any thing at all.

quote_text:
Let us be thankful that you are preserved from a state of such
insensibility.
question: What is the ironic point of Mr. Bennet's thanks?
answer: He pretends to be grateful she is spared from insensibility, mocking her claim that she would mind nothing.
evidence: I should not mind any thing at all.

quote_text:
I never can be thankful, Mr. Bennet, for any thing about the entail.
How any one could have the conscience to entail away an estate from
one's own daughters I cannot understand; and all for the sake of Mr.
Collins too!--Why should _he_ have it more than anybody else?
question: What does Mrs. Bennet reveal about her view of the entail and Mr. Collins?
answer: She thinks it unjust to disinherit daughters for Collins's sake and cannot feel grateful for any part of it.
evidence: How any one could have the conscience to entail away an estate from one's own daughters

quote_text: I leave it to yourself to determine,
question: What is the effect of Mr. Bennet's final reply to her complaint?
answer: He refuses to argue and leaves her to answer her own rhetorical question, ending the exchange with dry irony.
evidence: I leave it to yourself to determine

quote_text:
Oh! that my dear mother had more command over herself; she can have no
idea of the pain she gives me by her continual reflections on him. But I
will not repine. It cannot last long. He will be forgot, and we shall
all be as we were before.
question: Why does Jane wish her mother had more self-command?
answer: Because Mrs. Bennet's continual remarks about Bingley cause Jane pain, though Jane resolves not to repine.
evidence: she can have no idea of the pain she gives me by her continual reflections on him.

quote_text:
You doubt me, indeed you have no
reason. He may live in my memory as the most amiable man of my
acquaintance, but that is all. I have nothing either to hope or fear,
and nothing to reproach him with. Thank God! I have not _that_ pain. A
little time therefore.--I shall certainly try to get the better.
question: What prompts Jane to protest that Elizabeth doubts her?
answer: Elizabeth's silent, incredulous look makes Jane insist she has no hope or fear and only remembers Bingley as amiable.
evidence: Elizabeth looked at her sister with incredulous solicitude, but said nothing.

quote_text:
I have this comfort immediately,
that it has not been more than an error of fancy on my side, and that it
has done no harm to any one but myself.
question: What comfort does Jane find in her disappointment over Bingley?
answer: She believes her attachment was only an error of fancy and has harmed no one but herself.
evidence: it has not been more than an error of fancy on my side

quote_text:
My dear Jane! you are too good. Your sweetness
and disinterestedness are really angelic; I do not know what to say to
you. I feel as if I had never done you justice, or loved you as you
deserve.
question: Why is Elizabeth moved to call Jane angelic here?
answer: Jane has just blamed only herself and claimed her disappointment harmed no one else, so Elizabeth feels she has never done Jane justice.
evidence: it has done no harm to any one but myself

quote_text:
Nay, this is not fair. _You_ wish to think all the
world respectable, and are hurt if I speak ill of any body. _I_ only
want to think _you_ perfect, and you set yourself against it. Do not be
afraid of my running into any excess, of my encroaching on your
privilege of universal good will. You need not. There are few people
whom I really love, and still fewer of whom I think well. The more I see
of the world, the more am I dissatisfied with it; and every day confirms
my belief of the inconsistency of all human characters, and of the
little dependence that can be placed on the appearance of either merit
or sense. I have met with two instances lately; one I will not mention;
the other is Charlotte's marriage. It is unaccountable! in every view it
is unaccountable!
question: What does Elizabeth accuse Jane of in this playful protest?
answer: She says Jane is too charitable to everyone and refuses Elizabeth's praise, while Elizabeth wants to think Jane perfect.
evidence: You wish to think all the world respectable, and are hurt if I speak ill of any body.

quote_text:
My dear Lizzy, do not give way to such feelings as these. They will
ruin your happiness. You do not make allowance enough for difference of
situation and temper. Consider Mr. Collins's respectability, and
Charlotte's prudent, steady character. Remember that she is one of a
large family; that as to fortune, it is a most eligible match; and be
ready to believe, for every body's sake, that she may feel something
like regard and esteem for our cousin.
question: What does Jane urge Elizabeth to do about Charlotte's marriage?
answer: She asks Elizabeth to make allowances for Charlotte's situation and temper and to believe Charlotte may feel esteem for Mr. Collins.
