evidence: Consider Mr. Collins's respectability, and Charlotte's prudent, steady character.

quote_text:
To oblige you, I would try to believe almost any thing, but no one else
could be benefited by such a belief as this; for were I persuaded that
Charlotte had any regard for him, I should only think worse of her
understanding, than I now do of her heart. My dear Jane, Mr. Collins is
a conceited, pompous, narrow-minded, silly man; you know he is, as well
as I do; and you must feel, as well as I do, that the woman who marries
him, cannot have a proper way of thinking. You shall not defend her,
though it is Charlotte Lucas. You shall not, for the sake of one
individual, change the meaning of principle and integrity, nor
endeavour to persuade yourself or me, that selfishness is prudence, and
insensibility of danger, security for happiness.
question: Why does Elizabeth refuse to believe Charlotte has any regard for Mr. Collins?
answer: She says such a belief would make her think worse of Charlotte's understanding, since she considers Mr. Collins silly and the match mercenary.
evidence: Mr. Collins is a conceited, pompous, narrow-minded, silly man

quote_text:
I must think your language too strong in speaking of both, and I hope you will be convinced of it, by seeing them happy
together. But enough of this. You alluded to something else. You
mentioned _two_ instances. I cannot misunderstand you, but I intreat
you, dear Lizzy, not to pain me by thinking _that person_ to blame, and
saying your opinion of him is sunk. We must not be so ready to fancy
ourselves intentionally injured. We must not expect a lively young man
to be always so guarded and circumspect. It is very often nothing but
our own vanity that deceives us. Women fancy admiration means more than
it does.
question: What does Jane hope will convince Elizabeth to soften her judgment of Charlotte and Mr. Collins?
answer: She hopes Elizabeth will be convinced by seeing them happy together.
evidence: I hope you will be convinced of it, by seeing them happy together.

quote_text: And men take care that they should.
question: What does Elizabeth mean by her retort about men?
answer: She means men deliberately encourage women to read more into admiration than is intended, so women's illusions are partly men's fault.
evidence: Women fancy admiration means more than it does.

quote_text:
If it is designedly done, they cannot be justified; but I have no idea
of there being so much design in the world as some persons imagine.
question: What view of human scheming does Jane express here?
answer: She admits deliberate harm would be unjustifiable but doubts there is as much design in the world as Elizabeth imagines.
evidence: I have no idea of there being so much design in the world as some persons imagine.

quote_text:
I am far from attributing any part of Mr. Bingley's conduct to design, but without scheming to do wrong, or to make others
unhappy, there may be error, and there may be misery. Thoughtlessness,
want of attention to other people's feelings, and want of resolution,
will do the business.
question: How does Elizabeth explain Bingley's behavior without accusing him of deliberate scheming?
answer: She blames thoughtlessness, inattention to others' feelings, and want of resolution, which can cause misery without design.
evidence: Thoughtlessness, want of attention to other people's feelings, and want of resolution, will do the business.

quote_text: And do you impute it to either of those?
question: What is Jane asking Elizabeth to specify about Bingley's conduct?
answer: She asks which of the faults Elizabeth just listed—thoughtlessness or want of resolution—she attributes to Bingley.
evidence: Thoughtlessness, want of attention to other people's feelings, and want of resolution

quote_text:
Yes; to the last. But if I go on, I shall displease you by saying what
I think of persons you esteem. Stop me whilst you can.
question: Which fault does Elizabeth assign to Bingley, and why does she warn Jane?
answer: She assigns want of resolution and warns that continuing will criticize people Jane esteems.
evidence: Yes; to the last. But if I go on, I shall displease you

quote_text: You persist, then, in supposing his sisters influence him.
question: What belief of Elizabeth is Jane summarizing here?
answer: Jane asks whether Elizabeth still thinks Bingley's sisters influenced him against her.
evidence: his sisters influence him

quote_text: Yes, in conjunction with his friend.
question: Whom does Elizabeth add to the sisters as influencing Bingley?
answer: She adds Mr. Darcy, Bingley's friend.
evidence: in conjunction with his friend

quote_text:
I cannot believe it. Why should they try to influence him? They can
only wish his happiness, and if he is attached to me, no other woman can
secure it.
question: Why does Jane reject the idea that Bingley's sisters would interfere?
answer: She thinks they can only wish his happiness, and if he loves her no other woman can secure it.
evidence: They can only wish his happiness, and if he is attached to me, no other woman can secure it.

quote_text:
Your first position is false. They may wish many things besides his
happiness; they may wish his increase of wealth and consequence; they
may wish him to marry a girl who has all the importance of money, great
connections, and pride.
question: How does Elizabeth challenge Jane's belief about the sisters' motives?
answer: She says they may want wealth and consequence for Bingley and a match with money and pride, not merely his happiness.
evidence: They may wish many things besides his happiness; they may wish his increase of wealth and consequence

quote_text:
Beyond a doubt, they _do_ wish him to chuse Miss Darcy, but this may be from better feelings than you are supposing. They have
known her much longer than they have known me; no wonder if they love
her better. But, whatever may be their own wishes, it is very unlikely
they should have opposed their brother's. What sister would think
herself at liberty to do it, unless there were something very
objectionable? If they believed him attached to me, they would not try
to part us; if he were so, they could not succeed. By supposing such an
affection, you make every body acting unnaturally and wrong, and me most
unhappy. Do not distress me by the idea. I am not ashamed of having been
mistaken--or, at least, it is slight, it is nothing in comparison of
what I should feel in thinking ill of him or his sisters. Let me take it
in the best light, in the light in which it may be understood.
question: How does Jane try to excuse the Bingley sisters' preference for Miss Darcy?
answer: She says they have known Georgiana longer and may love her better, so their wish may come from better feelings.
evidence: They have known her much longer than they have known me; no wonder if they love her better.

quote_text:
So, Lizzy, your sister is crossed in love I find. I congratulate her. Next to
being married, a girl likes to be crossed in love a little now and then.
It is something to think of, and gives her a sort of distinction among
her companions. When is your turn to come? You will hardly bear to be
long outdone by Jane. Now is your time. Here are officers enough at
Meryton to disappoint all the young ladies in the country. Let Wickham
be _your_ man. He is a pleasant fellow, and would jilt you creditably.
question: What is Mr. Bennet's ironic reaction to Jane's disappointment?
answer: He congratulates Jane and treats being crossed in love as a distinction and a joke.
evidence: your sister is crossed in love I find. I congratulate her.

quote_text:
Thank you, Sir, but a less agreeable man would satisfy me. We must not
all expect Jane's good fortune.
question: How does Elizabeth answer her father's joke about Wickham jilting her?
answer: She thanks him but says a less agreeable man would satisfy her and that not everyone can expect Jane's good fortune.
evidence: a less agreeable man would satisfy me. We must not all expect Jane's good fortune.

quote_text:
True, but it is a comfort to think that, whatever of
that kind may befal you, you have an affectionate mother who will always
make the most of it.
question: What ironic comfort does Mr. Bennet offer Elizabeth about future disappointments?
answer: He says her affectionate mother will always make the most of any romantic misfortune that befalls her.
evidence: you have an affectionate mother who will always make the most of it.

quote_text:
I do not blame Jane, for Jane would have got Mr.
Bingley, if she could. But, Lizzy! Oh, sister! it is very hard to think
that she might have been Mr. Collins's wife by this time, had not it
been for her own perverseness. He made her an offer in this very room,
and she refused him. The consequence of it is, that Lady Lucas will have
a daughter married before I have, and that Longbourn estate is just as
much entailed as ever. The Lucases are very artful people indeed,
sister. They are all for what they can get. I am sorry to say it of
them, but so it is. It makes me very nervous and poorly, to be thwarted
so in my own family, and to have neighbours who think of themselves
before anybody else. However, your coming just at this time is the
greatest of comforts, and I am very glad to hear what you tell us, of
long sleeves.
question: What does Mrs. Bennet blame Elizabeth for in her complaint to Mrs. Gardiner?
answer: She blames Elizabeth's perverseness for refusing Mr. Collins, which she thinks could have secured the family.
evidence: she might have been Mr. Collins's wife by this time, had not it been for her own perverseness.

quote_text:
It
seems likely to have been a desirable match for Jane, I am
sorry it went off. But these things happen so often! A young man, such
as you describe Mr. Bingley, so easily falls in love with a pretty girl
for a few weeks, and when accident separates them, so easily forgets
her, that these sort of inconstancies are very frequent.
question: How does Mrs. Gardiner try to console Elizabeth about Jane and Bingley?
answer: She says such inconstancies are common and that a young man may easily forget a pretty girl after an accidental separation.
evidence: so easily falls in love with a pretty girl for a few weeks

quote_text:
An excellent consolation in its way, but it will not
do for _us_. We do not suffer by _accident_. It does not often happen
that the interference of friends will persuade a young man of
independent fortune to think no more of a girl, whom he was violently in
love with only a few days before.
question: Why does Elizabeth reject Mrs. Gardiner's consolation about Jane?
answer: She says Jane's case was not accidental; friends deliberately interfered with an independent man deeply in love.
evidence: We do not suffer by _accident_.

quote_text:
But that expression of 'violently in love' is so hackneyed, so
doubtful, so indefinite, that it gives me very little idea. It is as
often applied to feelings which arise from an half-hour's acquaintance,
as to a real, strong attachment. Pray, how _violent was_ Mr. Bingley's
love?
question: Why does Mrs. Gardiner question the phrase 'violently in love'?
answer: She thinks the phrase is vague and overused and wants concrete evidence of Bingley's strong attachment.
evidence: Pray, how _violent was_ Mr. Bingley's love?

quote_text:
I never saw a more promising inclination. He was growing quite
inattentive to other people, and wholly engrossed by her. Every time
they met, it was more decided and remarkable. At his own ball he
offended two or three young ladies, by not asking them to dance, and I
spoke to him twice myself, without receiving an answer. Could there be
finer symptoms? Is not general incivility the very essence of love?
question: What evidence does Elizabeth give that Bingley was in love with Jane?
answer: She cites his absorption in Jane and his rudeness to others, including ignoring other ladies and not answering Elizabeth at his ball.
evidence: He was growing quite inattentive to other people, and wholly engrossed by her.

quote_text:
Oh, yes!--of that kind of love which I suppose him to have felt. Poor
Jane! I am sorry for her, because, with her disposition, she may not get
over it immediately. It had better have happened to _you_, Lizzy; you
would have laughed yourself out of it sooner. But do you think she
would be prevailed on to go back with us? Change of scene might be of
service--and perhaps a little relief from home, may be as useful as
anything.
question: Why does Mrs. Gardiner think Jane's disappointment would have been easier for Elizabeth?
answer: She thinks Elizabeth would have laughed herself out of it sooner, while Jane may not get over it quickly.
evidence: you would have laughed yourself out of it sooner

quote_text:
I hope, that no consideration with regard to
this young man will influence her. We live in so different a part of
town, all our connections are so different, and, as you well know, we go
out so little, that it is very improbable they should meet at all,
unless he really comes to see her.
question: What does Mrs. Gardiner hope about Jane's stay in London?
answer: She hopes Jane will not be influenced by Bingley because their circles differ and they are unlikely to meet unless he seeks her out.
evidence: it is very improbable they should meet at all, unless he really comes to see her.

quote_text:
And _that_ is quite impossible; for he is now in the custody of his
friend, and Mr. Darcy would no more suffer him to call on Jane in such a
part of London! My dear aunt, how could you think of it? Mr. Darcy may
perhaps have _heard_ of such a place as Gracechurch Street, but he would
hardly think a month's ablution enough to cleanse him from its
impurities, were he once to enter it; and depend upon it, Mr. Bingley
never stirs without him.
question: Why does Elizabeth think Bingley cannot call on Jane in Gracechurch Street?
answer: She believes Darcy controls Bingley and would never allow a call in such an unfashionable part of London.
evidence: Mr. Darcy would no more suffer him to call on Jane in such a part of London

quote_text:
I like her appearance, She
looks sickly and cross.--Yes, she will do for him very well. She will
make him a very proper wife.
question: Why does Elizabeth say she likes Miss De Bourgh's appearance?
answer: She is thinking of Darcy's supposed match: the pale, cross-looking heiress strikes her as a fitting wife for him.
evidence: She looks sickly and cross.--Yes, she will do for him very well.

quote_text:
I confess, that I should not have been at all surprised by
her Ladyship's asking us on Sunday to drink tea and spend the evening at
Rosings. I rather expected, from my knowledge of her affability, that it
would happen. But who could have foreseen such an attention as this? Who
could have imagined that we should receive an invitation to dine there
(an invitation moreover including the whole party) so immediately after
your arrival!
question: Why is Mr. Collins not surprised by the invitation to dine at Rosings?
answer: He says his knowledge of Lady Catherine's affability made him expect at least a Sunday tea invitation; the dinner invitation exceeds even that.
evidence: I rather expected, from my knowledge of her affability, that it would happen.

quote_text:
I am the less surprised at what has happened, from that knowledge of what the manners of the great really are, which
my situation in life has allowed me to acquire. About the Court, such
instances of elegant breeding are not uncommon.
question: Why is Sir William less astonished by Lady Catherine's attention than the others?
answer: He claims his experience at Court has taught him how the great behave, so such elegant breeding seems ordinary to him.
evidence: from that knowledge of what the manners of the great really are, which my situation in life has allowed me to acquire

quote_text:
Do not make yourself uneasy, my dear cousin, about your apparel. Lady
Catherine is far from requiring that elegance of dress in us, which
becomes herself and daughter. I would advise you merely to put on
whatever of your clothes is superior to the rest, there is no occasion
for any thing more. Lady Catherine will not think the worse of you for
being simply dressed. She likes to have the distinction of rank
preserved.
question: What advice does Mr. Collins give Elizabeth about dressing for Rosings, and why?
answer: He tells her not to worry, merely to wear her best clothes, since Lady Catherine likes the distinction of rank preserved and will not think worse of plain dress.
evidence: Lady Catherine will not think the worse of you for being simply dressed. She likes to have the distinction of rank preserved.

quote_text:
Your father's estate is entailed on Mr. Collins, I think. For your
sake, I am glad of it; but otherwise I see no
occasion for entailing estates from the female line.--It was not thought
necessary in Sir Lewis de Bourgh's family.--Do you play and sing, Miss
Bennet?
question: Why does Lady Catherine say she is glad the Longbourn estate is entailed on Mr. Collins?
answer: Because it benefits Charlotte, who as his wife will one day have the estate; she adds that she sees no need for entails from the female line.
evidence: For your sake," turning to Charlotte, "I am glad of it

quote_text: A little.
question: What does Lady Catherine propose after Elizabeth admits she plays and sings a little?
answer: She says their instrument is capital and that Elizabeth shall try it some day, so they may hear her.
evidence: Our instrument is a capital one, probably superior to----You shall try it some day.

quote_text:
Oh! then--some time or other we shall be happy to hear you. Our
instrument is a capital one, probably superior to----You shall try it
some day.--Do your sisters play and sing?
question: What does Lady Catherine promise Elizabeth will soon be able to do at Rosings?
answer: She says Elizabeth shall try their superior instrument and that they will be happy to hear her play some time.
evidence: some time or other we shall be happy to hear you. Our instrument is a capital one

quote_text: One of them does.
question: How many of Elizabeth's sisters play and sing, according to her answer?
answer: Only one of her sisters does.
evidence: One of them does.

quote_text:
Why did not you all learn?--You ought all to have learned. The Miss
Webbs all play, and their father has not so good an income as
your's.--Do you draw?
question: Why does Lady Catherine think the Bennet sisters should all have learned music?
answer: Because even the Miss Webbs all play, though their father has a smaller income than Mr. Bennet.
evidence: The Miss Webbs all play, and their father has not so good an income as your's.

quote_text: No, not at all.
question: How does Elizabeth conduct herself under Lady Catherine's probing questions about her accomplishments?
answer: She feels the questions are impertinent but answers them all with great composure.
evidence: Elizabeth felt all the impertinence of her questions, but answered them very composedly.

quote_text: What, none of you?
question: What does Lady Catherine find hard to believe about the Bennet sisters' drawing?
answer: That none of the five sisters draws at all.
evidence: What, none of you?

quote_text: Not one.
question: What does Elizabeth's brief reply confirm about her family's accomplishments?
answer: That not one of the sisters can draw, which Lady Catherine calls very strange.
evidence: Not one.

quote_text:
That is very strange. But I suppose you had no opportunity. Your mother
should have taken you to town every spring for the benefit of masters.
question: What does Lady Catherine suggest Mrs. Bennet should have done for her daughters' education?
answer: She says Mrs. Bennet should have taken them to town every spring so they could have masters.
evidence: Your mother should have taken you to town every spring for the benefit of masters.

quote_text: My mother would have had no objection, but my father hates London.
question: Why does Elizabeth blame her father rather than her mother for the lack of London masters?
answer: She gently defends her mother, saying she would have had no objection, but her father hates London.
evidence: My mother would have had no objection, but my father hates London.

quote_text: Has your governess left you?
question: What does Lady Catherine assume about the Bennet household when she asks this?
answer: She assumes the girls had a governess who has since left them.
evidence: Has your governess left you?

quote_text: We never had any governess.
question: What does Elizabeth reveal about how she and her sisters were educated?
answer: That they never had a governess at all.
evidence: We never had any governess.

quote_text:
No governess! How was that possible? Five daughters brought up at home
without a governess!--I never heard of such a thing. Your mother must
have been quite a slave to your education.
question: Why is Lady Catherine so shocked by Elizabeth's account of her upbringing?
answer: She cannot conceive of five daughters being brought up at home without a governess, and assumes Mrs. Bennet must have slaved over their education.
evidence: Five daughters brought up at home without a governess!--I never heard of such a thing.

quote_text:
Then, who taught you? who attended to you? Without a governess you must
have been neglected.
question: What does Lady Catherine conclude must have happened to the Bennet girls without a governess?
answer: She assumes they must have been neglected and demands to know who taught them.
evidence: Without a governess you must have been neglected.

quote_text:
Compared with some families, I believe we were; but such of us as
wished to learn, never wanted the means. We were always encouraged to
read, and had all the masters that were necessary. Those who chose to be
idle, certainly might.
question: How does Elizabeth defend the education she and her sisters received at home?
answer: She says that though they may have been neglected compared with some families, those who wished to learn always had the means, being encouraged to read and given necessary masters.
evidence: We were always encouraged to read, and had all the masters that were necessary.

quote_text:
Aye, no doubt; but that is what a governess will prevent, and if I had
known your mother, I should have advised her most strenuously to engage
one. I always say that nothing is to be done in education without steady
and regular instruction, and nobody but a governess can give it. It is
wonderful how many families I have been the means of supplying in that
way. I am always glad to get a young person well placed out. Four nieces
of Mrs. Jenkinson are most delightfully situated through my means; and
it was but the other day, that I recommended another young person, who
was merely accidentally mentioned to me, and the family are quite
delighted with her. Mrs. Collins, did I tell you of Lady Metcalfe's
calling yesterday to thank me? She finds Miss Pope a treasure.
question: What principle does Lady Catherine insist on regarding education?
answer: That nothing can be done without steady, regular instruction, which only a governess can provide.
evidence: nothing is to be done in education without steady and regular instruction, and nobody but a governess can give it

quote_text: said she
question: Why does Lady Catherine repeat Lady Metcalfe's words of thanks?
answer: To boast of her success in recommending and placing young women, here Miss Pope, as governesses.
evidence: She finds Miss Pope a treasure.

quote_text:
Are any of your
younger sisters out, Miss Bennet?
question: What does Lady Catherine want to know about the Bennet sisters' social position?
answer: Whether any of Elizabeth's younger sisters are out in society.
evidence: Are any of your younger sisters out, Miss Bennet?

quote_text: Yes, Ma'am, all.
question: What surprises Lady Catherine about the Bennet sisters' coming out?
answer: That all five are out, including the younger ones before the elder are married.
evidence: Yes, Ma'am, all.

quote_text:
All!--What, all five out at once? Very odd!--And you only the
second.--The younger ones out before the elder are married!--Your
younger sisters must be very young?
question: Why does Lady Catherine call the Bennet sisters' situation very odd?
answer: Because all five are out at once and the younger ones are out before the elder are married, though they must be very young.
evidence: The younger ones out before the elder are married!

quote_text:
Yes, my youngest is not sixteen. Perhaps _she_ is full young to be much
in company. But really, Ma'am, I think it would be very hard upon
younger sisters, that they should not have their share of society and
amusement because the elder may not have the means or inclination to
marry early.--The last born has as good a right to the pleasures of
youth, as the first. And to be kept back on _such_ a motive!--I think it
would not be very likely to promote sisterly affection or delicacy of
mind.
question: What argument does Elizabeth make for her younger sisters being out in society?
answer: That the youngest has as much right to the pleasures of youth as the eldest, and holding them back would not promote sisterly affection.
evidence: The last born has as good a right to the pleasures of youth, as the first.

quote_text:
Upon my word, you give your opinion very
decidedly for so young a person.--Pray, what is your age?
question: How does Lady Catherine react to Elizabeth's outspoken defence of her sisters?
answer: She is startled that so young a person gives her opinion so decidedly, and demands to know Elizabeth's age.
evidence: you give your opinion very decidedly for so young a person

quote_text:
With three younger sisters grown up, your
Ladyship can hardly expect me to own it.
question: How does Elizabeth avoid answering Lady Catherine's question about her age?
answer: She smilingly says that with three grown-up younger sisters, Lady Catherine can hardly expect her to own it.
evidence: your Ladyship can hardly expect me to own it

quote_text:
You cannot be more than twenty, I am sure,--therefore you need not
conceal your age.
question: What does Lady Catherine insist about Elizabeth's age?
answer: That she cannot be more than twenty, so there is no need to conceal it.
evidence: You cannot be more than twenty, I am sure,--therefore you need not conceal your age.

quote_text: I am not one and twenty.
question: What makes Elizabeth's short reply about her age so bold?
answer: She is trifling with Lady Catherine's dignified impertinence, and Elizabeth suspects she is the first person ever to dare it.
evidence: Elizabeth suspected herself to be the first creature who had ever dared to trifle with so much dignified impertinence.

quote_text:
I may thank you, Eliza, for this piece of civility. Mr. Darcy would
never have come so soon to wait upon me.
question: Why does Charlotte teasingly thank Elizabeth for Mr. Darcy's visit?
answer: She implies Darcy would never have come so soon to wait on her if Elizabeth's presence had not drawn him.
evidence: Mr. Darcy would never have come so soon to wait upon me.

quote_text:
My eldest sister has been in town these three months. Have you never
happened to see her there?
question: Why does Elizabeth ask Mr. Darcy whether he has seen her eldest sister in town?
answer: She knows he has not, but wants to see whether he betrays any consciousness of the Bingley and Jane affair.
evidence: she wished to see whether he would betray any consciousness of what had passed between the Bingleys and Jane

quote_text:
What is that you are saying, Fitzwilliam? What is it you are talking
of? What are you telling Miss Bennet? Let me hear what it is.
question: Why does Lady Catherine call out to Colonel Fitzwilliam about his conversation with Elizabeth?
answer: Their lively talk drew her attention and she resents being left out, so she demands to hear what they are saying.
evidence: they conversed with so much spirit and flow, as to draw the attention of Lady Catherine herself

quote_text: We are speaking of music, Madam,
question: How does Colonel Fitzwilliam respond to his aunt's demand to know what they were discussing?
answer: He answers reluctantly, saying only that they were speaking of music, since he could no longer avoid replying.
evidence: said he, when no longer able to avoid a reply

quote_text:
Of music! Then pray speak aloud. It is of all subjects my delight. I
must have my share in the conversation, if you are speaking of music.
There are few people in England, I suppose, who have more true enjoyment
of music than myself, or a better natural taste. If I had ever learnt, I
should have been a great proficient. And so would Anne, if her health
had allowed her to apply. I am confident that she would have performed
delightfully. How does Georgiana get on, Darcy?
question: What claim does Lady Catherine make about her own musical abilities?
answer: She insists she has true enjoyment and natural taste, and would have been a great proficient had she ever learned.
evidence: If I had ever learnt, I should have been a great proficient.

quote_text:
I am very glad to hear such a good account of her, and pray tell her from me, that she cannot expect to excel,
if she does not practise a great deal.
question: What message does Lady Catherine ask Darcy to pass on to Georgiana?
answer: That she cannot expect to excel unless she practises a great deal.
evidence: she cannot expect to excel, if she does not practise a great deal

quote_text:
I assure you, Madam, that she does not need such advice.
She practises very constantly.
question: How does Mr. Darcy defend his sister against Lady Catherine's advice?
answer: He politely says Georgiana does not need such advice because she practises very constantly.
evidence: she does not need such advice. She practises very constantly.

quote_text:
So much the better. It cannot be done too much; and when I next write
to her, I shall charge her not to neglect it on any account. I often
tell young ladies, that no excellence in music is to be acquired,
without constant practice. I have told Miss Bennet several times, that
she will never play really well, unless she practises more; and though
Mrs. Collins has no instrument, she is very welcome, as I have often
told her, to come to Rosings every day, and play on the piano-forte in
Mrs. Jenkinson's room. She would be in nobody's way, you know, in that
part of the house.
question: What offer does Lady Catherine make to Mrs. Collins regarding the piano at Rosings?
answer: She says Mrs. Collins is welcome to come to Rosings every day and play the piano-forte in Mrs. Jenkinson's room.
evidence: she is very welcome, as I have often told her, to come to Rosings every day, and play on the piano-forte in Mrs. Jenkinson's room

quote_text:
You mean to frighten me, Mr. Darcy, by coming in all this state to hear
me? But I will not be alarmed though your sister _does_ play so well.
There is a stubbornness about me that never can bear to be frightened at
the will of others. My courage always rises with every attempt to
intimidate me.
question: Why does Elizabeth tease Mr. Darcy about trying to frighten her?
answer: Darcy has deliberately stationed himself by the piano to watch her perform, and she archly claims her courage rises with any attempt to intimidate her.
evidence: stationed himself so as to command a full view of the fair performer's countenance

quote_text:
I shall not say that you are mistaken, because you could
not really believe me to entertain any design of alarming you; and I
have had the pleasure of your acquaintance long enough to know, that you
find great enjoyment in occasionally professing opinions which in fact
are not your own.
question: What does Mr. Darcy accuse Elizabeth of in his reply?
answer: He says he knows her too well to be alarmed, and that she enjoys professing opinions she does not really hold.
evidence: you find great enjoyment in occasionally professing opinions which in fact are not your own

quote_text:
Your cousin will give you a very pretty notion of
me, and teach you not to believe a word I say. I am particularly unlucky
in meeting with a person so well able to expose my real character, in a
part of the world, where I had hoped to pass myself off with some degree
of credit. Indeed, Mr. Darcy, it is very ungenerous in you to mention
all that you knew to my disadvantage in Hertfordshire--and, give me
leave to say, very impolitic too--for it is provoking me to retaliate,
and such things may come out, as will shock your relations to hear.
question: What is Elizabeth doing when she complains to Colonel Fitzwilliam about his cousin?
answer: She jokingly says Darcy will expose her real character to the Colonel, and warns that she may retaliate by revealing shocking things about Darcy.
evidence: it is provoking me to retaliate, and such things may come out, as will shock your relations to hear

quote_text:
So much the better. I hope they will not meet at all. But does not Jane
correspond with the sister? _She_ will not be able to help calling.
question: Why does Mrs. Gardiner hope Bingley and Jane will not meet in London?
answer: She thinks a meeting could revive Jane’s attachment, so she hopes they avoid each other; she then asks whether Jane still corresponds with Miss Bingley.
evidence: I hope they will not meet at all. But does not Jane correspond with the sister?

quote_text: She will drop the acquaintance entirely.
question: What does Elizabeth predict Jane will do about Caroline Bingley?
answer: She says Jane will drop the acquaintance entirely rather than rely on Caroline’s friendship.
evidence: She will drop the acquaintance entirely.

quote_text:
You are too sensible a girl, Lizzy, to fall in love merely because you
are warned against it; and, therefore, I am not afraid of speaking
openly. Seriously, I would have you be on your guard. Do not involve
yourself, or endeavour to involve him in an affection which the want of
fortune would make so very imprudent. I have nothing to say against
_him_; he is a most interesting young man; and if he had the fortune he
ought to have, I should think you could not do better. But as it is--you
must not let your fancy run away with you. You have sense, and we all
expect you to use it. Your father would depend on _your_ resolution and
good conduct, I am sure. You must not disappoint your father.
question: Why does Mrs. Gardiner warn Elizabeth about encouraging Wickham?
answer: Because Wickham lacks fortune, an attachment would be imprudent; she urges Elizabeth to guard her feelings.
evidence: Do not involve yourself, or endeavour to involve him in an affection which the want of fortune would make so very imprudent

quote_text: My dear aunt, this is being serious indeed.
question: What tone does Elizabeth take toward her aunt’s serious warning?
answer: She answers lightly, acknowledging that her aunt is speaking seriously.
evidence: My dear aunt, this is being serious indeed.

quote_text: Yes, and I hope to engage you to be serious likewise.
question: What does Mrs. Gardiner hope Elizabeth will do after her warning?
answer: She wants Elizabeth to take the matter seriously and act prudently.
evidence: I hope to engage you to be serious likewise.

quote_text:
Well, then, you need not be under any alarm. I will take care of
myself, and of Mr. Wickham too. He shall not be in love with me, if I
can prevent it.
question: What does Elizabeth promise her aunt about Wickham?
answer: She promises to take care of herself and prevent Wickham from falling in love with her.
evidence: I will take care of myself, and of Mr. Wickham too. He shall not be in love with me, if I can prevent it.

quote_text: Elizabeth, you are not serious now.
question: Why does Mrs. Gardiner say Elizabeth is not serious?
answer: Elizabeth’s flippant promise to manage Wickham’s feelings shows she is joking rather than treating the warning seriously.
evidence: He shall not be in love with me, if I can prevent it.

quote_text:
I beg your pardon. I will try again. At present I am not in love with
Mr. Wickham; no, I certainly am not. But he is, beyond all comparison,
the most agreeable man I ever saw--and if he becomes really attached to
me--I believe it will be better that he should not. I see the imprudence
of it.--Oh! _that_ abominable Mr. Darcy!--My father's opinion of me does
me the greatest honour; and I should be miserable to forfeit it. My
father, however, is partial to Mr. Wickham. In short, my dear aunt, I
should be very sorry to be the means of making any of you unhappy; but
since we see every day that where there is affection, young people are
seldom withheld by immediate want of fortune, from entering into
engagements with each other, how can I promise to be wiser than so many
of my fellow creatures if I am tempted, or how am I even to know that it
would be wisdom to resist? All that I can promise you, therefore, is not
to be in a hurry. I will not be in a hurry to believe myself his first
object. When I am in company with him, I will not be wishing. In short,
I will do my best.
question: What limited promise does Elizabeth make about Wickham?
answer: She will not be in a hurry to believe herself his first object or to encourage an engagement.
evidence: All that I can promise you, therefore, is not to be in a hurry.

quote_text:
Perhaps it will be as well, if you discourage his coming here so very
often. At least, you should not _remind_ your Mother of inviting him.
question: What practical step does Mrs. Gardiner advise to keep Wickham from visiting so often?
answer: Elizabeth should discourage his visits and stop reminding her mother to invite him.
evidence: if you discourage his coming here so very often. At least, you should not _remind_ your Mother of inviting him.

quote_text:
As I did the other day, very
true, it will be wise in me to refrain from _that_. But do not imagine
that he is always here so often. It is on your account that he has been
so frequently invited this week. You know my mother's ideas as to the
necessity of constant company for her friends. But really, and upon my
honour, I will try to do what I think to be wisest; and now, I hope you
are satisfied.
question: What does Elizabeth admit about her own role in inviting Wickham?
answer: She admits she reminded her mother to invite him and agrees she should refrain from doing so.
evidence: it will be wise in me to refrain from _that_.

quote_text: _wished_ they might be happy.
question: How does Mrs. Bennet regard Charlotte’s marriage to Mr. Collins?
answer: She is resigned to it but speaks grudgingly, saying in an ill-natured tone that she wishes them happy.
evidence: in an ill-natured tone that she wished they might be happy

quote_text: I shall depend on hearing from you very often, Eliza.
question: What does Charlotte ask of Elizabeth before leaving for Kent?
answer: She asks Elizabeth to write to her often.
evidence: I shall depend on hearing from you very often, Eliza.

quote_text: _That_ you certainly shall.
question: How does Elizabeth answer Charlotte’s request for frequent letters?
answer: She promises that Charlotte certainly shall hear from her.
evidence: _That_ you certainly shall.

quote_text: And I have another favour to ask. Will you come and see me?
question: What second favor does Charlotte ask Elizabeth?
answer: She asks Elizabeth to come and visit her at Hunsford.
evidence: And I have another favour to ask. Will you come and see me?

quote_text: We shall often meet, I hope, in Hertfordshire.
question: How does Elizabeth avoid promising a visit to Hunsford?
answer: She suggests they will often meet in Hertfordshire instead.
evidence: We shall often meet, I hope, in Hertfordshire.

quote_text:
I am not likely to leave Kent for some time. Promise me, therefore, to
come to Hunsford.
question: Why does Charlotte press Elizabeth to promise a visit to Hunsford?
answer: Charlotte expects to remain in Kent for some time, so Hertfordshire meetings will not be enough.
evidence: I am not likely to leave Kent for some time. Promise me, therefore, to come to Hunsford.

quote_text:
My father and Maria are to come to me in March, and
I hope you will consent to be of the party. Indeed, Eliza, you will be
as welcome to me as either of them.
question: What plan does Charlotte propose for Elizabeth’s visit to Hunsford?
answer: Elizabeth should join Sir William and Maria when they visit Charlotte in March.
evidence: My father and Maria are to come to me in March

quote_text:
But, my dear Elizabeth, what sort of girl is Miss King? I
should be sorry to think our friend mercenary.
question: Why does Mrs. Gardiner ask Elizabeth about Miss King?
answer: She wants to know Miss King’s character because she hopes Wickham is not acting merely from mercenary motives.
evidence: I should be sorry to think our friend mercenary.

quote_text:
Pray, my dear aunt, what is the difference in matrimonial affairs,
between the mercenary and the prudent motive? Where does discretion end,
and avarice begin? Last Christmas you were afraid of his marrying me,
because it would be imprudent; and now, because he is trying to get a
girl with only ten thousand pounds, you want to find out that he is
mercenary.
question: What inconsistency does Elizabeth point out in her aunt’s view of Wickham?
answer: Her aunt once thought Wickham marrying Elizabeth imprudent for lack of fortune, but now calls him mercenary for seeking Miss King’s ten thousand pounds.
evidence: Last Christmas you were afraid of his marrying me, because it would be imprudent

quote_text:
If you will only tell me what sort of girl Miss King is, I shall know
what to think.
question: What information does Mrs. Gardiner need to judge Wickham’s conduct?
answer: She wants to know what sort of girl Miss King is before deciding what to think.
evidence: If you will only tell me what sort of girl Miss King is, I shall know what to think.

quote_text: She is a very good kind of girl, I believe. I know no harm of her.
question: What does Elizabeth say about Miss King’s character?
answer: She believes Miss King is a good kind of girl and knows no harm of her.
evidence: She is a very good kind of girl, I believe. I know no harm of her.

quote_text:
But he paid her not the smallest attention, till her grandfather's
death made her mistress of this fortune.
question: What timing makes Mrs. Gardiner suspicious of Wickham’s attentions to Miss King?
answer: He showed her no attention until her grandfather’s death made her rich.
evidence: he paid her not the smallest attention, till her grandfather's death made her mistress of this fortune

quote_text:
No--why should he? If it was not allowable for him to gain _my_
affections, because I had no money, what occasion could there be for
making love to a girl whom he did not care about, and who was equally
poor?
question: How does Elizabeth defend Wickham’s earlier neglect of Miss King?
answer: She says Miss King was poor and he did not care for her, so there was no reason to court her.
evidence: what occasion could there be for making love to a girl whom he did not care about, and who was equally poor?

quote_text:
But there seems indelicacy in directing his attentions towards her, so
soon after this event.
question: What objection does Mrs. Gardiner raise about Wickham’s courtship of Miss King?
answer: She thinks it indelicate that he courted her so soon after she gained her fortune.
evidence: there seems indelicacy in directing his attentions towards her, so soon after this event

quote_text:
A man in distressed circumstances has not time for all those elegant
decorums which other people may observe. If _she_ does not object to it,
why should _we_?
question: How does Elizabeth excuse Wickham’s haste in courting Miss King?
answer: She says a man in financial distress cannot afford elegant decorum, and Miss King’s lack of objection is what matters.
evidence: A man in distressed circumstances has not time for all those elegant decorums

quote_text:
_Her_ not objecting, does not justify _him_. It only shews her being
deficient in something herself--sense or feeling.
question: What does Mrs. Gardiner say Miss King’s lack of objection shows?
answer: It does not justify Wickham; it shows Miss King lacks sense or feeling.
evidence: _Her_ not objecting, does not justify _him_. It only shews her being deficient in something herself--sense or feeling.

quote_text:
Well, have it as you choose. _He_ shall be
mercenary, and _she_ shall be foolish.
question: How does Elizabeth conclude the argument about Wickham and Miss King?
answer: She sarcastically gives in, saying Wickham shall be called mercenary and Miss King foolish.
evidence: _He_ shall be mercenary, and _she_ shall be foolish.

quote_text:
No, Lizzy, that is what I do _not_ choose. I should be sorry, you know,
to think ill of a young man who has lived so long in Derbyshire.
question: Why does Mrs. Gardiner refuse Elizabeth’s sarcastic conclusion?
answer: She does not want to think ill of Wickham, having known him and Derbyshire friends for a long time.
evidence: I should be sorry, you know, to think ill of a young man who has lived so long in Derbyshire.

quote_text:
Oh! if that is all, I have a very poor opinion of young men who live in
Derbyshire; and their intimate friends who live in Hertfordshire are not
much better. I am sick of them all. Thank Heaven! I am going to-morrow
where I shall find a man who has not one agreeable quality, who has
neither manner nor sense to recommend him. Stupid men are the only ones
worth knowing, after all.
question: What does Elizabeth’s remark about stupid men suggest about her feelings?
answer: She is disillusioned and disappointed, sarcastically claiming dull men are preferable to agreeable ones like Wickham.
evidence: Stupid men are the only ones worth knowing, after all.

quote_text: Take care, Lizzy; that speech savours strongly of disappointment.
question: What does Mrs. Gardiner infer from Elizabeth’s bitter remark?
answer: She suspects Elizabeth is disappointed, probably over Wickham.
evidence: Take care, Lizzy; that speech savours strongly of disappointment.

quote_text: We have not quite determined how far it shall carry us, but perhaps to the Lakes.
question: What summer plan does Mrs. Gardiner invite Elizabeth to join?
answer: A tour whose destination is undecided but may include the Lakes.
evidence: We have not quite determined how far it shall carry us, but perhaps to the Lakes.

quote_text:
My dear, dear
aunt, what delight! what felicity! You give me
fresh life and vigour. Adieu to disappointment and spleen. What are men
to rocks and mountains? Oh! what hours of transport we shall spend! And
when we _do_ return, it shall not be like other travellers, without
being able to give one accurate idea of any thing. We _will_ know where
we have gone--we _will_ recollect what we have seen. Lakes, mountains,
and rivers, shall not be jumbled together in our imaginations; nor, when
we attempt to describe any particular scene, will we begin quarrelling
about its relative situation. Let _our_ first effusions be less
insupportable than those of the generality of travellers.
question: How does Elizabeth react to the invitation to tour with her aunt and uncle?
answer: She is rapturous, saying it gives her fresh life and drives away disappointment.
evidence: what delight! what felicity! You give me fresh life and vigour.

quote_text:
Yes, Miss Elizabeth, you will have the honour of seeing Lady Catherine
de Bourgh on the ensuing Sunday at church, and I need not say you will
be delighted with her. She is all affability and condescension, and I
doubt not but you will be honoured with some portion of her notice when
service is over. I have scarcely any hesitation in saying that she will
include you and my sister Maria in every invitation with which she
honours us during your stay here. Her behaviour to my dear Charlotte is
charming. We dine at Rosings twice every week, and are never allowed to
walk home. Her ladyship's carriage is regularly ordered for us. I
_should_ say, one of her ladyship's carriages, for she has several.
question: What does Mr. Collins predict will happen during Elizabeth’s stay near Rosings?
answer: He says she will see Lady Catherine at church and be delighted, and likely receive invitations from her.
evidence: you will have the honour of seeing Lady Catherine de Bourgh on the ensuing Sunday at church

quote_text: Lady Catherine is a very respectable, sensible woman indeed, and a most attentive neighbour.
question: How does Charlotte characterize Lady Catherine to the company?
answer: She calls her a respectable, sensible woman and an attentive neighbor.
evidence: Lady Catherine is a very respectable, sensible woman indeed, and a most attentive neighbour.

quote_text:
Very true, my dear, that is exactly what I say. She is the sort of
woman whom one cannot regard with too much deference.
question: How does Mr. Collins respond to Charlotte’s praise of Lady Catherine?
answer: He agrees emphatically and says Lady Catherine deserves the utmost deference.
evidence: that is exactly what I say. She is the sort of woman whom one cannot regard with too much deference.

quote_text:
Oh, my dear Eliza! pray make haste and come into the dining-room, for
there is such a sight to be seen! I will not tell you what it is. Make
haste, and come down this moment.
question: Why does Maria urgently call Elizabeth to the dining-room?
answer: She refuses to explain, only urging Elizabeth to hurry downstairs to see a surprising sight.
evidence: there is such a sight to be seen! I will not tell you what it is. Make haste, and come down this moment.

quote_text:
And is this all? I expected at least that the pigs
were got into the garden, and here is nothing but Lady Catherine and her
daughter!
question: What does Elizabeth think of the sight Maria summoned her for?
answer: She is disappointed and amused, having expected something more dramatic than Lady Catherine and her daughter.
evidence: I expected at least that the pigs were got into the garden, and here is nothing but Lady Catherine and her daughter!

quote_text:
La! my dear, it is not Lady
Catherine. The old lady is Mrs. Jenkinson, who lives with them. The
other is Miss De Bourgh. Only look at her. She is quite a little
creature. Who would have thought she could be so thin and small!
question: What correction does Maria make about the visitors in the phaeton?
answer: She says the older lady is Mrs. Jenkinson, not Lady Catherine, and the other is Miss De Bourgh.
evidence: it is not Lady Catherine. The old lady is Mrs. Jenkinson, who lives with them. The other is Miss De Bourgh.

quote_text:
She is abominably rude to keep Charlotte out of doors in all this wind.
Why does she not come in?
question: Why does Elizabeth call Miss De Bourgh rude?
answer: Because she keeps Charlotte outside in the wind instead of coming indoors.
evidence: She is abominably rude to keep Charlotte out of doors in all this wind. Why does she not come in?

quote_text:
Oh! Charlotte says, she hardly ever does. It is the greatest of favours
when Miss De Bourgh comes in.
question: What does Maria explain about Miss De Bourgh’s willingness to enter the parsonage?
answer: She says Miss De Bourgh hardly ever comes in; it is considered a great favor when she does.
evidence: Charlotte says, she hardly ever does. It is the greatest of favours when Miss De Bourgh comes in.

quote_text: I am not afraid of you,
question: Why does Darcy reply that he is not afraid of Elizabeth's threat to retaliate?
answer: He is amused and confident, treating her warning as playful teasing rather than a real threat.
evidence: said he, smilingly

quote_text: Pray let me hear what you have to accuse him of, I should like to know how he behaves among strangers.
question: What does Colonel Fitzwilliam want to learn from Elizabeth's account of Darcy?
answer: He is curious to hear how Darcy behaves among strangers and wants Elizabeth to expose him.
evidence: I should like to know how he behaves among strangers.

quote_text:
You shall hear then--but prepare yourself for something very dreadful.
The first time of my ever seeing him in Hertfordshire, you must know,
was at a ball--and at this ball, what do you think he did? He danced
only four dances! I am sorry to pain you--but so it was. He danced only
four dances, though gentlemen were scarce; and, to my certain knowledge,
more than one young lady was sitting down in want of a partner. Mr.
Darcy, you cannot deny the fact.
question: What does Elizabeth warn Colonel Fitzwilliam to expect before she tells her story about Darcy?
answer: She warns him to expect a shocking account of Darcy's conduct at the Meryton ball, where Darcy danced only four dances.
evidence: He danced only four dances, though gentlemen were scarce

quote_text:
I had not at that time the honour of knowing any lady in the assembly
beyond my own party.
question: How does Darcy explain why he did not dance with more ladies at the Meryton assembly?
answer: He says he knew no ladies there beyond his own party, so he could not dance with others.
evidence: I had not at that time the honour of knowing any lady in the assembly beyond my own party.

quote_text:
True; and nobody can ever be introduced in a ball room. Well, Colonel
Fitzwilliam, what do I play next? My fingers wait your orders.
question: How does Elizabeth respond to Darcy's excuse about not being introduced at the ball?
answer: She ironically agrees that no one can be introduced in a ballroom, then changes the subject to music.
evidence: nobody can ever be introduced in a ball room.

quote_text:
Perhaps, I should have judged better, had I sought an
introduction, but I am ill qualified to recommend myself to strangers.
question: What does Darcy admit about his ability to socialize with strangers?
answer: He admits he should perhaps have sought an introduction, but he is poor at recommending himself to strangers.
evidence: I am ill qualified to recommend myself to strangers.

quote_text:
Shall we ask your cousin the reason of this? Shall we ask him why a man of sense and
education, and who has lived in the world, is ill qualified to recommend
himself to strangers?
question: Why does Elizabeth propose asking Colonel Fitzwilliam to explain Darcy's reserve?
answer: She wants to tease Darcy by having his cousin explain why a sensible man is so ill qualified to recommend himself to strangers.
evidence: why a man of sense and education, and who has lived in the world, is ill qualified to recommend himself to strangers?

quote_text:
I can answer your question, without applying to
him. It is because he will not give himself the trouble.
question: What reason does Colonel Fitzwilliam give for Darcy's awkwardness with strangers?
answer: He says it is because Darcy will not give himself the trouble to converse easily.
evidence: It is because he will not give himself the trouble.

quote_text:
I certainly have not the talent which some people possess, of conversing easily with those I have never seen before. I cannot
catch their tone of conversation, or appear interested in their
concerns, as I often see done.
question: What specific social skill does Darcy say he lacks?
answer: He says he lacks the talent of conversing easily with people he has never seen before.
evidence: of conversing easily with those I have never seen before.

quote_text:
My fingers, do not move over this instrument in the
masterly manner which I see so many women's do. They have not the same
force or rapidity, and do not produce the same expression. But then I
have always supposed it to be my own fault--because I would not take the
trouble of practising. It is not that I do not believe _my_ fingers as
capable as any other woman's of superior execution.
question: How does Elizabeth compare her piano playing to Darcy's social manner?
answer: She says her fingers lack masterly execution because she would not take the trouble to practice, paralleling his unwillingness to converse easily.
evidence: because I would not take the trouble of practising.

quote_text:
You are perfectly right. You have employed your
time much better. No one admitted to the privilege of hearing you, can
think any thing wanting. We neither of us perform to strangers.
question: What compliment does Darcy give Elizabeth after her self-deprecating remark about practice?
answer: He says she has employed her time better and that no one hearing her could think anything wanting; neither of them performs to strangers.
evidence: We neither of us perform to strangers.

quote_text:
Miss Bennet would not play at all amiss, if she practised more, and
could have the advantage of a London master. She has a very good notion
of fingering, though her taste is not equal to Anne's. Anne would have
been a delightful performer, had her health allowed her to learn.
question: How does Lady Catherine faintly praise Elizabeth's playing while criticizing it?
answer: She says Elizabeth would not play amiss if she practiced more and had a London master, and that her taste is inferior to Anne's.
evidence: if she practised more, and could have the advantage of a London master.

quote_text:
How very suddenly you all quitted Netherfield last November, Mr. Darcy!
It must have been a most agreeable surprise to Mr. Bingley to see you
all after him so soon; for, if I recollect right, he went but the day
before. He and his sisters were well, I hope, when you left London.
question: Why does Elizabeth mention the sudden departure from Netherfield?
answer: She is curious to hear Darcy's account of their hasty departure and Bingley's intentions, hoping for news relevant to Jane.
evidence: feeling curious to know what he would say on the subject of their hasty departure

quote_text: Perfectly so--I thank you.
question: How does Darcy answer Elizabeth's inquiry about Bingley and his sisters?
answer: He answers briefly and formally that they were perfectly well.
evidence: Perfectly so--I thank you.

quote_text:
I think I have understood that Mr. Bingley has not much idea of ever
returning to Netherfield again?
question: What does Elizabeth hope to learn by asking whether Bingley will return to Netherfield?
answer: She wants to discover Bingley's intentions toward Netherfield, which bear on Jane's hopes and Darcy's influence.
evidence: has not much idea of ever returning to Netherfield again

quote_text:
I have never heard him say so; but it is probable that he may spend
very little of his time there in future. He has many friends, and he is
at a time of life when friends and engagements are continually
increasing.
question: What does Darcy's reply suggest about Bingley's future at Netherfield?
answer: He has not heard Bingley say he will never return, but thinks Bingley may spend little time there because of friends and engagements.
evidence: he may spend very little of his time there in future

quote_text:
If he means to be but little at Netherfield, it would be better for the
neighbourhood that he should give up the place entirely, for then we
might possibly get a settled family there. But perhaps Mr. Bingley did
not take the house so much for the convenience of the neighbourhood as
for his own, and we must expect him to keep or quit it on the same
principle.
question: What does Elizabeth argue Bingley should do if he will seldom be at Netherfield?
answer: She says it would be better for the neighbourhood if he gave up the place so a settled family could live there.
evidence: it would be better for the neighbourhood that he should give up the place entirely

quote_text:
I should not be surprised, if he were to give it up, as
soon as any eligible purchase offers.
question: What does Darcy predict about Bingley's keeping Netherfield?
answer: He says he would not be surprised if Bingley gave it up as soon as a suitable purchase offered.
evidence: if he were to give it up, as soon as any eligible purchase offers.

quote_text:
This seems a very comfortable
house. Lady Catherine, I believe, did a great deal to it when Mr.
Collins first came to Hunsford.
question: How does Darcy try to revive conversation after the awkward talk about Bingley?
answer: He remarks that the parsonage seems comfortable and that Lady Catherine improved it for Mr. Collins.
evidence: This seems a very comfortable house.

quote_text:
I believe she did--and I am sure she could not have bestowed her
kindness on a more grateful object.
question: What does Elizabeth imply about Mr. Collins in agreeing about Lady Catherine's kindness?
answer: She implies Lady Catherine could not have chosen a more grateful recipient than Mr. Collins.
evidence: could not have bestowed her kindness on a more grateful object.

quote_text: Mr. Collins appears very fortunate in his choice of a wife.
question: Why does Darcy remark that Mr. Collins is fortunate in his choice of wife?
answer: He is making polite conversation and acknowledging Charlotte's good sense, indirectly complimenting Elizabeth's friend.
evidence: Mr. Collins appears very fortunate in his choice of a wife.

quote_text:
Yes, indeed; his friends may well rejoice in his having met with one of
the very few sensible women who would have accepted him, or have made
him happy if they had. My friend has an excellent understanding--though
I am not certain that I consider her marrying Mr. Collins as the wisest
thing she ever did. She seems perfectly happy, however, and in a
prudential light, it is certainly a very good match for her.
question: What is Elizabeth's opinion of Charlotte's marriage to Mr. Collins?
answer: She thinks Charlotte is sensible and one of the few women who could make Collins happy, but she doubts it was the wisest thing Charlotte ever did.
evidence: one of the very few sensible women who would have accepted him

quote_text:
It must be very agreeable to her to be settled within so easy a
distance of her own family and friends.
question: What does Darcy assume Charlotte feels about living near her family?
answer: He assumes she must be pleased to be settled within an easy distance of her family and friends.
evidence: settled within so easy a distance of her own family and friends.

quote_text: An easy distance do you call it? It is nearly fifty miles.
question: Why does Elizabeth dispute Darcy's idea that Hunsford is an easy distance from Charlotte's family?
answer: She thinks nearly fifty miles is far, especially given the Collinses' limited income for travel.
evidence: It is nearly fifty miles.

quote_text:
And what is fifty miles of good road? Little more than half a day's
journey. Yes, I call it a _very_ easy distance.
question: How does Darcy defend calling fifty miles an easy distance?
answer: He says it is little more than half a day's journey on good roads.
evidence: Little more than half a day's journey.

quote_text:
I should never have considered the distance as one of the _advantages_
of the match, I should never have said Mrs. Collins
was settled _near_ her family.
question: What does Elizabeth say she would never call an advantage of Charlotte's match?
answer: She says she would never consider the distance an advantage or call Charlotte settled near her family.
evidence: I should never have said Mrs. Collins was settled _near_ her family.

quote_text:
It is a proof of your own attachment to Hertfordshire. Any thing beyond
the very neighbourhood of Longbourn, I suppose, would appear far.
question: What does Darcy suggest is the real reason Elizabeth thinks fifty miles is far?
answer: He suggests her strong attachment to Hertfordshire makes anything beyond Longbourn seem far.
evidence: a proof of your own attachment to Hertfordshire.

quote_text:
I do not mean to say that a woman may not be settled too near her
family. The far and the near must be relative, and depend on many
varying circumstances. Where there is fortune to make the expence of
travelling unimportant, distance becomes no evil. But that is not the
case _here_. Mr. and Mrs. Collins have a comfortable income, but not
such a one as will allow of frequent journeys--and I am persuaded my
friend would not call herself _near_ her family under less than _half_
the present distance.
question: How does Elizabeth qualify her objection to Darcy's idea of distance?
answer: She says distance is relative and depends on circumstances; with fortune travel is easy, but the Collinses cannot afford frequent journeys.
evidence: The far and the near must be relative, and depend on many varying circumstances.

quote_text:
_You_ cannot
have a right to such very strong local attachment. _You_ cannot have
been always at Longbourn.
question: What does Darcy hint about Elizabeth's future at Longbourn?
answer: He hints that she cannot always have lived at Longbourn and may not always remain there, perhaps suggesting marriage.
evidence: _You_ cannot have been always at Longbourn.

quote_text: Are you pleased with Kent?
question: Why does Darcy suddenly ask Elizabeth about Kent?
answer: He becomes uncomfortable after his forward remark and retreats into formal, colder conversation.
evidence: he drew back his chair, took a newspaper from the table, and, glancing over it, said, in a colder voice

quote_text:
What can be the meaning of this! My dear Eliza he must be in love with you, or he would never have
called on us in this familiar way.
question: What does Charlotte infer from Darcy's familiar call at the parsonage?
answer: She concludes he must be in love with Elizabeth, or he would never have called so familiarly.
evidence: he must be in love with you, or he would never have called on us in this familiar way.

quote_text: I did not know before that you ever walked this way.
question: Why is Elizabeth surprised to meet Colonel Fitzwilliam on her walk?
answer: She did not know he ever walked that way, which she had thought was her own favorite haunt.
evidence: I did not know before that you ever walked this way.

quote_text:
I have been making the tour of the Park, as I generally
do every year, and intend to close it with a call at the Parsonage. Are
you going much farther?
question: What reason does Colonel Fitzwilliam give for being on Elizabeth's walking path?
answer: He is making his annual tour of the park and intends to end it with a call at the parsonage.
evidence: as I generally do every year, and intend to close it with a call at the Parsonage

quote_text: No, I should have turned in a moment.
question: What does Elizabeth mean when she says she would have turned in a moment?
answer: She means she was already about to turn back toward the parsonage, so she can walk with him.
evidence: No, I should have turned in a moment.

quote_text: Do you certainly leave Kent on Saturday?
question: Why does Elizabeth ask Colonel Fitzwilliam whether he leaves Kent on Saturday?
answer: She is making conversation and perhaps testing whether Darcy's party will leave, which matters to her feelings.
evidence: Do you certainly leave Kent on Saturday?

quote_text:
Yes--if Darcy does not put it off again. But I am at his disposal. He
arranges the business just as he pleases.
question: What does Colonel Fitzwilliam reveal about how travel plans are made?
answer: He says he is at Darcy's disposal and Darcy arranges business as he pleases.
evidence: I am at his disposal. He arranges the business just as he pleases.

quote_text:
And if not able to please himself in the arrangement, he has at least
great pleasure in the power of choice. I do not know any body who seems
more to enjoy the power of doing what he likes than Mr. Darcy.
question: What does Elizabeth imply about Darcy's character in her remark about his power of choice?
answer: She implies Darcy takes great pleasure in having his own way and doing as he likes.
evidence: more to enjoy the power of doing what he likes than Mr. Darcy.

quote_text:
He likes to have his own way very well, But so we all do. It is only that he has better means of having it than
many others, because he is rich, and many others are poor. I speak
feelingly. A younger son, you know, must be inured to self-denial and
dependence.
question: How does Colonel Fitzwilliam defend Darcy against Elizabeth's charge of liking his own way?
answer: He says everyone likes their own way, but Darcy has better means of getting it because he is rich.
evidence: But so we all do. It is only that he has better means of having it than many others, because he is rich

quote_text:
In my opinion, the younger son of an Earl can know very little of
either. Now, seriously, what have you ever known of self-denial and
dependence? When have you been prevented by want of money from going
wherever you chose, or procuring any thing you had a fancy for?
question: Why does Elizabeth doubt Colonel Fitzwilliam's claim to know self-denial?
answer: As an earl's younger son he has money and freedom, so she challenges him to name any real hardship.
evidence: what have you ever known of self-denial and dependence?

quote_text:
These are home questions--and perhaps I cannot say that I have
experienced many hardships of that nature. But in matters of greater
weight, I may suffer from the want of money. Younger sons cannot marry
where they like.
question: What serious limitation does Colonel Fitzwilliam admit as a younger son?
answer: He admits that in important matters he may suffer from want of money, since younger sons cannot marry where they like.
evidence: Younger sons cannot marry where they like.

quote_text:
Unless where they like women of fortune, which I think they very often
do.
question: How does Elizabeth answer Fitzwilliam's complaint that younger sons cannot marry where they like?
answer: She teases him that younger sons can often marry women of fortune instead.
evidence: Younger sons cannot marry where they like.

quote_text:
Our habits of expence make us too dependant, and there are not many in
my rank of life who can afford to marry without some attention to
money.
question: Why does Fitzwilliam say younger sons cannot marry where they like?
answer: He says their expensive habits make them dependent, so few can afford marriage without attention to money.
evidence: Our habits of expence make us too dependant

quote_text: "Is this," "meant for me?"
question: What does Elizabeth privately wonder about Fitzwilliam's remarks on younger sons and money?
answer: She wonders whether his comment about younger sons needing fortunes is aimed at her.
evidence: Younger sons cannot marry where they like.

quote_text:
And pray, what is
the usual price of an Earl's younger son? Unless the elder brother is
very sickly, I suppose you would not ask above fifty thousand pounds.
question: What joking question does Elizabeth ask Fitzwilliam about younger sons who marry for money?
answer: She asks the going price for an Earl's younger son, teasing him about marrying a fortune.
evidence: Unless where they like women of fortune

quote_text:
I imagine your cousin brought you down with him chiefly for the sake of
having somebody at his disposal. I wonder he does not marry, to secure a
lasting convenience of that kind. But, perhaps his sister does as well
for the present, and, as she is under his sole care, he may do what he
likes with her.
question: What does Elizabeth suggest about Darcy's reason for bringing Fitzwilliam to Kent?
answer: She suggests Darcy wanted someone at his disposal and wonders why he does not marry to secure such convenience.
evidence: chiefly for the sake of having somebody at his disposal

quote_text:
No, that is an advantage which he must
divide with me. I am joined with him in the guardianship of Miss Darcy.
question: How does Fitzwilliam correct Elizabeth's assumption about Darcy's control over Miss Darcy?
answer: He says he shares the guardianship of Miss Darcy with Darcy.
evidence: I am joined with him in the guardianship of Miss Darcy.

quote_text:
Are you, indeed? And pray what sort of guardians do you make? Does your
charge give you much trouble? Young ladies of her age, are sometimes a
little difficult to manage, and if she has the true Darcy spirit, she
may like to have her own way.
question: What does Elizabeth teasingly ask Fitzwilliam about their guardianship of Miss Darcy?
answer: She asks whether their charge gives trouble and hints that Miss Darcy may have the Darcy willfulness.
evidence: if she has the true Darcy spirit, she may like to have her own way.

quote_text:
You need not be frightened. I never heard any harm of her; and I dare
say she is one of the most tractable creatures in the world. She is a
very great favourite with some ladies of my acquaintance, Mrs. Hurst and
Miss Bingley. I think I have heard you say that you know them.
question: Why does Elizabeth reassure Fitzwilliam after asking about Miss Darcy?
answer: Because he looked earnest, she says she has heard no harm of Georgiana and calls her tractable.
evidence: You need not be frightened.

quote_text:
I know them a little. Their brother is a pleasant gentleman-like
man--he is a great friend of Darcy's.
question: How does Fitzwilliam describe Bingley to Elizabeth?
answer: He calls Bingley a pleasant gentleman-like man and a great friend of Darcy.
evidence: Their brother is a pleasant gentleman-like man--he is a great friend of Darcy's.

quote_text:
Oh! yes, Mr. Darcy is uncommonly kind to Mr.
Bingley, and takes a prodigious deal of care of him.
question: Why is Elizabeth drily sarcastic about Darcy's kindness to Bingley?
answer: She already believes Darcy interfered to separate Bingley from Jane, so she means the opposite.
evidence: I had detached Mr. Bingley from your sister

quote_text:
Care of him!--Yes, I really believe Darcy _does_ take care of him in
those points where he most wants care. From something that he told me in
our journey hither, I have reason to think Bingley very much indebted to
him. But I ought to beg his pardon, for I have no right to suppose that
Bingley was the person meant. It was all conjecture.
question: What does Fitzwilliam reveal about Darcy's role in Bingley's life?
answer: He says Darcy takes care of Bingley where he most needs care and that Bingley is much indebted to him.
evidence: Bingley very much indebted to him.

quote_text: What is it you mean?
question: What makes Elizabeth press Fitzwilliam for details about Darcy and Bingley?
answer: His hint that Bingley is much indebted to Darcy makes her want the specifics.
evidence: Bingley very much indebted to him.

quote_text:
It is a circumstance which Darcy of course would not wish to be
generally known, because if it were to get round to the lady's family,
it would be an unpleasant thing.
question: Why does Fitzwilliam hesitate to explain the circumstance about Darcy and Bingley?
answer: He says Darcy would not want it generally known and it would be unpleasant for the lady's family.
evidence: Darcy of course would not wish to be generally known

quote_text: You may depend upon my not mentioning it.
question: What does Elizabeth promise when Fitzwilliam says the matter is sensitive?
answer: She assures him she will not mention it.
evidence: You may depend upon my not mentioning it.

quote_text:
And remember that I have not much reason for supposing it to be
Bingley. What he told me was merely this; that he congratulated himself
on having lately saved a friend from the inconveniences of a most
imprudent marriage, but without mentioning names or any other
particulars, and I only suspected it to be Bingley from believing him
the kind of young man to get into a scrape of that sort, and from
knowing them to have been together the whole of last summer.
question: Why does Fitzwilliam suspect Bingley is the friend Darcy saved from an imprudent marriage?
answer: He thinks Bingley fits the sort of young man who could get into such a scrape and was with Darcy that summer.
evidence: knowing them to have been together the whole of last summer

quote_text: Did Mr. Darcy give you his reasons for this interference?
question: What does Elizabeth want to learn about Darcy's interference?
answer: She asks whether Darcy gave his reasons for opposing the match.
evidence: Did Mr. Darcy give you his reasons for this interference?

quote_text:
I understood that there were some very strong objections against the
lady.
question: What reason does Fitzwilliam report for Darcy's opposition to the match?
answer: He says there were very strong objections against the lady.
evidence: there were some very strong objections against the lady

quote_text: And what arts did he use to separate them?
question: What does Elizabeth ask about Darcy's method of separating Bingley and the lady?
answer: She asks what arts Darcy used to separate them.
evidence: what arts did he use to separate them?

quote_text:
He did not talk to me of his own arts, He
only told me, what I have now told you.
question: How does Fitzwilliam answer Elizabeth's question about Darcy's methods?
answer: He says Darcy never discussed his own arts and only told him what he has now repeated.
evidence: He only told me, what I have now told you.

quote_text:
I am thinking of what you have been telling me, Your
cousin's conduct does not suit my feelings. Why was he to be the judge?
question: Why is Elizabeth indignant after hearing Fitzwilliam's account?
answer: She thinks Darcy had no right to judge and direct Bingley's happiness.
evidence: Why was he to be the judge?

quote_text: You are rather disposed to call his interference officious?
question: How does Fitzwilliam interpret Elizabeth's reaction to Darcy's interference?
answer: He suggests she is disposed to call the interference officious.
evidence: call his interference officious

quote_text:
I do not see what right Mr. Darcy had to decide on the propriety of
his friend's inclination, or why, upon his own judgment alone, he was to
determine and direct in what manner that friend was to be happy. But, as we know none of the
particulars, it is not fair to condemn him. It is not to be supposed
that there was much affection in the case.
question: What is Elizabeth's objection to Darcy's conduct toward Bingley?
answer: She says Darcy had no right to decide Bingley's happiness by his own judgment alone.
evidence: I do not see what right Mr. Darcy had to decide

quote_text:
That is not an unnatural surmise, but it is
lessening the honour of my cousin's triumph very sadly.
question: How does Fitzwilliam try to soften Elizabeth's condemnation of Darcy?
answer: He jestingly says her surmise lessens the honor of Darcy's triumph.
evidence: lessening the honour of my cousin's triumph very sadly

quote_text: There were some very strong objections against the lady,
question: Why does Elizabeth repeat Fitzwilliam's phrase about strong objections to herself?
answer: She uses it to conclude that Darcy objected to Jane's low family connections.
evidence: the situation of your mother's family, though objectionable

quote_text:
To Jane herself, "there could be no possibility of
objection. All loveliness and goodness as she is! Her understanding
excellent, her mind improved, and her manners captivating. Neither could
any thing be urged against my father, who, though with some
peculiarities, has abilities which Mr. Darcy himself need not disdain,
and respectability which he will probably never reach."
question: Why does Elizabeth defend Jane in her private reflections on Darcy's objections?
answer: She is convinced Jane herself is faultless, so the objections must concern her family.
evidence: All loveliness and goodness as she is!

quote_text:
In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be
repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love
you.
question: Why does Darcy finally confess his feelings to Elizabeth?
