answer: He says he can no longer repress his feelings despite struggling against them.
evidence: My feelings will not be repressed.

quote_text:
In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to
express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however
unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be
felt, and if I could _feel_ gratitude, I would now thank you. But I
cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly
bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to any
one. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of
short duration. The feelings which, you tell me, have long prevented the
acknowledgment of your regard, can have little difficulty in overcoming
it after this explanation.
question: How does Elizabeth answer Darcy's proposal?
answer: She coldly refuses and says she cannot feel gratitude because she never desired his good opinion.
evidence: I have never desired your good opinion

quote_text:
And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I
might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little _endeavour_ at
civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.
question: What does Darcy want to know after Elizabeth's refusal?
answer: He asks why he is rejected with so little effort at civility.
evidence: why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected

quote_text:
I might as well enquire, why with so evident a design of
offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me
against your will, against your reason, and even against your character?
Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I _was_ uncivil? But I have
other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided
against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been
favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept
the man, who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the
happiness of a most beloved sister?
question: What does Elizabeth cite as provocation for her incivility toward Darcy?
answer: She says he insulted her by declaring he liked her against his will, reason, and character.
evidence: against your will, against your reason, and even against your character

quote_text:
I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can
excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted _there_. You dare not,
you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means
of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the
world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for
disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest
kind.
question: What serious accusation does Elizabeth make about Darcy's treatment of Jane and Bingley?
answer: She accuses him of being the principal means of dividing them and ruining Jane's happiness.
evidence: means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister

quote_text: Can you deny that you have done it?
question: What does Elizabeth demand that Darcy admit?
answer: She demands he admit his role in separating Bingley and Jane.
evidence: you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them

quote_text:
I have no wish of denying
that I did every thing in my power to separate my friend from your
sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards _him_ I have been
kinder than towards myself.
question: How does Darcy respond to the accusation about separating Bingley and Jane?
answer: He admits he did everything in his power to separate them and says he rejoices in his success.
evidence: I rejoice in my success.

quote_text:
But it is not merely this affair, on which my dislike
is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was
decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received
many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to
say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself?
or under what misrepresentation, can you here impose upon others?
question: What second grievance does Elizabeth add to her dislike of Darcy?
answer: She cites Wickham's recital of Darcy's mistreatment of him.
evidence: Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham.

quote_text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman's concerns,
question: What does Darcy observe about Elizabeth's interest in Wickham?
answer: He notes that she takes an eager interest in Wickham's concerns.
evidence: You take an eager interest in that gentleman's concerns

quote_text:
Who that knows what his misfortunes have been, can help feeling an
interest in him?
question: How does Elizabeth justify her sympathy for Wickham?
answer: She says anyone who knows his misfortunes cannot help feeling interest in him.
evidence: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been

quote_text:
His misfortunes! yes, his misfortunes
have been great indeed.
question: How does Darcy react to Elizabeth's claim about Wickham's misfortunes?
answer: He repeats the word contemptuously, implying Wickham's misfortunes were deserved.
evidence: yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed

quote_text:
And of your infliction, You have reduced
him to his present state of poverty, comparative poverty. You have
withheld the advantages, which you must know to have been designed for
him. You have deprived the best years of his life, of that independence
which was no less his due than his desert. You have done all this! and
yet you can treat the mention of his misfortunes with contempt and
ridicule.
question: What does Elizabeth accuse Darcy of doing to Wickham?
answer: She says he reduced Wickham to poverty and withheld advantages designed for him.
evidence: You have reduced him to his present state of poverty

quote_text:
And this, is your opinion of me! This is the estimation in which you hold me! I
thank you for explaining it so fully. My faults, according to this
calculation, are heavy indeed! But perhaps, these offences might have been
overlooked, had not your pride been hurt by my honest confession of the
scruples that had long prevented my forming any serious design. These
bitter accusations might have been suppressed, had I with greater policy
concealed my struggles, and flattered you into the belief of my being
impelled by unqualified, unalloyed inclination; by reason, by
reflection, by every thing. But disguise of every sort is my abhorrence.
Nor am I ashamed of the feelings I related. They were natural and just.
Could you expect me to rejoice in the inferiority of your connections?
To congratulate myself on the hope of relations, whose condition in life
is so decidedly beneath my own?
question: Why does Darcy think Elizabeth's accusations are influenced by wounded pride?
answer: He believes she resents his honest confession of the scruples that restrained him.
evidence: your pride been hurt by my honest confession of the scruples

quote_text:
You are mistaken, Mr. Darcy, if you suppose that the mode of your
declaration affected me in any other way, than as it spared me the
concern which I might have felt in refusing you, had you behaved in a
more gentleman-like manner.
question: What does Elizabeth say about the manner of Darcy's proposal?
answer: She says his ungentlemanlike manner spared her the concern she might have felt in refusing him.
evidence: had you behaved in a more gentleman-like manner

quote_text:
You could not have made me the offer of your hand in any possible way
that would have tempted me to accept it.
question: What does Elizabeth declare about any possible offer from Darcy?
answer: She says no possible manner of offer would have tempted her to accept him.
evidence: You could not have made me the offer of your hand in any possible way

quote_text:
From the very beginning, from the first moment I may almost say, of my
acquaintance with you, your manners impressing me with the fullest
belief of your arrogance, your conceit, and your selfish disdain of the
feelings of others, were such as to form that ground-work of
disapprobation, on which succeeding events have built so immoveable a
dislike; and I had not known you a month before I felt that you were the
last man in the world whom I could ever be prevailed on to marry.
question: Why does Elizabeth tell Darcy he is the last man she could ever marry?
answer: She says his arrogance, conceit, and selfish disdain of others from their first acquaintance created an immovable dislike in her.
evidence: your manners impressing me with the fullest belief of your arrogance, your conceit

quote_text:
You have said quite enough, madam. I perfectly comprehend your
feelings, and have now only to be ashamed of what my own have been.
Forgive me for having taken up so much of your time, and accept my best
wishes for your health and happiness.
question: What does Darcy's reply show about how he receives Elizabeth's refusal?
answer: He says he understands her feelings and is ashamed of his own, then accepts that he has said enough and leaves.
evidence: I perfectly comprehend your feelings, and have now only to be ashamed of what my own have been.

quote_text:
I
have been walking in the grove some time in the hope of meeting you.
Will you do me the honour of reading that letter?
question: Why does Darcy approach Elizabeth in the grove?
answer: He has been waiting to meet her so he can give her a letter explaining his conduct after her accusations.
evidence: holding out a letter, which she instinctively took

quote_text:
This must be false!
This cannot be! This must be the grossest falsehood!
question: Why does Elizabeth keep rejecting Darcy's account of Wickham?
answer: The account contradicts her cherished opinion of Wickham and alarms her, so she wishes to discredit it entirely.
evidence: She wished to discredit it entirely, repeatedly exclaiming

quote_text:
How despicably have I acted! I, who have prided myself on
my discernment!--I, who have valued myself on my abilities! who have
often disdained the generous candour of my sister, and gratified my
vanity, in useless or blameable distrust.--How humiliating is this
discovery!--Yet, how just a humiliation!--Had I been in love, I could
not have been more wretchedly blind. But vanity, not love, has been my
folly.--Pleased with the preference of one, and offended by the neglect
of the other, on the very beginning of our acquaintance, I have courted
prepossession and ignorance, and driven reason away, where either were
concerned. Till this moment, I never knew myself.
question: What realization causes Elizabeth's cry of self-reproach after reading Darcy's letter?
answer: She sees that her vanity and prejudice, not love, blinded her to the truth about Darcy and Wickham.
evidence: vanity, not love, has been my folly

quote_text:
I assure
you, I feel it exceedingly, I believe nobody
feels the loss of friends so much as I do. But I am particularly
attached to these young men; and know them to be so much attached to
me!--They were excessively sorry to go! But so they always are. The dear
colonel rallied his spirits tolerably till just at last; but Darcy
seemed to feel it most acutely, more I think than last year. His
attachment to Rosings, certainly increases.
question: Why does Lady Catherine say she feels the nephews' departure so much?
answer: She claims particular attachment to the young men and believes nobody feels the loss of friends as she does.
evidence: I am particularly attached to these young men

quote_text:
But if that is the case, you must write to your mother to beg that you
may stay a little longer. Mrs. Collins will be very glad of your
company, I am sure.
question: Why does Lady Catherine suggest Elizabeth write to her mother?
answer: She thinks Elizabeth seems out of spirits because she dislikes returning home and offers to let her stay longer.
evidence: supposing that she did not like to go home again

quote_text:
I am much obliged to your ladyship for your kind invitation, but it is not in my power to accept it.--I must be in town
next Saturday.
question: Why does Elizabeth decline Lady Catherine's invitation to stay longer?
answer: She says she must be in town the next Saturday and cannot accept the extension.
evidence: I must be in town next Saturday.

quote_text:
Why, at that rate, you will have been here only six weeks. I expected
you to stay two months. I told Mrs. Collins so before you came. There
can be no occasion for your going so soon. Mrs. Bennet could certainly
spare you for another fortnight.
question: Why is Lady Catherine surprised by Elizabeth's planned departure?
answer: She had expected Elizabeth to stay two months and sees no occasion for her to leave so soon.
evidence: I expected you to stay two months. I told Mrs. Collins so before you came.

quote_text: But my father cannot.--He wrote last week to hurry my return.
question: What reason does Elizabeth give for not staying longer at Hunsford?
answer: Her father cannot spare her and recently wrote to hurry her return.
evidence: He wrote last week to hurry my return.

quote_text:
Oh! your father of course may spare you, if your mother can.--Daughters
are never of so much consequence to a father. And if you will stay
another _month_ complete, it will be in my power to take one of you as
far as London, for I am going there early in June, for a week; and as
Dawson does not object to the Barouche box, there will be very good room
for one of you--and indeed, if the weather should happen to be cool, I
should not object to taking you both, as you are neither of you large.
question: What plan does Lady Catherine propose if Elizabeth stays another month?
answer: She offers to take one or both of the young women as far as London on her own journey in June.
evidence: if you will stay another month complete, it will be in my power to take one of you as far as London

quote_text:
You are all kindness, Madam; but I believe we must abide by our
original plan.
question: How does Elizabeth respond to Lady Catherine's proposed change of plans?
answer: She thanks her for the kindness but politely insists that they must keep their original travel plan.
evidence: I believe we must abide by our original plan.

quote_text:
Mrs. Collins, you must send a servant with them. You know I always
speak my mind, and I cannot bear the idea of two young women travelling
post by themselves. It is highly improper. You must contrive to send
somebody. I have the greatest dislike in the world to that sort of
thing.--Young women should always be properly guarded and attended,
according to their situation in life. When my niece Georgiana went to
Ramsgate last summer, I made a point of her having two men servants go
with her.--Miss Darcy, the daughter of Mr. Darcy, of Pemberley, and Lady
Anne, could not have appeared with propriety in a different manner.--I
am excessively attentive to all those things. You must send John with
the young ladies, Mrs. Collins. I am glad it occurred to me to mention
it; for it would really be discreditable to _you_ to let them go alone.
question: Why does Lady Catherine insist that a servant accompany the young women?
answer: She thinks it highly improper for two young women to travel post by themselves and wants them properly guarded.
evidence: I cannot bear the idea of two young women travelling post by themselves. It is highly improper.

quote_text: My uncle is to send a servant for us.
question: What arrangement has Elizabeth's family already made for their journey?
answer: Her uncle is going to send a servant for them.
evidence: My uncle is to send a servant for us.

quote_text:
Oh!--Your uncle!--He keeps a man-servant, does he?--I am very glad you
have somebody who thinks of those things. Where shall you change
horses?--Oh! Bromley, of course.--If you mention my name at the Bell,
you will be attended to.
question: How does Lady Catherine react to hearing that Elizabeth's uncle keeps a servant?
answer: She is surprised and pleased, saying she is glad somebody thinks of such proprieties, then advises mentioning her name at the Bell.
evidence: I am very glad you have somebody who thinks of those things.

quote_text:
I know not, Miss Elizabeth, whether Mrs. Collins has yet
expressed her sense of your kindness in coming to us, but I am very
certain you will not leave the house without receiving her thanks for
it. The favour of your company has been much felt, I assure you. We know
how little there is to tempt any one to our humble abode. Our plain
manner of living, our small rooms, and few domestics, and the little we
see of the world, must make Hunsford extremely dull to a young lady like
yourself; but I hope you will believe us grateful for the condescension,
and that we have done every thing in our power to prevent your spending
your time unpleasantly.
question: What does Mr. Collins want to assure Elizabeth before she leaves Hunsford?
answer: He wants her to know that Charlotte and he are grateful for her visit and that she will receive Charlotte's thanks.
evidence: you will not leave the house without receiving her thanks for it

quote_text:
It gives me the greatest pleasure to hear that you have passed your
time not disagreeably. We have certainly done our best; and most
fortunately having it in our power to introduce you to very superior
society, and from our connection with Rosings, the frequent means of
varying the humble home scene, I think we may flatter ourselves that
your Hunsford visit cannot have been entirely irksome. Our situation
with regard to Lady Catherine's family is indeed the sort of
extraordinary advantage and blessing which few can boast. You see on
what a footing we are. You see how continually we are engaged there. In
truth I must acknowledge that, with all the disadvantages of this humble
parsonage, I should not think any one abiding in it an object of
compassion, while they are sharers of our intimacy at Rosings.
question: How does Mr. Collins describe the Collinses' efforts to entertain Elizabeth?
answer: He claims they did their best and that their connection with Rosings made her visit far from irksome.
evidence: we have certainly done our best

quote_text:
You may, in fact, carry a very favourable report of us into
Hertfordshire, my dear cousin. I flatter myself at least that you will
be able to do so. Lady Catherine's great attentions to Mrs. Collins you
have been a daily witness of; and altogether I trust it does not appear
that your friend has drawn an unfortunate--but on this point it will be
as well to be silent. Only let me assure you, my dear Miss Elizabeth,
that I can from my heart most cordially wish you equal felicity in
marriage. My dear Charlotte and I have but one mind and one way of
thinking. There is in every thing a most remarkable resemblance of
character and ideas between us. We seem to have been designed for each
other.
question: What kind of report does Mr. Collins hope Elizabeth will carry back to Hertfordshire?
answer: He hopes she will carry a very favourable report of their happiness and of Lady Catherine's attentions.
evidence: carry a very favourable report of us into Hertfordshire

quote_text:
But, you will of course wish to have your humble respects
delivered to them, with your grateful thanks for their kindness to you
while you have been here.
question: What does Mr. Collins suddenly remind the departing young women they have forgotten?
answer: He reminds them to leave their respects and thanks for the ladies at Rosings.
evidence: you will of course wish to have your humble respects delivered to them

quote_text:
Good gracious! it seems but
a day or two since we first came!--and yet how many things have
happened!
question: What makes Maria exclaim about how short the visit seems?
answer: She reflects that it feels only a day or two since they arrived, though many things have happened.
evidence: it seems but a day or two since we first came

quote_text: A great many indeed,
question: What does Elizabeth's sigh suggest about her feelings as they leave Hunsford?
answer: She agrees many things have happened, but her sigh reflects private turmoil and the need to conceal much.
evidence: said her companion with a sigh

quote_text:
We have dined nine times at Rosings, besides drinking tea there
twice!--How much I shall have to tell!
question: What does Maria count as the main events of their Hunsford visit?
answer: She counts nine dinners at Rosings and two teas there, showing how much she has to tell.
evidence: We have dined nine times at Rosings, besides drinking tea there twice

quote_text: And how much I shall have to conceal.
question: What does Elizabeth privately mean she will have to conceal?
answer: She means she must hide Darcy's proposal, his letter, and the truth about Wickham from general gossip.
evidence: And how much I shall have to conceal.

quote_text:
And we mean to treat you all, but you must lend us the
money, for we have just spent ours at the shop out there. Look here, I have bought this bonnet. I do not think it
is very pretty; but I thought I might as well buy it as not. I shall
pull it to pieces as soon as I get home, and see if I can make it up any
better.
question: What does Lydia's request for money reveal about her behavior at the inn?
answer: She has already spent her money on purchases and expects her sisters to pay for the treat.
evidence: we have just spent ours at the shop out there

quote_text:
Oh! but there were two or three much uglier in the shop; and
when I have bought some prettier-coloured satin to trim it with fresh, I
think it will be very tolerable. Besides, it will not much signify what
one wears this summer, after the ----shire have left Meryton, and they
are going in a fortnight.
question: Why does Lydia defend buying an ugly bonnet?
answer: She plans to trim it with prettier satin and thinks it hardly matters before the militia leaves Meryton.
evidence: when I have bought some prettier-coloured satin to trim it with fresh

quote_text: Are they indeed?
question: Why is Elizabeth so satisfied to hear the militia is leaving in a fortnight?
answer: Their removal will relieve her from Wickham's presence and the troubles connected with him.
evidence: they are going in a fortnight

quote_text:
They are going to be encamped near Brighton; and I do so want papa to
take us all there for the summer! It would be such a delicious scheme,
and I dare say would hardly cost any thing at all. Mamma would like to
go too of all things! Only think what a miserable summer else we shall
have!
question: What scheme does Lydia urge on her father and why?
answer: She wants him to take the family to Brighton near the camp, fearing a miserable summer otherwise.
evidence: I do so want papa to take us all there for the summer

quote_text:
Yes, _that_ would be a delightful scheme, indeed,
and completely do for us at once. Good Heaven! Brighton, and a whole
campful of soldiers, to us, who have been overset already by one poor
regiment of militia, and the monthly balls of Meryton.
question: What does Elizabeth privately think of Lydia's Brighton plan?
answer: She thinks it would be disastrous, since Brighton and a campful of soldiers would only increase their folly.
evidence: Brighton, and a whole campful of soldiers

quote_text:
Now I have got some news for you, What do you think? It is excellent news, capital news, and about
a certain person that we all like.
question: What important news about Wickham does Lydia announce at the inn?
answer: She says there is no danger of Wickham marrying Mary King because Mary King has gone to Liverpool.
evidence: There is no danger of Wickham's marrying Mary King.

quote_text:
Aye, that is just like your formality and discretion. You thought the
waiter must not hear, as if he cared! I dare say he often hears worse
things said than I am going to say. But he is an ugly fellow! I am glad
he is gone. I never saw such a long chin in my life. Well, but now for
my news: it is about dear Wickham; too good for the waiter, is not it?
There is no danger of Wickham's marrying Mary King. There's for you! She
is gone down to her uncle at Liverpool; gone to stay. Wickham is safe.
question: Why does Lydia mock her sisters' concern about the waiter hearing her news?
answer: She thinks their formality is unnecessary and that the waiter would not care about their gossip.
evidence: You thought the waiter must not hear, as if he cared!

quote_text:
And Mary King is safe! safe from a connection
imprudent as to fortune.
question: What does Elizabeth mean by saying Mary King is safe?
answer: She means Mary King has escaped a financially imprudent connection with Wickham.
evidence: safe from a connection imprudent as to fortune

quote_text: She is a great fool for going away, if she liked him.
question: Why does Lydia call Mary King a fool?
answer: She thinks Mary King foolishly went away if she actually liked Wickham.
evidence: She is a great fool for going away, if she liked him.

quote_text: But I hope there is no strong attachment on either side,
question: What does Jane hope about Wickham and Mary King's feelings?
answer: She hopes neither of them had any strong attachment.
evidence: I hope there is no strong attachment on either side

quote_text:
I am sure there is not on _his_. I will answer for it he never cared
three straws about her. Who _could_ about such a nasty little freckled
thing?
question: Why is Lydia certain Wickham did not care for Mary King?
answer: She claims he never cared three straws about her and disparages Mary King's appearance.
evidence: he never cared three straws about her

quote_text:
How nicely we are crammed in! I am glad I bought my
bonnet, if it is only for the fun of having another bandbox! Well, now
let us be quite comfortable and snug, and talk and laugh all the way
home. And in the first place, let us hear what has happened to you all,
since you went away. Have you seen any pleasant men? Have you had any
flirting? I was in great hopes that one of you would have got a husband
before you came back. Jane will be quite an old maid soon, I declare.
She is almost three and twenty! Lord, how ashamed I should be of not
being married before three and twenty! My aunt Philips wants you so to
get husbands, you can't think. She says Lizzy had better have taken Mr.
Collins; but _I_ do not think there would have been any fun in it. Lord!
how I should like to be married before any of you; and then I would
chaperon you about to all the balls. Dear me! we had such a good piece
of fun the other day at Colonel Forster's. Kitty and me were to spend
the day there, and Mrs. Forster promised to have a little dance in the
evening; (by the bye, Mrs. Forster and me are _such_ friends!) and so
she asked the two Harringtons to come, but Harriet was ill, and so Pen
was forced to come by herself; and then, what do you think we did? We
dressed up Chamberlayne in woman's clothes, on purpose to pass for a
lady,--only think what fun! Not a soul knew of it, but Col. and Mrs.
Forster, and Kitty and me, except my aunt, for we were forced to borrow
one of her gowns; and you cannot imagine how well he looked! When Denny,
and Wickham, and Pratt, and two or three more of the men came in, they
did not know him in the least. Lord! how I laughed! and so did Mrs.
Forster. I thought I should have died. And _that_ made the men suspect
something, and then they soon found out what was the matter.
question: What does Lydia's delight in the crowded carriage show about her mood?
answer: She is frivolously amused by the bandbox and the snug crowding, treating the journey as fun.
evidence: I am glad I bought my bonnet, if it is only for the fun of having another bandbox

quote_text: I am glad you are come back, Lizzy.
question: Why does Mr. Bennet voluntarily tell Elizabeth he is glad she is back?
answer: He has missed her and shows his affection more openly than usual now that she has returned.
evidence: I am glad you are come back, Lizzy.

quote_text:
Oh! Mary, I wish you had gone with us, for we had such fun!
as we went along, Kitty and me drew up all the blinds, and pretended
there was nobody in the coach; and I should have gone so all the way, if
Kitty had not been sick; and when we got to the George, I do think we
behaved very handsomely, for we treated the other three with the nicest
cold luncheon in the world, and if you would have gone, we would have
treated you too. And then when we came away it was such fun! I thought
we never should have got into the coach. I was ready to die of laughter.
And then we were so merry all the way home! we talked and laughed so
loud, that any body might have heard us ten miles off!
question: Why does Lydia wish Mary had gone with them to the inn?
answer: She thinks Mary missed the fun of their coach journey and the cold luncheon they arranged.
evidence: we had such fun!

quote_text:
Far be it from me, my dear sister,
to depreciate such pleasures. They would doubtless be congenial with
the generality of female minds. But I confess they would have no charms
for _me_. I should infinitely prefer a book.
question: What does Mary's reply reveal about her attitude toward Lydia's pleasures?
answer: She claims such frivolous pleasures have no charms for her and that she would prefer a book.
evidence: I should infinitely prefer a book.

quote_text:
His being so sure of succeeding, was wrong, and certainly
ought not to have appeared; but consider how much it must increase his
disappointment.
question: What is Jane's reaction to hearing how Darcy proposed to Elizabeth?
answer: She thinks Darcy was wrong to seem so sure of success but pities the disappointment his refusal must cause him.
evidence: consider how much it must increase his disappointment

quote_text:
Indeed, I am heartily sorry for him; but he has
other feelings which will probably soon drive away his regard for me.
You do not blame me, however, for refusing him?
question: Why does Elizabeth say she is heartily sorry for Darcy?
answer: She pities his disappointment but believes his other feelings will soon drive away his regard for her.
evidence: I am heartily sorry for him

quote_text: Blame you! Oh, no.
question: Why does Jane immediately absolve Elizabeth of blame for refusing Mr. Darcy?
answer: Jane is so sympathetic that she does not condemn Elizabeth's refusal, even though she pities Darcy.
evidence: You do not blame me, however, for refusing him?

quote_text: But you blame me for having spoken so warmly of Wickham.
question: Why does Elizabeth expect Jane may blame her for having spoken warmly of Wickham?
answer: Elizabeth now knows from Darcy's letter that Wickham's character is bad, so her earlier praise will look mistaken.
evidence: The extravagance and general profligacy which he scrupled not to lay to Mr. Wickham's charge, exceedingly shocked her

quote_text: No--I do not know that you were wrong in saying what you did.
question: How does Jane respond to Elizabeth's fear that her warm praise of Wickham was wrong?
answer: Jane refuses to condemn Elizabeth, saying she cannot see that Elizabeth was wrong in what she said.
evidence: No--I do not know that you were wrong in saying what you did.

quote_text:
But you _will_ know it, when I have told you what happened the very
next day.
question: Why does Elizabeth insist that Jane will change her mind about blaming her?
answer: Elizabeth knows the next day's revelations about Wickham will make her former praise of him seem foolish.
evidence: The extravagance and general profligacy which he scrupled not to lay to Mr. Wickham's charge

quote_text:
This will not do, You never will be able to make both
of them good for any thing. Take your choice, but you must be satisfied
with only one. There is but such a quantity of merit between them; just
enough to make one good sort of man; and of late it has been shifting
about pretty much. For my part, I am inclined to believe it all Mr.
Darcy's, but you shall do as you chuse.
question: What is Elizabeth trying to persuade Jane to accept about Darcy and Wickham?
answer: She says Jane cannot make both men good and must choose one, and Elizabeth favors Darcy's merit.
evidence: You never will be able to make both of them good for any thing.

quote_text:
I do not know when I have been more shocked, Wickham so
very bad! It is almost past belief. And poor Mr. Darcy! dear Lizzy, only
consider what he must have suffered. Such a disappointment! and with the
knowledge of your ill opinion too! and having to relate such a thing of
his sister! It is really too distressing. I am sure you must feel it
so.
question: Why is Jane shocked after hearing the account of Wickham and Darcy?
answer: She is shocked because Wickham, whom she thought amiable, is revealed as very bad, while Darcy suffered greatly.
evidence: Wickham so very bad! It is almost past belief. And poor Mr. Darcy!

quote_text:
Oh! no, my regret and compassion are all done away by seeing you so
full of both. I know you will do him such ample justice, that I am
growing every moment more unconcerned and indifferent. Your profusion
makes me saving; and if you lament over him much longer, my heart will
be as light as a feather.
question: How does Elizabeth react to Jane's great compassion for Darcy?
answer: She teasingly says Jane's abundant pity leaves her no regret of her own and makes her feel more indifferent.
evidence: Your profusion makes me saving; and if you lament over him much longer, my heart will be as light as a feather.

quote_text:
Poor Wickham; there is such an expression of goodness in his
countenance! such an openness and gentleness in his manner.
question: What does Jane's remark reveal about her judgment of Wickham despite the letter?
answer: She still clings to his pleasing appearance and manner and finds it hard to believe him wholly bad.
evidence: there is such an expression of goodness in his countenance! such an openness and gentleness in his manner.

quote_text:
There certainly was some great mismanagement in the education of those
two young men. One has got all the goodness, and the other all the
appearance of it.
question: What does Elizabeth mean by contrasting the two young men's goodness and appearance?
answer: She suggests Darcy has the real goodness while Wickham has only its appearance, owing to their upbringing.
evidence: One has got all the goodness, and the other all the appearance of it.

quote_text:
I never thought Mr. Darcy so deficient in the _appearance_ of it as you
used to do.
question: How does Jane gently correct Elizabeth's former view of Darcy?
answer: Jane says she never thought Darcy lacked even the appearance of goodness as much as Elizabeth used to claim.
evidence: I never thought Mr. Darcy so deficient in the appearance of it as you used to do.

quote_text:
And yet I meant to be uncommonly clever in taking so decided a dislike
to him, without any reason. It is such a spur to one's genius, such an
opening for wit to have a dislike of that kind. One may be continually
abusive without saying any thing just; but one cannot be always laughing
at a man without now and then stumbling on something witty.
question: What does Elizabeth admit about her former dislike of Darcy?
answer: She admits she prided herself on cleverly disliking him without reason, which was vanity rather than discernment.
evidence: It is such a spur to one's genius, such an opening for wit to have a dislike of that kind.

quote_text:
Lizzy, when you first read that letter, I am sure you could not treat
the matter as you do now.
question: Why does Jane doubt Elizabeth's present lightness about Darcy's letter?
answer: Jane believes Elizabeth must have been deeply upset when she first read it, before she could laugh at it.
evidence: when you first read that letter, I am sure you could not treat the matter as you do now.

quote_text:
Indeed I could not. I was uncomfortable enough. I was very
uncomfortable, I may say unhappy. And with no one to speak to, of what I
felt, no Jane to comfort me and say that I had not been so very weak and
vain and nonsensical as I knew I had! Oh! how I wanted you!
question: What does Elizabeth reveal about her feelings when she first read Darcy's letter?
answer: She was very uncomfortable and unhappy and wished for Jane to comfort her.
evidence: I was very uncomfortable, I may say unhappy.

quote_text:
How unfortunate that you should have used such very strong expressions
in speaking of Wickham to Mr. Darcy, for now they _do_ appear wholly
undeserved.
question: Why does Jane call Elizabeth's strong words to Darcy unfortunate?
answer: Because Darcy's letter shows Wickham's bad character, so Elizabeth's earlier abuse of Darcy now seems undeserved.
evidence: for now they do appear wholly undeserved.

quote_text:
Certainly. But the misfortune of speaking with bitterness, is a most
natural consequence of the prejudices I had been encouraging. There is
one point, on which I want your advice. I want to be told whether I
ought, or ought not to make our acquaintance in general understand
Wickham's character.
question: What does Elizabeth say caused her bitter speech to Darcy?
answer: She says it was the natural result of the prejudices she had been encouraging against him.
evidence: a most natural consequence of the prejudices I had been encouraging.

quote_text:
Surely there can be no
occasion for exposing him so dreadfully. What is your own opinion?
question: What does Jane ask Elizabeth to consider about revealing Wickham's character?
answer: Jane questions whether there is any need to expose Wickham so harshly and asks Elizabeth's own opinion.
evidence: Surely there can be no occasion for exposing him so dreadfully. What is your own opinion?

quote_text:
That it ought not to be attempted. Mr. Darcy has not authorised me to
make his communication public. On the contrary every particular relative
to his sister, was meant to be kept as much as possible to myself; and
if I endeavour to undeceive people as to the rest of his conduct, who
will believe me? The general prejudice against Mr. Darcy is so violent,
that it would be the death of half the good people in Meryton, to
attempt to place him in an amiable light. I am not equal to it. Wickham
will soon be gone; and therefore it will not signify to anybody here,
what he really is. Sometime hence it will be all found out, and then we
may laugh at their stupidity in not knowing it before. At present I will
say nothing about it.
question: Why does Elizabeth decide not to make Wickham's character public?
answer: Because Darcy did not authorize it, his sister's part must be secret, and people would not believe her against their prejudice.
evidence: Mr. Darcy has not authorised me to make his communication public.

quote_text:
You are quite right. To have his errors made public might ruin him for
ever. He is now perhaps sorry for what he has done, and anxious to
re-establish a character. We must not make him desperate.
question: Why does Jane agree with Elizabeth's decision to stay silent about Wickham?
answer: Jane fears public exposure might ruin Wickham forever and prevent him from reforming.
evidence: To have his errors made public might ruin him for ever.

quote_text:
And then, if that very
improbable event should ever take place, I shall merely be able to tell
what Bingley may tell in a much more agreeable manner himself. The
liberty of communication cannot be mine till it has lost all its value!
question: What does Elizabeth mean by saying she cannot reveal the rest of Darcy's letter until a very improbable event?
answer: She means she cannot tell Jane of Darcy's love until Jane and Bingley are securely engaged, when secrecy would no longer matter.
evidence: The liberty of communication cannot be mine till it has lost all its value!

quote_text:
Well, Lizzy, what is your opinion _now_ of
this sad business of Jane's? For my part, I am determined never to speak
of it again to anybody. I told my sister Philips so the other day. But I
cannot find out that Jane saw any thing of him in London. Well, he is a
very undeserving young man--and I do not suppose there is the least
chance in the world of her ever getting him now. There is no talk of his
coming to Netherfield again in the summer; and I have enquired of every
body too, who is likely to know.
question: What does Mrs. Bennet ask Elizabeth about Jane and Bingley?
answer: She asks Elizabeth's opinion of Jane's sad business and says she has resolved not to speak of it again.
evidence: what is your opinion now of this sad business of Jane's?

quote_text: I do not believe that he will ever live at Netherfield any more.
question: Why does Elizabeth say Bingley will not live at Netherfield again?
answer: She believes his sisters and Darcy have kept him in London and that he will not return to Jane.
evidence: his sisters would be successful in keeping him away

quote_text:
Oh, well! it is just as he chooses. Nobody wants him to come. Though I
shall always say that he used my daughter extremely ill; and if I was
her, I would not have put up with it. Well, my comfort is, I am sure
Jane will die of a broken heart, and then he will be sorry for what he
has done.
question: How does Mrs. Bennet try to hide her disappointment over Bingley?
answer: She pretends not to care whether he returns, though she insists he used Jane ill and predicts Jane will die of a broken heart.
evidence: Nobody wants him to come. Though I shall always say that he used my daughter extremely ill

quote_text:
Well, Lizzy, and so the
Collinses live very comfortable, do they? Well, well, I only hope it
will last. And what sort of table do they keep? Charlotte is an
excellent manager, I dare say. If she is half as sharp as her mother,
she is saving enough. There is nothing extravagant in _their_
housekeeping, I dare say.
question: What does Mrs. Bennet turn the conversation to after discussing Jane?
answer: She asks about the Collinses' household and Charlotte's management, hoping to find something to criticize.
evidence: And what sort of table do they keep? Charlotte is an excellent manager, I dare say.

quote_text: No, nothing at all.
question: How does Elizabeth answer her mother's suggestion that the Collinses are extravagant?
answer: She agrees that there is no extravagance in their housekeeping.
evidence: There is nothing extravagant in their housekeeping, I dare say.

quote_text:
A great deal of good management, depend upon it. Yes, yes. _They_ will
take care not to outrun their income. _They_ will never be distressed
for money. Well, much good may it do them! And so, I suppose, they often
talk of having Longbourn when your father is dead. They look upon it
quite as their own, I dare say, whenever that happens.
question: What does Mrs. Bennet imply about the Collinses and Longbourn?
answer: She says they will manage carefully and probably already regard Longbourn as theirs after Mr. Bennet's death.
evidence: They look upon it quite as their own, I dare say, whenever that happens.

quote_text: It was a subject which they could not mention before me.
question: Why does Elizabeth say the Collinses could not mention Longbourn before her?
answer: Because it would be indelicate to talk of inheriting Longbourn in front of the daughter who might have married Mr. Collins.
evidence: It was a subject which they could not mention before me.

quote_text:
No. It would have been strange if they had. But I make no doubt, they
often talk of it between themselves. Well, if they can be easy with an
estate that is not lawfully their own, so much the better. _I_ should be
ashamed of having one that was only entailed on me.
question: What does Mrs. Bennet suspect the Collinses do privately regarding Longbourn?
answer: She believes they often talk of inheriting it and are easy with an estate not lawfully their own.
evidence: they often talk of it between themselves.

quote_text:
I am sure, I cried for two days together when Colonel
Millar's regiment went away. I thought I should have broke my heart.
question: Why does Mrs. Bennet tell the story about Colonel Millar's regiment?
answer: She is sharing the girls' grief over the militia's departure and claims she suffered similarly years ago.
evidence: she remembered what she had herself endured on a similar occasion, five and twenty years ago.

quote_text: I am sure I shall break _mine_,
question: How does Lydia respond to her mother's claim of heartbreak?
answer: She declares that her own heart will break when the regiment leaves.
evidence: I am sure I shall break mine

quote_text: If one could but go to Brighton!
question: What does Mrs. Bennet wish for as a relief from the regiment's departure?
answer: She wishes they could go to Brighton, thinking sea-bathing would restore her.
evidence: A little sea-bathing would set me up for ever.

quote_text:
Oh, yes!--if one could but go to Brighton! But papa is so
disagreeable.
question: Why does Lydia blame her father in this exchange?
answer: Because he refuses to take the family to Brighton, which she believes would be delightful.
evidence: if one could but go to Brighton! But papa is so disagreeable.

quote_text: And my aunt Philips is sure it would do _me_ a great deal of good,
question: What does Kitty add to the wish to go to Brighton?
answer: She says Aunt Philips believes sea-bathing would benefit Kitty too.
evidence: And my aunt Philips is sure it would do me a great deal of good

quote_text:
I cannot see why Mrs. Forster should not ask _me_ as well as Lydia, though I am _not_ her particular friend. I have just as much
right to be asked as she has, and more too, for I am two years older.
question: Why is Kitty upset about Lydia's Brighton invitation?
answer: She feels she has as much right to be invited and is older than Lydia.
evidence: I have just as much right to be asked as she has, and more too, for I am two years older.

quote_text:
Lydia will never be easy till she has exposed herself in some public
place or other, and we can never expect her to do it with so little
expense or inconvenience to her family as under the present
circumstances.
question: What is Mr. Bennet's reason for allowing Lydia to go to Brighton?
answer: He thinks she will inevitably expose herself somewhere, and Brighton is the cheapest and most convenient place for it.
evidence: we can never expect her to do it with so little expense or inconvenience to her family as under the present circumstances.

quote_text:
If you were aware, of the very great disadvantage to
us all, which must arise from the public notice of Lydia's unguarded and
imprudent manner; nay, which has already arisen from it, I am sure you
would judge differently in the affair.
question: What does Elizabeth warn her father about Lydia's behavior?
answer: She says Lydia's unguarded manner already damages the family's respectability and will worsen unless checked.
evidence: which must arise from the public notice of Lydia's unguarded and imprudent manner

quote_text:
Already arisen! What, has she frightened away
some of your lovers? Poor little Lizzy! But do not be cast down. Such
squeamish youths as cannot bear to be connected with a little absurdity,
are not worth a regret. Come, let me see the list of the pitiful fellows
who have been kept aloof by Lydia's folly.
question: How does Mr. Bennet tease Elizabeth about her warning?
answer: He jokingly asks whether Lydia has scared away Elizabeth's suitors and says such squeamish youths are not worth regretting.
evidence: What, has she frightened away some of your lovers?

quote_text:
Indeed you are mistaken. I have no such injuries to resent. It is not
of peculiar, but of general evils, which I am now complaining. Our
importance, our respectability in the world, must be affected by the
wild volatility, the assurance and disdain of all restraint which mark
Lydia's character. Excuse me--for I must speak plainly. If you, my dear
father, will not take the trouble of checking her exuberant spirits, and
of teaching her that her present pursuits are not to be the business of
her life, she will soon be beyond the reach of amendment. Her character
will be fixed, and she will, at sixteen, be the most determined flirt
that ever made herself and her family ridiculous. A flirt too, in the
worst and meanest degree of flirtation; without any attraction beyond
youth and a tolerable person; and from the ignorance and emptiness of
her mind, wholly unable to ward off any portion of that universal
contempt which her rage for admiration will excite. In this danger Kitty
is also comprehended. She will follow wherever Lydia leads. Vain,
ignorant, idle, and absolutely uncontrouled! Oh! my dear father, can you
suppose it possible that they will not be censured and despised wherever
they are known, and that their sisters will not be often involved in the
disgrace?
question: What is Elizabeth's real concern in warning her father about Lydia?
answer: She is worried about general family disgrace from Lydia's wild behavior, not about her own lost suitors.
evidence: It is not of peculiar, but of general evils, which I am now complaining.

quote_text:
Do not make yourself uneasy, my love. Wherever you and Jane are known,
you must be respected and valued; and you will not appear to less
advantage for having a couple of--or I may say, three very silly
sisters. We shall have no peace at Longbourn if Lydia does not go to
Brighton. Let her go then. Colonel Forster is a sensible man, and will
keep her out of any real mischief; and she is luckily too poor to be an
object of prey to any body. At Brighton she will be of less importance
even as a common flirt than she has been here. The officers will find
women better worth their notice. Let us hope, therefore, that her being
there may teach her her own insignificance. At any rate, she cannot grow
many degrees worse, without authorizing us to lock her up for the rest
of her life.
question: How does Mr. Bennet reassure Elizabeth about the family's reputation?
answer: He says she and Jane will be respected wherever they are known, despite having silly sisters, and lets Lydia go.
evidence: Wherever you and Jane are known, you must be respected and valued

quote_text:
How long did you
say that he was at Rosings?
question: Why does Wickham ask Elizabeth how long Colonel Fitzwilliam stayed at Rosings?
answer: He is surprised and uneasy to learn that Darcy and Fitzwilliam were near Elizabeth, and wants to gauge what she may have learned.
evidence: He looked surprised, displeased, alarmed

quote_text: Nearly three weeks.
question: What effect does Elizabeth's answer about Colonel Fitzwilliam's stay have on Wickham?
answer: It increases his alarm, prompting him to ask more about Darcy and whether Elizabeth saw him often.
evidence: He looked surprised, displeased, alarmed

quote_text: And you saw him frequently?
question: Why does Wickham press Elizabeth about how often she saw Colonel Fitzwilliam at Rosings?
answer: He is unsettled by her account of Rosings and wants to learn how much she knows about Darcy's visit.
evidence: He looked surprised, displeased, alarmed; but with a moment's recollection and a returning smile

quote_text: Yes, almost every day.
question: What does Elizabeth's willingness to confirm frequent meetings with Colonel Fitzwilliam suggest about her attitude toward Wickham now?
answer: She is no longer trying to spare him and answers in a way that tests his unease.
evidence: so little was Elizabeth disposed to part from him in good humour

quote_text: His manners are very different from his cousin's.
question: Why does Wickham introduce a comparison between Colonel Fitzwilliam's manners and his cousin's?
answer: He is fishing for Elizabeth's opinion of Darcy after hearing that she liked Fitzwilliam.
evidence: asked her how she had liked him. Her answer was warmly in his favour.

quote_text: Yes, very different. But I think Mr. Darcy improves on acquaintance.
question: Why does Elizabeth's remark that Mr. Darcy improves on acquaintance startle Wickham?
answer: It hints that her former contempt has softened, threatening his account of Darcy's character.
evidence: cried Wickham with a look which did not escape her

quote_text:
Indeed! And pray
may I ask? Is it in
address that he improves? Has he deigned to add ought of civility to his
ordinary style? for I dare not hope, that he is improved in essentials.
question: What does Wickham fear when he asks whether Darcy has improved 'in essentials'?
answer: He fears Elizabeth has learned something that undermines his story of Darcy's character.
evidence: Wickham looked as if scarcely knowing whether to rejoice over her words, or to distrust their meaning.

quote_text:
Oh, no! In essentials, I believe, he is very much
what he ever was.
question: How does Elizabeth's answer about Darcy's 'essentials' affect Wickham?
answer: It leaves him uncertain whether to be relieved or suspicious because her meaning is not clear.
evidence: Wickham looked as if scarcely knowing whether to rejoice over her words, or to distrust their meaning.

quote_text:
When I said that he improved on acquaintance, I did not mean that
either his mind or manners were in a state of improvement, but that from
knowing him better, his disposition was better understood.
question: What does Elizabeth mean by saying that Mr. Darcy improves on acquaintance?
answer: She means she now understands his disposition better, not that his mind or manners have changed.
evidence: from knowing him better, his disposition was better understood.

quote_text:
You, who so well know my feelings towards Mr. Darcy, will readily
comprehend how sincerely I must rejoice that he is wise enough to assume
even the _appearance_ of what is right. His pride, in that direction,
may be of service, if not to himself, to many others, for it must deter
him from such foul misconduct as I have suffered by. I only fear that
the sort of cautiousness, to which you, I imagine, have been alluding,
is merely adopted on his visits to his aunt, of whose good opinion and
judgment he stands much in awe. His fear of her, has always operated, I
know, when they were together; and a good deal is to be imputed to his
wish of forwarding the match with Miss De Bourgh, which I am certain he
has very much at heart.
question: How does Wickham reinterpret Darcy's improved behavior toward Elizabeth?
answer: He claims it is merely caution adopted to please Lady Catherine and promote the match with Miss de Bourgh.
evidence: a good deal is to be imputed to his wish of forwarding the match with Miss De Bourgh

quote_text:
But it is fortunate, that I have something to wish for.
Were the whole arrangement complete, my disappointment would be certain.
But here, by carrying with me one ceaseless source of regret in my
sister's absence, I may reasonably hope to have all my expectations of
pleasure realized. A scheme of which every part promises delight, can
never be successful; and general disappointment is only warded off by
the defence of some little peculiar vexation.
question: Why does Elizabeth consider it fortunate that she still has something to wish for?
answer: She believes a small, particular regret helps ward off general disappointment.
evidence: general disappointment is only warded off by the defence of some little peculiar vexation.

quote_text:
But surely, I may enter his county with impunity,
and rob it of a few petrified spars without his perceiving me.
question: Why does Elizabeth reassure herself about entering Derbyshire?
answer: The tour has been changed to Derbyshire, Darcy's county, and she hopes to avoid encountering him.
evidence: It was impossible for her to see the word without thinking of Pemberley and its owner.

quote_text:
My love, should not you like to see a place of which you have heard so
much? A place too, with which so many of your
acquaintance are connected. Wickham passed all his youth there, you
know.
question: Why does Mrs. Gardiner think Elizabeth would like to see Pemberley?
answer: She says Elizabeth has heard much of it and that many of her acquaintance, especially Wickham, are connected with it.
evidence: A place too, with which so many of your acquaintance are connected. Wickham passed all his youth there

quote_text:
If it were merely a fine house
richly furnished, I should not care about it myself; but the
grounds are delightful. They have some of the finest woods in the
country.
question: What reason does Mrs. Gardiner give for wanting to visit Pemberley despite Elizabeth's reluctance?
answer: She cares less for the furnished house than for the celebrated grounds and woods.
evidence: but the grounds are delightful. They have some of the finest woods in the country.

quote_text:
And of this place, I might have been mistress! With
these rooms I might now have been familiarly acquainted! Instead of
viewing them as a stranger, I might have rejoiced in them as my own, and
welcomed to them as visitors my uncle and aunt.--But no, that could never be: my uncle and aunt would have been lost
to me: I should not have been allowed to invite them.
question: What mixed feeling does Elizabeth have while touring Pemberley?
answer: She briefly imagines being its mistress but then recalls she could never have invited her uncle and aunt there.
evidence: my uncle and aunt would have been lost to me: I should not have been allowed to invite them.

quote_text:
but we expect him to-morrow, with a
large party of friends.
question: Why is Elizabeth relieved by Mrs. Reynolds's news about Mr. Darcy's return?
answer: She learns he is absent that day, so their visit can proceed without meeting him.
evidence: How rejoiced was Elizabeth that their own journey had not by any circumstance been delayed a day!

quote_text: He is now gone into the army, but I am afraid he has turned out very wild.
question: What does Mrs. Reynolds's remark about Wickham reveal about his reputation at Pemberley?
answer: The housekeeper believes he has gone into the army and become wild, contradicting his polished self-presentation.
evidence: but I am afraid he has turned out very wild.

quote_text:
And that, is my master--and very like him. It was drawn at the same time as the
other--about eight years ago.
question: Whose miniature does Mrs. Reynolds identify as her master, and how does she describe it?
answer: She identifies Darcy's picture and says it is very like him, drawn about eight years earlier.
evidence: is my master--and very like him. It was drawn at the same time as the other

quote_text:
I have heard much of your master's fine person, it is a handsome face. But, Lizzy, you can tell
us whether it is like or not.
question: Why does Mrs. Gardiner turn to Elizabeth after praising Darcy's portrait?
answer: She knows Elizabeth has actually met Darcy and can judge whether the likeness is accurate.
evidence: But, Lizzy, you can tell us whether it is like or not.

quote_text: Does that young lady know Mr. Darcy?
question: Why does Mrs. Reynolds's manner toward Elizabeth change after hearing she knows Darcy?
answer: She becomes more respectful, treating Elizabeth as someone connected with her master.
evidence: Mrs. Reynolds's respect for Elizabeth seemed to increase on this intimation of her knowing her master.

quote_text: A little.
question: How does Elizabeth downplay her acquaintance with Darcy to the housekeeper?
answer: She answers evasively and colors, unwilling to reveal how well she knows him.
evidence: Elizabeth coloured, and said

quote_text: And do not you think him a very handsome gentleman, Ma'am?
question: Why does Mrs. Reynolds ask Elizabeth whether she thinks Darcy handsome?
answer: She is eager to praise her master and expects Elizabeth to agree with her admiration.
evidence: had evidently great pleasure in talking of her master and his sister.

quote_text: Yes, very handsome.
question: Why does Elizabeth simply agree that Darcy is handsome?
answer: She is caught between honesty and embarrassment before the admiring housekeeper.
evidence: Yes, very handsome.

quote_text:
I am sure _I_ know none so handsome; but in the gallery up stairs you
will see a finer, larger picture of him than this. This room was my late
master's favourite room, and these miniatures are just as they used to
be then. He was very fond of them.
question: What does Mrs. Reynolds offer to show the visitors after praising Darcy's looks?
answer: She directs them to a larger portrait of Darcy in the gallery upstairs.
evidence: in the gallery up stairs you will see a finer, larger picture of him than this.

quote_text: And is Miss Darcy as handsome as her brother?
question: Why does Mr. Gardiner ask about Miss Darcy's looks?
answer: The housekeeper has been praising the family, and he encourages her talk about Darcy's sister.
evidence: Mr. Gardiner, whose manners were easy and pleasant, encouraged her communicativeness by his questions

quote_text:
Oh! yes--the handsomest young lady that ever was seen; and so
accomplished!--She plays and sings all day long. In the next room is a
new instrument just come down for her--a present from my master; she
comes here to-morrow with him.
question: How does Mrs. Reynolds describe Miss Darcy?
answer: She calls her extremely handsome and accomplished, saying she plays and sings constantly.
evidence: the handsomest young lady that ever was seen; and so accomplished!

quote_text: Is your master much at Pemberley in the course of the year?
question: What does Mr. Gardiner's question about Darcy's time at Pemberley draw out?
answer: It invites the housekeeper to praise Darcy's character and attachment to the estate.
evidence: Mrs. Reynolds, either from pride or attachment, had evidently great pleasure in talking of her master

quote_text:
Not so much as I could wish, Sir; but I dare say he may spend half his
time here; and Miss Darcy is always down for the summer months.
question: What does Mrs. Reynolds reveal about Darcy's habits at Pemberley?
answer: He spends about half the year there, and his sister stays for the summer months.
evidence: I dare say he may spend half his time here; and Miss Darcy is always down for the summer months.

quote_text: Except, when she goes to Ramsgate.
question: What does Elizabeth privately recall about Miss Darcy's summer plans?
answer: She remembers Miss Darcy went to Ramsgate, where Wickham tried to elope with her.
evidence: when she goes to Ramsgate.

quote_text: If your master would marry, you might see more of him.
question: Why does Mr. Gardiner suggest Darcy should marry?
answer: He teases the housekeeper that a wife would keep Darcy at Pemberley more often.
evidence: you might see more of him.

quote_text:
Yes, Sir; but I do not know when _that_ will be. I do not know who is
good enough for him.
question: What does the housekeeper's reply about Darcy marrying show about her view of him?
answer: She thinks no woman is good enough for him and speaks with devoted admiration.
evidence: I do not know who is good enough for him.

quote_text:
It is
very much to his credit, I am sure, that you should think so.
question: Why does Elizabeth compliment Mrs. Reynolds on her high opinion of Darcy?
answer: She is struck by such unusual praise and acknowledges it as a credit to Darcy.
evidence: Elizabeth thought this was going pretty far

quote_text:
I say no more than the truth, and what every body will say that knows
him, I have never had a cross word from him in my life, and I have known him
ever since he was four years old.
question: What makes Mrs. Reynolds's praise of Darcy especially surprising to Elizabeth?
answer: The housekeeper has known Darcy since childhood and says she never had a cross word from him.
evidence: I have never had a cross word from him in my life, and I have known him ever since he was four years old.

quote_text:
There are very few people of whom so much can be said. You are lucky in
having such a master.
question: How does Mr. Gardiner respond to the housekeeper's extraordinary praise of Darcy?
answer: He agrees such praise is rare and says she is lucky to have such a master.
evidence: There are very few people of whom so much can be said.

quote_text:
Yes, Sir, I know I am. If I was to go through the world, I could not
meet with a better. But I have always observed, that they who are
good-natured when children, are good-natured when they grow up; and he
was always the sweetest-tempered, most generous-hearted, boy in the
world.
question: What does Mrs. Reynolds say about Darcy's temperament as a boy?
answer: She claims he was always the sweetest-tempered, most generous-hearted boy.
evidence: he was always the sweetest-tempered, most generous-hearted, boy in the world.

quote_text: Can this be Mr. Darcy!
question: Why is Elizabeth astonished by the housekeeper's account of Darcy?
answer: It contradicts her fixed opinion that Darcy was not good-tempered.
evidence: That he was not a good-tempered man, had been her firmest opinion.

quote_text: His father was an excellent man,
question: How does Mrs. Gardiner steer the housekeeper's praise toward Darcy's father?
answer: She affirms the late Mr. Darcy's goodness, prompting further praise of the son.
evidence: His father was an excellent man

quote_text:
Yes, Ma'am, that he was indeed; and his son will be just like him--just
as affable to the poor.
question: What does Mrs. Reynolds predict about Darcy's character compared with his father's?
answer: She says he will be just like his father, especially in being affable to the poor.
evidence: his son will be just like him--just as affable to the poor.

quote_text:
He is the best landlord, and the best master, that ever
lived. Not like the wild young men now-a-days, who think of nothing but
themselves. There is not one of his tenants or servants but what will
give him a good name. Some people call him proud; but I am sure I never
saw any thing of it. To my fancy, it is only because he does not rattle
away like other young men.
question: How does Mrs. Reynolds defend Darcy against the charge of pride?
answer: She says he is the best landlord and master and that his supposed pride is only reserve.
evidence: Some people call him proud; but I am sure I never saw any thing of it.

quote_text: In what an amiable light does this place him!
question: What effect does the housekeeper's testimony have on Elizabeth's view of Darcy?
answer: It makes her see him in a newly amiable light and reconsider her former prejudice.
evidence: Elizabeth listened, wondered, doubted, and was impatient for more.

quote_text:
This fine account of him, is not
quite consistent with his behaviour to our poor friend.
question: Why does Mrs. Gardiner find the housekeeper's praise hard to reconcile?
answer: It clashes with what she believes about Darcy's cruel treatment of Wickham.
evidence: is not quite consistent with his behaviour to our poor friend.

quote_text: Perhaps we might be deceived.
question: What does Elizabeth suggest about their earlier judgment of Darcy's treatment of Wickham?
answer: She hints that their information about Wickham may have been wrong and Darcy misjudged.
evidence: Perhaps we might be deceived.

quote_text: That is not very likely; our authority was too good.
question: Why does Mrs. Gardiner refuse to doubt the earlier account of Mr. Darcy's conduct?
answer: She thinks their previous informant was too reliable to dismiss, even though Pemberley's housekeeper praises Darcy.
evidence: our authority was too good.

quote_text: He is certainly a good brother,
question: What has just led Elizabeth to call Mr. Darcy a good brother?
answer: The housekeeper has shown them a room newly fitted up to please Miss Darcy, revealing Darcy's kindness to his sister.
evidence: it was but just done, to give pleasure to Miss Darcy

quote_text:
And this is always the way with him, Whatever
can give his sister any pleasure, is sure to be done in a moment. There
is nothing he would not do for her.
question: What does the housekeeper mean by saying this is always Mr. Darcy's way?
answer: She means Darcy invariably does anything he can to give his sister pleasure.
evidence: Whatever can give his sister any pleasure, is sure to be done in a moment.

quote_text: delightful, charming,
question: Why does Elizabeth stop after beginning to praise Pemberley to Mr. Darcy?
answer: She suddenly fears her praise might be taken as fishing for his approval or as a mischievous hint.
evidence: she fancied that praise of Pemberley from her, might be mischievously construed.

quote_text:
What will be his surprise, when he knows who they are! He takes them now for people of
fashion.
question: Why does Elizabeth expect Mr. Darcy to be surprised when he learns who her companions are?
answer: He is seeking an introduction while supposing them to be fashionable strangers, not Elizabeth's uncle and aunt in trade.
evidence: He takes them now for people of fashion.

quote_text:
Why is he so altered? From
what can it proceed? It cannot be for _me_, it cannot be for _my_ sake
that his manners are thus softened. My reproofs at Hunsford could not
work such a change as this. It is impossible that he should still love
me.
question: Why does Elizabeth doubt that Mr. Darcy's softened manners are caused by regard for her?
answer: She thinks her reproofs at Hunsford could not have produced such a change and cannot believe he still loves her.
evidence: My reproofs at Hunsford could not work such a change as this.

quote_text:
for your housekeeper, informed us that
you would certainly not be here till to-morrow; and indeed, before we
left Bakewell, we understood that you were not immediately expected in
the country.
question: Why does Elizabeth mention the housekeeper when explaining why she is at Pemberley?
answer: She wants Darcy to know she had been assured he was absent before she came, so her visit was not designed to meet him.
evidence: she wished him to know that she had been assured of his absence before she came

quote_text:
They
will join me early to-morrow, and among them are some
who will claim an acquaintance with you,--Mr. Bingley and his sisters. There is also one other person in the party, who more particularly wishes to be known to you,--Will you allow
me, or do I ask too much, to introduce my sister to your acquaintance
during your stay at Lambton?
question: What does Darcy reveal when he says his party will join him tomorrow?
answer: He reveals that Bingley and his sisters will soon arrive, and he asks permission to introduce his sister to Elizabeth.
evidence: among them are some who will claim an acquaintance with you,--Mr. Bingley and his sisters.

quote_text: He is perfectly well behaved, polite, and unassuming,
question: What behavior prompts Mr. Gardiner to call Mr. Darcy polite and unassuming?
answer: Darcy has just been strikingly civil to the Gardiners at Pemberley, even inviting Mr. Gardiner to fish there.
evidence: Mr. Darcy invite him, with the greatest civility, to fish there as often as he chose

quote_text:
There _is_ something a little stately in him to be sure, but it is confined to his air, and is not unbecoming. I can now
say with the housekeeper, that though some people may call him proud,
_I_ have seen nothing of it.
question: How does Mrs. Gardiner explain away Darcy's stateliness after meeting him?
answer: She says his stateliness is only in his air and not unbecoming, since she saw no actual pride.
evidence: though some people may call him proud, I have seen nothing of it.

quote_text:
I was never more surprised than by his behaviour to us. It was more
than civil; it was really attentive; and there was no necessity for such
attention. His acquaintance with Elizabeth was very trifling.
question: Why is Mr. Gardiner surprised by Mr. Darcy's attentions to them?
answer: Because Darcy barely knew Elizabeth, yet treated her relatives with more than mere civility.
evidence: His acquaintance with Elizabeth was very trifling.

quote_text:
To be sure, Lizzy, he is not so handsome as Wickham;
or rather he has not Wickham's countenance, for his features are
perfectly good. But how came you to tell us that he was so
disagreeable?
question: What does Mrs. Gardiner ask Elizabeth to explain after seeing Darcy at Pemberley?
answer: She asks why Elizabeth had described Darcy as so disagreeable when he is actually handsome and pleasant.
evidence: how came you to tell us that he was so disagreeable?

quote_text:
But perhaps he may be a little whimsical in his civilities, Your great men often are; and therefore I shall not take him
at his word about fishing, as he might change his mind another day, and
warn me off his grounds.
question: Why does Mr. Gardiner hesitate to rely on Darcy's invitation to fish?
answer: He suspects great men like Darcy may be whimsical and could change their minds later.
evidence: I shall not take him at his word about fishing

quote_text:
From what we have seen of him, I really
should not have thought that he could have behaved in so cruel a way by
any body, as he has done by poor Wickham. He has not an ill-natured
look. On the contrary, there is something pleasing about his mouth when
he speaks. And there is something of dignity in his countenance, that
would not give one an unfavourable idea of his heart. But to be sure,
the good lady who shewed us the house, did give him a most flaming
character! I could hardly help laughing aloud sometimes. But he is a
liberal master, I suppose, and _that_ in the eye of a servant
comprehends every virtue.
question: Why does Mrs. Gardiner begin to doubt that Darcy could have treated Wickham cruelly?
answer: Darcy's pleasing looks and manner, plus the housekeeper's praise, do not seem to fit Wickham's account.
evidence: He has not an ill-natured look.

quote_text:
It
is above eight months. We have not met since the 26th of November, when
we were all dancing together at Netherfield.
question: What does Bingley's exact memory of his last meeting with the Bennets suggest to Elizabeth?
answer: It suggests he still remembers Jane and their time together with particular tenderness.
evidence: Elizabeth was pleased to find his memory so exact

quote_text:
Pray, Miss Eliza, are not the ----shire militia removed from Meryton?
They must be a great loss to _your_ family.
question: Why does Miss Bingley bring up the militia in front of Mr. Darcy?
answer: She wants to discompose Elizabeth by hinting at Wickham and her family's connection with the officers.
evidence: she had merely intended to discompose Elizabeth, by bringing forward the idea of a man to whom she believed her partial

quote_text:
How very ill Eliza Bennet looks this morning, Mr. Darcy, I
never in my life saw any one so much altered as she is since the winter.
She is grown so brown and coarse! Louisa and I were agreeing that we
should not have known her again.
question: Why does Miss Bingley criticize Elizabeth's looks to Darcy?
answer: Jealous of Darcy's admiration, she hopes to lessen his good opinion of Elizabeth.
evidence: Persuaded as Miss Bingley was that Darcy admired Elizabeth, this was not the best method of recommending herself

quote_text:
For my own part, I must confess that I never could see
any beauty in her. Her face is too thin; her complexion has no
brilliancy; and her features are not at all handsome. Her nose wants
character; there is nothing marked in its lines. Her teeth are
tolerable, but not out of the common way; and as for her eyes, which
have sometimes been called so fine, I never could perceive any thing
extraordinary in them. They have a sharp, shrewish look, which I do not
like at all; and in her air altogether, there is a self-sufficiency
without fashion, which is intolerable.
question: What does Miss Bingley's detailed fault-finding with Elizabeth's appearance reveal?
answer: It reveals her jealousy and her wish to persuade Darcy that Elizabeth has no beauty.
evidence: I never could see any beauty in her.

quote_text:
I remember, when we first knew her in Hertfordshire, how amazed we all
were to find that she was a reputed beauty; and I particularly recollect
your saying one night, after they had been dining at Netherfield, But afterwards she
seemed to improve on you, and I believe you thought her rather pretty at
one time.
question: Why does Miss Bingley quote Darcy's earlier insult about Elizabeth?
answer: She wants to remind him of his former low opinion and undermine his present admiration.
evidence: _She_ a beauty!--I should as soon call her mother a wit.

quote_text:
Yes, but _that_
was only when I first knew her, for it is many months since I have
considered her as one of the handsomest women of my acquaintance.
question: What does Darcy's reply to Miss Bingley reveal about his present feelings for Elizabeth?
answer: He openly contradicts her by saying he now considers Elizabeth one of the handsomest women he knows.
evidence: it is many months since I have considered her as one of the handsomest women of my acquaintance.

quote_text: Oh! where, where is my uncle?
question: Why is Elizabeth desperately looking for her uncle after reading Jane's letters?
answer: Lydia has eloped with Wickham, and Elizabeth knows Mr. Gardiner's help is urgently needed.
evidence: she was gone off to Scotland with one of his officers; to own the truth, with Wickham!

quote_text:
I beg your pardon, but I must leave you.
I must find Mr. Gardiner this moment, on business that cannot be
delayed; I have not an instant to lose.
question: What urgent business makes Elizabeth unable to stay with Darcy?
answer: She must find Mr. Gardiner at once because Lydia's elopement requires immediate family action.
evidence: I must find Mr. Gardiner this moment, on business that cannot be delayed

quote_text:
Good God! what is the matter? I will not detain you a minute,
but let me, or let the servant, go after Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner. You are
not well enough;--you cannot go yourself.
question: How does Darcy react when he sees Elizabeth's distress?
answer: He is alarmed and offers to fetch the Gardiners himself or send a servant, saying she is too unwell to go.
evidence: let me, or let the servant, go after Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner.

quote_text:
Let me call your maid. Is there nothing you could take, to give you
present relief?--A glass of wine;--shall I get you one?--You are very
ill.
question: What do Darcy's offers of a maid and wine show about him here?
answer: They show genuine compassionate concern for Elizabeth's health despite the awkward situation.
evidence: Is there nothing you could take, to give you present relief?

quote_text:
No, I thank you; There
is nothing the matter with me. I am quite well. I am only distressed by
some dreadful news which I have just received from Longbourn.
question: Why does Elizabeth say she is quite well despite looking ill?
answer: She is not physically ill; she is distressed by dreadful news from Longbourn.
evidence: I am only distressed by some dreadful news which I have just received from Longbourn.

quote_text:
I have just had a letter from
Jane, with such dreadful news. It cannot be concealed from any one. My
youngest sister has left all her friends--has eloped;--has thrown
herself into the power of--of Mr. Wickham. They are gone off together
from Brighton. _You_ know him too well to doubt the rest. She has no
money, no connections, nothing that can tempt him to--she is lost for
ever.
question: Why does Elizabeth tell Darcy about Lydia's elopement despite the disgrace?
answer: She is overwhelmed and knows the scandal cannot be concealed; Lydia has thrown herself into Wickham's power.
evidence: My youngest sister has left all her friends--has eloped

quote_text:
When I consider, that _I_ might have prevented it!--_I_ who knew
what he was. Had I but explained some part of it only--some part of what
