I learnt, to my own family! Had his character been known, this could not
have happened. But it is all, all too late now.
question: What does Elizabeth blame herself for in the midst of the crisis?
answer: She blames herself for not warning her family about Wickham's true character, which might have prevented the elopement.
evidence: Had his character been known, this could not have happened.

quote_text:
I am grieved, indeed, grieved--shocked. But is it
certain, absolutely certain?
question: Why does Darcy ask whether the news is absolutely certain?
answer: He is shocked and wants confirmation before accepting that Lydia has run off with Wickham.
evidence: But is it certain, absolutely certain?

quote_text:
Oh yes!--They left Brighton together on Sunday night, and were traced
almost to London, but not beyond; they are certainly not gone to
Scotland.
question: What detail makes Elizabeth certain Lydia has not gone to Scotland to marry?
answer: The couple was traced toward London but not beyond, so there is no sign they went to Scotland.
evidence: they are certainly not gone to Scotland.

quote_text: And what has been done, what has been attempted, to recover her?
question: Why does Darcy ask what has been done to recover Lydia?
answer: He is trying to understand the situation and what practical steps the family has already taken.
evidence: And what has been done, what has been attempted, to recover her?

quote_text:
My father is gone to London, and Jane has written to beg my uncle's
immediate assistance, and we shall be off, I hope, in half an hour. But
nothing can be done; I know very well that nothing can be done. How is
such a man to be worked on? How are they even to be discovered? I have
not the smallest hope. It is every way horrible!
question: What plan does Elizabeth describe for dealing with Lydia's elopement?
answer: Her father has gone to London, Jane has asked Mr. Gardiner for help, and the family hopes to leave shortly.
evidence: My father is gone to London, and Jane has written to beg my uncle's immediate assistance

quote_text:
When _my_ eyes were opened to his real character.--Oh! had I known what
I ought, what I dared, to do! But I knew not--I was afraid of doing too
much. Wretched, wretched, mistake!
question: What mistake does Elizabeth regret most in hindsight?
answer: She regrets hesitating to expose Wickham's real character because she feared doing too much.
evidence: I was afraid of doing too much.

quote_text:
I am afraid you have been
long desiring my absence, nor have I any thing to plead in excuse of my
stay, but real, though unavailing, concern. Would to heaven that any
thing could be either said or done on my part, that might offer
consolation to such distress.--But I will not torment you with vain
wishes, which may seem purposely to ask for your thanks. This
unfortunate affair will, I fear, prevent my sister's having the pleasure
of seeing you at Pemberley to-day.
question: How does Darcy respond to Elizabeth's grief while trying not to intrude?
answer: He expresses real but unavailing concern, avoids empty consolation, and withdraws politely.
evidence: real, though unavailing, concern

quote_text:
Oh, yes. Be so kind as to apologize for us to Miss Darcy. Say that
urgent business calls us home immediately. Conceal the unhappy truth as
long as it is possible.--I know it cannot be long.
question: What does Elizabeth ask Darcy to tell Miss Darcy after canceling their Pemberley visit?
answer: She asks him to apologize and say urgent family business calls them home, while concealing the scandal as long as possible.
evidence: Conceal the unhappy truth as long as it is possible.

quote_text:
But what is to be
done about Pemberley? John told us Mr. Darcy was
here when you sent for us;--was it so?
question: Why does Mrs. Gardiner ask about Pemberley after the hurried return?
answer: She wonders how Elizabeth handled the canceled engagement after Darcy unexpectedly found her there.
evidence: John told us Mr. Darcy was here when you sent for us;--was it so?

quote_text:
Yes; and I told him we should not be able to keep our engagement.
_That_ is all settled.
question: What does Elizabeth mean when she says their Pemberley engagement is all settled?
answer: She means she has already told Darcy that they cannot keep their dinner engagement.
evidence: I told him we should not be able to keep our engagement.

quote_text: That is all settled;
question: How does Mrs. Gardiner react to Elizabeth's casual claim that everything is settled?
answer: She repeats the phrase doubtfully as she hurries to prepare, suspecting more passed between Elizabeth and Darcy.
evidence: repeated the other, as she ran into her room to prepare.

quote_text:
And are they upon such terms as for her to disclose the real
truth! Oh, that I knew how it was!
question: What does Mrs. Gardiner privately wonder about Elizabeth and Darcy?
answer: She wonders whether they are close enough for Elizabeth to have told Darcy the real reason for their sudden departure.
evidence: And are they upon such terms as for her to disclose the real truth!

quote_text:
I have been thinking it over again, Elizabeth, and really, upon serious consideration, I am much
more inclined than I was to judge as your eldest sister does of the
matter. It appears to me so very unlikely, that any young man should
form such a design against a girl who is by no means unprotected or
friendless, and who was actually staying in his colonel's family, that I
am strongly inclined to hope the best. Could he expect that her friends
would not step forward? Could he expect to be noticed again by the
regiment, after such an affront to Colonel Forster? His temptation is
not adequate to the risk.
question: What hopeful view of Lydia's situation does Mr. Gardiner offer in the carriage?
answer: He thinks Wickham is unlikely to risk such a scheme because Lydia is not unprotected or friendless, so he hopes for the best.
evidence: I am strongly inclined to hope the best.

quote_text: Do you really think so?
question: Why does Elizabeth brighten when her uncle gives his opinion?
answer: His hope that Wickham may still marry Lydia gives her a moment of relief.
evidence: brightening up for a moment

quote_text:
Upon my word, I begin to be of your uncle's
opinion. It is really too great a violation of decency, honour, and
interest, for him to be guilty of it. I cannot think so very ill of
Wickham. Can you, yourself, Lizzy, so wholly give him up, as to believe
him capable of it?
question: Why does Mrs. Gardiner begin by agreeing with her husband about Wickham's likely intentions?
answer: She thinks Wickham's elopement is too dishonourable and risky to be believed, so she shares her husband's hopeful view.
evidence: I begin to be of your uncle's opinion. It is really too great a violation of decency

quote_text:
Not perhaps of neglecting his own interest. But of every other neglect
I can believe him capable. If, indeed, it should be so! But I dare not
hope it. Why should they not go on to Scotland, if that had been the
case?
question: What distinction does Elizabeth make about Wickham's capacity for neglect?
answer: She thinks he would not neglect his own interest but could neglect every other duty.
evidence: Not perhaps of neglecting his own interest. But of every other neglect I can believe him capable.

quote_text:
In the first place, there is no absolute proof
that they are not gone to Scotland.
question: What reason does Mr. Gardiner give for hoping Lydia and Wickham may still have gone to Scotland?
answer: He says there is no absolute proof that they did not go to Scotland.
evidence: there is no absolute proof that they are not gone to Scotland

quote_text:
Oh! but their removing from the chaise into an hackney coach is such a
presumption! And, besides, no traces of them were to be found on the
Barnet road.
question: What evidence makes Elizabeth doubt that the couple went on to Scotland?
answer: They left the chaise for a hackney coach, and no traces were found on the Barnet road.
evidence: their removing from the chaise into an hackney coach is such a presumption

quote_text:
Well, then--supposing them to be in London. They may be there, though
for the purpose of concealment, for no more exceptionable purpose. It is
not likely that money should be very abundant on either side; and it
might strike them that they could be more economically, though less
expeditiously, married in London, than in Scotland.
question: How does Mr. Gardiner explain the couple's possible presence in London without assuming a wicked design?
answer: He suggests they may have chosen a private London marriage because it was cheaper, though slower than Scotland.
evidence: they could be more economically, though less expeditiously, married in London, than in Scotland

quote_text:
But why all this secrecy? Why any fear of detection? Why must their
marriage be private? Oh! no, no, this is not likely. His most particular
friend, you see by Jane's account, was persuaded of his never intending
to marry her. Wickham will never marry a woman without some money. He
cannot afford it. And what claims has Lydia, what attractions has she
beyond youth, health, and good humour, that could make him for her sake,
forego every chance of benefiting himself by marrying well? As to what
restraint the apprehension of disgrace in the corps might throw on a
dishonourable elopement with her, I am not able to judge; for I know
nothing of the effects that such a step might produce. But as to your
other objection, I am afraid it will hardly hold good. Lydia has no
brothers to step forward; and he might imagine, from my father's
behaviour, from his indolence and the little attention he has ever
seemed to give to what was going forward in his family, that _he_ would
do as little, and think as little about it, as any father could do, in
such a matter.
question: Why does Elizabeth think the secrecy surrounding the trip rules out an intended marriage?
answer: She believes Wickham will never marry a woman without money, so secrecy points to a dishonourable elopement.
evidence: Wickham will never marry a woman without some money. He cannot afford it.

quote_text:
But can you think that Lydia is so lost to every thing but love of him,
as to consent to live with him on any other terms than marriage?
question: What doubt does Mr. Gardiner raise about Lydia's willingness to compromise?
answer: He asks whether Lydia would consent to live with Wickham without marriage.
evidence: as to consent to live with him on any other terms than marriage

quote_text:
It does seem, and it is most shocking indeed, that a sister's sense of decency and virtue in such
a point should admit of doubt. But, really, I know not what to say.
Perhaps I am not doing her justice. But she is very young; she has never
been taught to think on serious subjects; and for the last half year,
nay, for a twelvemonth, she has been given up to nothing but amusement
and vanity. She has been allowed to dispose of her time in the most idle
and frivolous manner, and to adopt any opinions that came in her way.
Since the ----shire were first quartered in Meryton, nothing but love,
flirtation, and officers, have been in her head. She has been doing
every thing in her power by thinking and talking on the subject, to give
greater--what shall I call it? susceptibility to her feelings; which are
naturally lively enough. And we all know that Wickham has every charm of
person and address that can captivate a woman.
question: How does Elizabeth explain her fear that Lydia might have consented to a non-marital elopement?
answer: She says Lydia is young, untaught on serious subjects, and given up to amusement and vanity.
evidence: she is very young; she has never been taught to think on serious subjects

quote_text:
But you see that Jane, does not think so ill of
Wickham, as to believe him capable of the attempt.
question: Why does Mrs. Gardiner mention Jane's opinion of Wickham?
answer: She notes Jane is more charitable and does not believe Wickham capable of such an attempt.
evidence: does not think so ill of Wickham, as to believe him capable of the attempt

quote_text:
Of whom does Jane ever think ill? And who is there, whatever might be
their former conduct, that she would believe capable of such an attempt,
till it were proved against them? But Jane knows, as well as I do, what
Wickham really is. We both know that he has been profligate in every
sense of the word. That he has neither integrity nor honour. That he is
as false and deceitful, as he is insinuating.
question: How does Elizabeth defend Jane's charitable view while insisting Wickham is truly bad?
answer: She says Jane never thinks ill of anyone, but both sisters know Wickham is profligate and deceitful.
evidence: he has been profligate in every sense of the word

quote_text: And do you really know all this?
question: Why is Mrs. Gardiner so eager to hear Elizabeth's answer?
answer: She is curious how Elizabeth learned so much about Wickham's real character.
evidence: whose curiosity as to the mode of her intelligence was all alive

quote_text:
I do, indeed, I told you the other day,
of his infamous behaviour to Mr. Darcy; and you, yourself, when last at
Longbourn, heard in what manner he spoke of the man, who had behaved
with such forbearance and liberality towards him. And there are other
circumstances which I am not at liberty--which it is not worth while to
relate; but his lies about the whole Pemberley family are endless. From
what he said of Miss Darcy, I was thoroughly prepared to see a proud,
reserved, disagreeable girl. Yet he knew to the contrary himself. He
must know that she was as amiable and unpretending as we have found
her.
question: What sources does Elizabeth cite for her knowledge of Wickham's misconduct?
answer: She cites Wickham's infamous behaviour to Darcy, his lies about the Pemberley family, and other circumstances she cannot reveal.
evidence: I told you the other day, of his infamous behaviour to Mr. Darcy

quote_text:
But does Lydia know nothing of this? Can she be ignorant of what you
and Jane seem so well to understand?
question: What concern does Mrs. Gardiner raise about Lydia's knowledge of Wickham?
answer: She asks whether Lydia could be ignorant of the character flaws Elizabeth and Jane know.
evidence: Can she be ignorant of what you and Jane seem so well to understand?

quote_text:
Oh, yes!--that, that is the worst of all. Till I was in Kent, and saw
so much both of Mr. Darcy and his relation, Colonel Fitzwilliam, I was
ignorant of the truth myself. And when I returned home, the ----shire
was to leave Meryton in a week or fortnight's time. As that was the
case, neither Jane, to whom I related the whole, nor I, thought it
necessary to make our knowledge public; for of what use could it
apparently be to any one, that the good opinion which all the
neighbourhood had of him, should then be overthrown? And even when it
was settled that Lydia should go with Mrs. Forster, the necessity of
opening her eyes to his character never occurred to me. That _she_ could
be in any danger from the deception never entered my head. That such a
consequence as _this_ should ensue, you may easily believe was far
enough from my thoughts.
question: Why does Elizabeth blame herself most for not warning Lydia?
answer: She learned the truth in Kent but thought no danger could come from Lydia being near Wickham.
evidence: the necessity of opening her eyes to his character never occurred to me

quote_text:
When they all removed to Brighton, therefore, you had no reason, I
suppose, to believe them fond of each other.
question: What does Mrs. Gardiner ask about the couple's behaviour before they left for Brighton?
answer: She asks whether Elizabeth had any reason to think Lydia and Wickham were fond of each other.
evidence: you had no reason, I suppose, to believe them fond of each other

quote_text:
Not the slightest. I can remember no symptom of affection on either
side; and had any thing of the kind been perceptible, you must be aware
that ours is not a family, on which it could be thrown away. When first
he entered the corps, she was ready enough to admire him; but so we all
were. Every girl in, or near Meryton, was out of her senses about him
for the first two months; but he never distinguished _her_ by any
particular attention, and, consequently, after a moderate period of
extravagant and wild admiration, her fancy for him gave way, and others
of the regiment, who treated her with more distinction, again became her
favourites.
question: How does Elizabeth describe Lydia's early admiration for Wickham?
answer: She says Lydia admired him at first like other girls, but he never singled her out, so her fancy faded.
evidence: he never distinguished her by any particular attention

quote_text:
Not yet, But now that my dear uncle is come, I hope
every thing will be well.
question: What hope does Jane express when Elizabeth first returns home?
answer: Jane hopes Mr. Gardiner's arrival will help resolve the crisis.
evidence: But now that my dear uncle is come, I hope every thing will be well

quote_text: Is my father in town?
question: Why does Elizabeth ask whether her father is in town?
answer: She is checking whether Mr. Bennet is still in London searching for Lydia.
evidence: My father is going to London with Colonel Forster instantly

quote_text: Yes, he went on Tuesday as I wrote you word.
question: What does Jane report about their father's whereabouts?
answer: He went to London on Tuesday as she had written.
evidence: he went on Tuesday as I wrote you word

quote_text: And have you heard from him often?
question: Why is Elizabeth eager to know whether Jane has often heard from their father?
answer: She is anxious for news from the London search for Lydia.
evidence: lost not a moment in asking whether any thing had been heard of the fugitives

quote_text:
We have heard only once. He wrote me a few lines on Wednesday, to say
that he had arrived in safety, and to give me his directions, which I
particularly begged him to do. He merely added, that he should not write
again, till he had something of importance to mention.
question: What has Mr. Bennet written so far?
answer: Only once; a few lines saying he arrived safely and giving directions.
evidence: We have heard only once. He wrote me a few lines on Wednesday

quote_text: And my mother--How is she? How are you all?
question: Why does Elizabeth ask about her mother and the rest of the family?
answer: She knows the elopement has distressed them and wants to know how they are bearing it.
evidence: Our distress, my dear Lizzy, is very great

quote_text:
My mother is tolerably well, I trust; though her spirits are greatly
shaken. She is up stairs, and will have great satisfaction in seeing you
all. She does not yet leave her dressing-room. Mary and Kitty, thank
Heaven! are quite well.
question: What is Mrs. Bennet's condition when Elizabeth returns?
answer: She is tolerably well physically but her spirits are greatly shaken, and she stays in her dressing-room.
evidence: My mother is tolerably well, I trust; though her spirits are greatly shaken

quote_text:
But you--How are you? You look pale. How much you
must have gone through!
question: Why does Elizabeth single out Jane's health for concern?
answer: Jane looks pale and Elizabeth fears she has suffered under the strain.
evidence: You look pale. How much you must have gone through!

quote_text:
If I had been able, to carry my point of going to Brighton,
with all my family, _this_ would not have happened; but poor dear Lydia
had nobody to take care of her. Why did the Forsters ever let her go out
of their sight? I am sure there was some great neglect or other on their
side, for she is not the kind of girl to do such a thing, if she had
been well looked after. I always thought they were very unfit to have
the charge of her; but I was over-ruled, as I always am. Poor dear
child! And now here's Mr. Bennet gone away, and I know he will fight
Wickham, wherever he meets him, and then he will be killed, and what is
to become of us all? The Collinses will turn us out, before he is cold
in his grave; and if you are not kind to us, brother, I do not know what
we shall do.
question: Whom does Mrs. Bennet blame for Lydia's elopement?
answer: She blames the Forsters for negligence and herself for being overruled about going to Brighton.
evidence: this would not have happened; but poor dear Lydia had nobody to take care of her

quote_text:
Do not give way to useless alarm, though it is right to be
prepared for the worst, there is no occasion to look on it as certain.
It is not quite a week since they left Brighton. In a few days more, we
may gain some news of them, and till we know that they are not married,
and have no design of marrying, do not let us give the matter over as
lost. As soon as I get to town, I shall go to my brother, and make him
come home with me to Gracechurch Street, and then we may consult
together as to what is to be done.
question: What practical hope does Mr. Gardiner offer the family?
answer: He says they may soon get news and should not assume the worst before they know the couple is not married.
evidence: there is no occasion to look on it as certain

quote_text:
Oh! my dear brother, that is exactly what I
could most wish for. And now do, when you get to town, find them out,
wherever they may be; and if they are not married already, _make_ them
marry. And as for wedding clothes, do not let them wait for that, but
tell Lydia she shall have as much money as she chuses, to buy them,
after they are married. And, above all things, keep Mr. Bennet from
fighting. Tell him what a dreadful state I am in,--that I am frightened
out of my wits; and have such tremblings, such flutterings, all over me,
such spasms in my side, and pains in my head, and such beatings at
heart, that I can get no rest by night nor by day. And tell my dear
Lydia, not to give any directions about her clothes, till she has seen
me, for she does not know which are the best warehouses. Oh, brother,
how kind you are! I know you will contrive it all.
question: What does Mrs. Bennet beg Mr. Gardiner to do in London?
answer: She asks him to find the couple, make them marry if needed, and keep Mr. Bennet from fighting.
evidence: keep Mr. Bennet from fighting

quote_text:
This is a most unfortunate affair; and will probably be much talked of.
But we must stem the tide of malice, and pour into the wounded bosoms of
each other, the balm of sisterly consolation.
question: Why does Mary whisper this to Elizabeth at dinner?
answer: She wants to offer sisterly consolation and treat the scandal as a moral lesson.
evidence: we must stem the tide of malice

quote_text:
Unhappy as the event must be for Lydia, we may draw from it this useful
lesson; that loss of virtue in a female is irretrievable--that one false
step involves her in endless ruin--that her reputation is no less
brittle than it is beautiful,--and that she cannot be too much guarded
in her behaviour towards the undeserving of the other sex.
question: What moral lesson does Mary draw from Lydia's ruin?
answer: She says a woman's loss of virtue is irretrievable and her reputation fragile.
evidence: loss of virtue in a female is irretrievable

quote_text:
But tell me all and every thing about it, which
I have not already heard. Give me farther particulars. What did Colonel
Forster say? Had they no apprehension of any thing before the elopement
took place? They must have seen them together for ever.
question: Why does Elizabeth ask Jane for every particular?
answer: She wants to understand how the elopement happened and what the Forsters knew.
evidence: What did Colonel Forster say?

quote_text:
Colonel Forster did own that he had often suspected some partiality,
especially on Lydia's side, but nothing to give him any alarm. I am so
grieved for him. His behaviour was attentive and kind to the utmost. He
_was_ coming to us, in order to assure us of his concern, before he had
any idea of their not being gone to Scotland: when that apprehension
first got abroad, it hastened his journey.
question: What does Jane say Colonel Forster had suspected before the elopement?
answer: He had suspected some partiality, especially on Lydia's side, but nothing alarming.
evidence: he had often suspected some partiality, especially on Lydia's side, but nothing to give him any alarm

quote_text:
And was Denny convinced that Wickham would not marry? Did he know of
their intending to go off? Had Colonel Forster seen Denny himself?
question: Why does Elizabeth ask about Denny's conviction?
answer: She wants to know whether Wickham's intention not to marry was known beforehand.
evidence: was Denny convinced that Wickham would not marry?

quote_text:
Yes; but when questioned by _him_ Denny denied knowing any thing of
their plan, and would not give his real opinion about it. He did not
repeat his persuasion of their not marrying--and from _that_, I am
inclined to hope, he might have been misunderstood before.
question: What does Jane say Denny did when questioned by Colonel Forster?
answer: Denny denied knowing their plan and did not repeat his persuasion, so Jane hopes he was misunderstood.
evidence: Denny denied knowing any thing of their plan

quote_text:
And till Colonel Forster came himself, not one of you entertained a
doubt, I suppose, of their being really married?
question: What does Elizabeth find hard to believe about the family's prior expectations?
answer: She asks whether none of them doubted that Lydia and Wickham would really marry.
evidence: not one of you entertained a doubt, I suppose, of their being really married?

quote_text:
How was it possible that such an idea should enter our brains! I felt a
little uneasy--a little fearful of my sister's happiness with him in
marriage, because I knew that his conduct had not been always quite
right. My father and mother knew nothing of that, they only felt how
imprudent a match it must be. Kitty then owned, with a very natural
triumph on knowing more than the rest of us, that in Lydia's last
letter, she had prepared her for such a step. She had known, it seems,
of their being in love with each other, many weeks.
question: Why does Jane say the family never suspected a non-marital elopement?
answer: She says such an idea could not enter their minds; they only feared imprudence and knew nothing of Wickham's bad conduct.
evidence: How was it possible that such an idea should enter our brains!

quote_text: But not before they went to Brighton?
question: What timing does Elizabeth try to clarify about Kitty's knowledge?
answer: She asks whether Kitty knew of the attachment before Lydia went to Brighton.
evidence: But not before they went to Brighton?

quote_text: No, I believe not.
question: What does Jane answer about Kitty's prior knowledge?
answer: She believes Kitty did not know before Brighton.
evidence: No, I believe not.

quote_text:
And did Colonel Forster appear to think ill of Wickham himself? Does he
know his real character?
question: Why does Elizabeth ask about Colonel Forster's opinion of Wickham?
answer: She wants to know whether Forster had begun to think badly of Wickham.
evidence: did Colonel Forster appear to think ill of Wickham himself?

quote_text:
I must confess that he did not speak so well of Wickham as he formerly
did. He believed him to be imprudent and extravagant. And since this sad
affair has taken place, it is said, that he left Meryton greatly in
debt; but I hope this may be false.
question: What had Colonel Forster come to believe about Wickham?
answer: He thought Wickham imprudent and extravagant, and heard he left Meryton in debt.
evidence: He believed him to be imprudent and extravagant

quote_text:
Oh, Jane, had we been less secret, had we told what we knew of him,
this could not have happened!
question: What does Elizabeth regret about their silence concerning Wickham?
answer: She believes that if they had warned the family, Lydia's elopement could have been prevented.
evidence: had we told what we knew of him, this could not have happened

quote_text:
Perhaps it would have been better; But to expose
the former faults of any person, without knowing what their present
feelings were, seemed unjustifiable. We acted with the best intentions.
question: Why does Jane partly agree that secrecy was a mistake yet still defend their choice to keep Wickham's faults quiet?
answer: She admits that speaking out might have been better, but she felt it unjustifiable to expose anyone's former faults without knowing their present feelings; they acted with good intentions.
evidence: to expose the former faults of any person, without knowing what their present feelings were, seemed unjustifiable

quote_text:
Could Colonel Forster repeat the particulars of Lydia's note to his
wife?
question: What information is Elizabeth trying to obtain from Jane about Colonel Forster's account of Lydia's disappearance?
answer: She wants the exact particulars of Lydia's note so she can understand how the elopement was arranged and discovered.
evidence: Colonel Forster did own that he had often suspected some partiality, especially on Lydia's side

quote_text: He brought it with him for us to see.
question: How does Jane explain that the family has Lydia's note available to inspect?
answer: She says Colonel Forster brought Lydia's note with him so the Bennets could see it.
evidence: He brought it with him for us to see.

quote_text:
Oh! thoughtless, thoughtless Lydia! What a letter is this, to be written at such a moment. But
at least it shews, that _she_ was serious in the object of her journey.
Whatever he might afterwards persuade her to, it was not on her side a
_scheme_ of infamy. My poor father! how he must have felt it!
question: What does Elizabeth conclude about Lydia's intentions after reading Lydia's flippant letter?
answer: She calls Lydia thoughtless, but the letter shows Lydia seriously meant to marry Wickham; the scheme of infamy was not on Lydia's side.
evidence: it was not on her side a scheme of infamy

quote_text:
I never saw any one so shocked. He could not speak a word for full ten
minutes. My mother was taken ill immediately, and the whole house in
such confusion!
question: How does Jane describe her parents' immediate reaction to Lydia's elopement?
answer: She says Mr. Bennet was so shocked he could not speak for ten minutes, while Mrs. Bennet was taken ill and the house fell into confusion.
evidence: He could not speak a word for full ten minutes. My mother was taken ill immediately

quote_text:
Oh! Jane, was there a servant belonging to it, who
did not know the whole story before the end of the day?
question: What anxiety does Elizabeth express about how widely the scandal became known at Longbourn?
answer: She fears the servants knew the whole story before the day ended, which would deepen the family's humiliation.
evidence: was there a servant belonging to it, who did not know the whole story before the end of the day?

quote_text:
I do not know.--I hope there was.--But to be guarded at such a time, is
very difficult. My mother was in hysterics, and though I endeavoured to
give her every assistance in my power, I am afraid I did not do so much
as I might have done! But the horror of what might possibly happen,
almost took from me my faculties.
question: Why does Jane hope the servants did not all learn the news, and what difficulty does she admit?
answer: She hopes the story was contained, but says it was very hard to be guarded while Mrs. Bennet was in hysterics.
evidence: But to be guarded at such a time, is very difficult. My mother was in hysterics

quote_text:
Your attendance upon her, has been too much for you. You do not look
well. Oh! that I had been with you, you have had every care and anxiety
upon yourself alone.
question: What does Elizabeth infer about Jane's health from her appearance and recent duties?
answer: Elizabeth thinks nursing Mrs. Bennet has been too much for Jane and that Jane looks unwell.
evidence: Your attendance upon her, has been too much for you. You do not look well.

quote_text:
Mary and Kitty have been very kind, and would have shared in every
fatigue, I am sure, but I did not think it right for either of them.
Kitty is slight and delicate, and Mary studies so much, that her hours
of repose should not be broken in on. My aunt Philips came to Longbourn
on Tuesday, after my father went away; and was so good as to stay till
Thursday with me. She was of great use and comfort to us all, and lady
Lucas has been very kind; she walked here on Wednesday morning to
condole with us, and offered her services, or any of her daughters, if
they could be of use to us.
question: Why did Jane not let Mary and Kitty share the fatigues of caring for Mrs. Bennet?
answer: She thought Kitty was delicate and Mary needed rest because she studied so much.
evidence: Kitty is slight and delicate, and Mary studies so much, that her hours of repose should not be broken in on.

quote_text:
She had better have stayed at home, perhaps she
_meant_ well, but, under such a misfortune as this, one cannot see too
little of one's neighbours. Assistance is impossible; condolence,
insufferable. Let them triumph over us at a distance, and be satisfied.
question: Why does Elizabeth think Lady Lucas should have stayed away rather than visit to condole?
answer: She believes that in such a misfortune neighbors should be seen as little as possible, since condolence is insufferable and assistance impossible.
evidence: one cannot see too little of one's neighbours

quote_text:
He meant, I believe, to go to Epsom, the place where
they last changed horses, see the postilions, and try if any thing could
be made out from them. His principal object must be, to discover the
number of the hackney coach which took them from Clapham. It had come
with a fare from London; and as he thought the circumstance of a
gentleman and lady's removing from one carriage into another, might be
remarked, he meant to make enquiries at Clapham. If he could any how
discover at what house the coachman had before set down his fare, he
determined to make enquiries there, and hoped it might not be impossible
to find out the stand and number of the coach. I do not know of any
other designs that he had formed: but he was in such a hurry to be gone,
and his spirits so greatly discomposed, that I had difficulty in finding
out even so much as this.
question: What practical plan did Mr. Bennet intend to follow in London to trace Lydia and Wickham?
answer: He meant to question postilions at Epsom and try to identify the hackney coach that took them from Clapham.
evidence: His principal object must be, to discover the number of the hackney coach which took them from Clapham.

quote_text:
A gamester! This is
wholly unexpected. I had not an idea of it.
question: What newly revealed fact about Wickham shocks Jane, and why is it unexpected to her?
answer: She is horrified to learn he is a gamester with considerable gaming debts, which she had never suspected.
evidence: he had left gaming debts behind him, to a very considerable amount

quote_text:
What, is he coming home, and without poor Lydia! Sure he
will not leave London before he has found them. Who is to fight Wickham,
and make him marry her, if he comes away?
question: Why is Mrs. Bennet distressed that Mr. Bennet is returning without Lydia?
answer: She wants him to stay in London to find Lydia and force Wickham to marry her, or fight him if necessary.
evidence: Who is to fight Wickham, and make him marry her, if he comes away?

quote_text:
Say
nothing of that. Who should suffer but myself? It has been my own doing,
and I ought to feel it.
question: What does Mr. Bennet mean about responsibility for Lydia's ruin?
answer: He takes the blame entirely on himself, saying it was his own doing and that he ought to feel the suffering.
evidence: It has been my own doing, and I ought to feel it.

quote_text: You must not be too severe upon yourself,
question: Why does Elizabeth try to restrain her father's self-accusation?
answer: She sees him blaming himself for Lydia's elopement and tries to moderate his severity toward himself.
evidence: It has been my own doing, and I ought to feel it.

quote_text:
You may well warn me against such an evil. Human nature is so prone to
fall into it! No, Lizzy, let me once in my life feel how much I have
been to blame. I am not afraid of being overpowered by the impression.
It will pass away soon enough.
question: What does Mr. Bennet say he wants from his self-reproach, despite Elizabeth's warning?
answer: He wants once in his life to feel how much he has been to blame, believing the impression will soon pass.
evidence: let me once in my life feel how much I have been to blame

quote_text: Do you suppose them to be in London?
question: Why does Elizabeth ask her father whether Lydia and Wickham are in London?
answer: She is trying to determine where the couple has gone after being traced only as far as London.
evidence: were traced almost to London, but not beyond

quote_text: Yes; where else can they be so well concealed?
question: Why does Mr. Bennet think London is the likeliest place for Lydia and Wickham to be?
answer: He thinks it is the best place for them to hide because they can be so well concealed there.
evidence: where else can they be so well concealed?

quote_text: And Lydia used to want to go to London,
question: What irony does Kitty point out about Lydia's present situation?
answer: She notes that Lydia used to want to go to London, and now she may be there under disgraceful circumstances.
evidence: And Lydia used to want to go to London

quote_text:
She is happy, then, and her residence there
will probably be of some duration.
question: What does Mr. Bennet imply by saying Lydia is happy and may stay in London for some time?
answer: He is speaking bitterly and ironically, suggesting Lydia's wish has been fulfilled in a disgraceful and lasting way.
evidence: and her residence there will probably be of some duration

quote_text:
Lizzy, I bear you no
ill-will for being justified in your advice to me last May, which,
considering the event, shews some greatness of mind.
question: What advice of Elizabeth's is Mr. Bennet referring to, and how does he regard it now?
answer: He admits Elizabeth was justified in warning him about Lydia's behavior last May and says he bears her no ill will for being right.
evidence: being justified in your advice to me last May

quote_text:
This is a parade, which does one good; it gives such an
elegance to misfortune! Another day I will do the same; I will sit in
my library, in my night cap and powdering gown, and give as much trouble
as I can,--or, perhaps, I may defer it, till Kitty runs away.
question: What is Mr. Bennet mocking when he calls the tea visit a parade?
answer: He sarcastically calls the ceremony of having tea brought to him a parade that lends elegance to misfortune.
evidence: it gives such an elegance to misfortune!

quote_text:
I am not going to run away, Papa, if _I_
should ever go to Brighton, I would behave better than Lydia.
question: How does Kitty defend herself when her father teases her about running away?
answer: She protests that she is not going to run away and claims she would behave better than Lydia if she went to Brighton.
evidence: if I should ever go to Brighton, I would behave better than Lydia

quote_text:
_You_ go to Brighton!--I would not trust you so near it as East Bourne
for fifty pounds! No, Kitty, I have at last learnt to be cautious, and
you will feel the effects of it. No officer is ever to enter my house
again, nor even to pass through the village. Balls will be absolutely
prohibited, unless you stand up with one of your sisters. And you are
never to stir out of doors, till you can prove, that you have spent ten
minutes of every day in a rational manner.
question: What strict new rules does Mr. Bennet impose on Kitty after Lydia's elopement?
answer: He forbids officers from entering the house or village, bans balls unless she dances with a sister, and restricts her going out.
evidence: No officer is ever to enter my house again, nor even to pass through the village.

quote_text:
Well, well, do not make yourself unhappy. If you are a good
girl for the next ten years, I will take you to a review at the end of
them.
question: How does Mr. Bennet soften the harshness of his restrictions on Kitty?
answer: He tells her not to be unhappy and jokingly promises to take her to a review after ten years of good behavior.
evidence: If you are a good girl for the next ten years, I will take you to a review

quote_text:
I beg your pardon,
madam, for interrupting you, but I was in hopes you might have got some
good news from town, so I took the liberty of coming to ask.
question: Why does Mrs. Hill interrupt Jane and Elizabeth in the shrubbery?
answer: She hopes they have received good news from London and comes to ask about it.
evidence: I was in hopes you might have got some good news from town

quote_text: What do you mean, Hill? We have heard nothing from town.
question: Why is Jane confused by Mrs. Hill's question about good news?
answer: Jane believes the family has heard nothing from London, so Hill's question surprises her.
evidence: We have heard nothing from town.

quote_text:
Dear madam, don't you know
there is an express come for master from Mr. Gardiner? He has been here
this half hour, and master has had a letter.
question: What important news does Mrs. Hill reveal that Jane and Elizabeth had not known?
answer: She tells them an express has arrived for Mr. Bennet from Mr. Gardiner, and he has had the letter for half an hour.
evidence: there is an express come for master from Mr. Gardiner

quote_text:
If you are looking for my master, ma'am, he is walking towards the
little copse.
question: Where does the butler say Mr. Bennet has gone, prompting the sisters to follow him?
answer: He says Mr. Bennet is walking toward the little copse, so the sisters run after him for news.
evidence: he is walking towards the little copse

quote_text: Oh, Papa, what news? what news? have you heard from my uncle?
question: Why is Elizabeth so urgent in asking her father for news?
answer: She has just learned that an express came from Mr. Gardiner and is desperate to hear what it says about Lydia.
evidence: there is an express come for master from Mr. Gardiner

quote_text: Yes, I have had a letter from him by express.
question: What does Mr. Bennet confirm about how he received Mr. Gardiner's message?
answer: He confirms that he has received a letter from Mr. Gardiner by express.
evidence: I have had a letter from him by express

quote_text: Well, and what news does it bring? good or bad?
question: What does Elizabeth want her father to tell her about the letter's contents?
answer: She asks whether the news it brings is good or bad.
evidence: what news does it bring? good or bad?

quote_text: What is there of good to be expected? but perhaps you would like to read it.
question: What does Mr. Bennet's response reveal about his expectations for the letter?
answer: He expects no good news and offers the letter to Elizabeth to read for herself.
evidence: What is there of good to be expected?

quote_text:
Read it aloud, for I hardly know myself what it is
about.
question: Why does Mr. Bennet want Elizabeth to read Mr. Gardiner's letter aloud?
answer: He says he hardly knows what the letter is about, suggesting his mind is too distracted to read it himself.
evidence: for I hardly know myself what it is about

quote_text: Then it is, as I always hoped, they are married!
question: What hopeful conclusion does Jane jump to when she hears the couple has been found?
answer: She assumes Lydia and Wickham are married, which is what she had always hoped.
evidence: Then it is, as I always hoped

quote_text:
Is it possible! Can it be
possible that he will marry her?
question: Why is Elizabeth astonished after reading the letter?
answer: She is startled that Wickham, who had no intention of marrying Lydia, may now actually marry her if the terms are met.
evidence: They are not married, nor can I find there was any intention of being so

quote_text: Wickham is not so undeserving, then, as we have thought him; My dear father, I congratulate you.
question: How does Jane reinterpret Wickham's character after hearing he will marry Lydia?
answer: She hopes his consent to marry Lydia shows he is not as undeserving as they had thought, and she congratulates her father.
evidence: Wickham is not so undeserving, then, as we have thought him

quote_text: And have you answered the letter?
question: What practical concern does Elizabeth immediately raise after hearing the marriage terms?
answer: She asks whether her father has already answered Mr. Gardiner's letter.
evidence: And have you answered the letter?

quote_text: No; but it must be done soon.
question: What does Mr. Bennet admit about replying to Mr. Gardiner's letter?
answer: He has not yet answered, but he acknowledges that it must be done soon.
evidence: No; but it must be done soon.

quote_text:
Oh! my dear father, come back, and write immediately.
Consider how important every moment is, in such a case.
question: Why does Elizabeth urge her father to return to the house and write immediately?
answer: She believes every moment is important for securing Lydia's marriage and wants him to waste no time.
evidence: Consider how important every moment is, in such a case.

quote_text:
Let me write for you, if you dislike the trouble
yourself.
question: Why does Jane offer to write the letter in her father's place?
answer: Mr. Bennet has just admitted he hates writing but that the reply to Mr. Gardiner must be sent at once, so Jane offers to spare him the trouble.
evidence: "I dislike it very much," he replied; "but it must be done."

quote_text: I dislike it very much, but it must be done.
question: What does Mr. Bennet's reply to Jane's offer reveal about his mood?
answer: He is reluctant and low-spirited about the whole business, yet still feels the letter cannot be delayed.
evidence: "but it must be done."

quote_text:
And may I ask? but the terms, I suppose, must be
complied with.
question: What prompts Elizabeth to ask her father this question?
answer: He has just said the settlement terms must be complied with, and she wants to hear what those terms actually are.
evidence: "but the terms, I suppose, must be complied with."

quote_text: Complied with! I am only ashamed of his asking so little.
question: Why does Mr. Bennet say he is ashamed rather than pleased by the terms?
answer: Because Mr. Gardiner asked for so little on Lydia's behalf that it humiliates him to accept such a small settlement.
evidence: "I am only ashamed of his asking so little."

quote_text: And they _must_ marry! Yet he is _such_ a man!
question: What feeling lies behind Elizabeth's exclamation about the marriage?
answer: She is astonished and dismayed that they must rejoice over a match to a man of Wickham's character.
evidence: "How strange this is! And for _this_ we are to be thankful."

quote_text:
Yes, yes, they must marry. There is nothing else to be done. But there
are two things that I want very much to know:--one is, how much money
your uncle has laid down, to bring it about; and the other, how I am
ever to pay him.
question: What two things does Mr. Bennet say he wants to find out?
answer: How much money Mr. Gardiner laid down to bring the marriage about, and how he is ever to repay him.
evidence: how much money your uncle has laid down, to bring it about; and the other, how I am ever to pay him.

quote_text: Money! my uncle! what do you mean, Sir?
question: Why is Jane so bewildered by her father's talk of money?
answer: She never imagined that her uncle had paid Wickham money to marry Lydia.
evidence: what do you mean, Sir?

quote_text:
I mean, that no man in his senses, would marry Lydia on so slight a
temptation as one hundred a-year during my life, and fifty after I am
gone.
question: What is Mr. Bennet implying about Wickham with these figures?
answer: That no sensible man would marry Lydia for so small a settlement, so Wickham must have been given far more than one hundred a year.
evidence: no man in his senses, would marry Lydia on so slight a temptation as one hundred a-year

quote_text:
That is very true, though it had not occurred to me
before. His debts to be discharged, and something still to remain! Oh!
it must be my uncle's doings! Generous, good man, I am afraid he has
distressed himself. A small sum could not do all this.
question: What does Elizabeth suddenly realize from her father's reasoning?
answer: That Wickham's debts must have been cleared and money settled on him besides, so only her uncle could be behind it.
evidence: His debts to be discharged, and something still to remain! Oh! it must be my uncle's doings!

quote_text:
No, Wickham's a fool, if he takes her with a
farthing less than ten thousand pounds. I should be sorry to think so
ill of him, in the very beginning of our relationship.
question: What does Mr. Bennet mean by answering "No" here?
answer: He means Wickham would be a fool to take Lydia for anything less than ten thousand pounds.
evidence: Wickham's a fool, if he takes her with a farthing less than ten thousand pounds.

quote_text:
Ten thousand pounds! Heaven forbid! How is half such a sum to be
repaid?
question: Why is Elizabeth so horrified by the sum her father names?
answer: She cannot imagine how such a huge debt of gratitude could ever be repaid to her uncle.
evidence: How is half such a sum to be repaid?

quote_text:
And they are really to be married! How strange this is! And for _this_ we are to be
thankful. That they should marry, small as is their chance of happiness,
and wretched as is his character, we are forced to rejoice! Oh, Lydia!
question: What makes Elizabeth's cry about the wedding so bitter?
answer: She is forced to be grateful for a marriage that is wretched in itself, simply because it averts worse disgrace.
evidence: small as is their chance of happiness, and wretched as is his character, we are forced to rejoice!

quote_text:
I comfort myself with thinking, that he certainly would
not marry Lydia, if he had not a real regard for her. Though our kind
uncle has done something towards clearing him, I cannot believe that ten
thousand pounds, or any thing like it, has been advanced. He has
children of his own, and may have more. How could he spare half ten
thousand pounds?
question: What comfort does Jane draw from Wickham's consenting to the marriage?
answer: She believes he would not marry Lydia unless he had a genuine regard for her.
evidence: he certainly would not marry Lydia, if he had not a real regard for her.

quote_text:
If we are ever able to learn what Wickham's debts have been, and how much is settled on his side on our sister, we shall
exactly know what Mr. Gardiner has done for them, because Wickham has
not sixpence of his own. The kindness of my uncle and aunt can never be
requited. Their taking her home, and affording her their personal
protection and countenance, is such a sacrifice to her advantage, as
years of gratitude cannot enough acknowledge. By this time she is
actually with them! If such goodness does not make her miserable now,
she will never deserve to be happy! What a meeting for her, when she
first sees my aunt!
question: How does Elizabeth propose to discover exactly what her uncle did for the couple?
answer: By learning the size of Wickham's debts and of the settlement made on him, since he has no money of his own.
evidence: we shall exactly know what Mr. Gardiner has done for them, because Wickham has not sixpence of his own.

quote_text:
We must endeavour to forget all that has passed on either side, I hope and trust they will yet be happy. His consenting to marry
her is a proof, I will believe, that he is come to a right way of
thinking. Their mutual affection will steady them; and I flatter myself
they will settle so quietly, and live in so rational a manner, as may in
time make their past imprudence forgotten.
question: What future does Jane hope for Lydia and Wickham?
answer: She hopes their mutual affection will steady them and that they will live quietly enough for the past to be forgotten.
evidence: Their mutual affection will steady them

quote_text:
Their conduct has been such, as neither you, nor
I, nor any body, can ever forget. It is useless to talk of it.
question: How does Elizabeth answer Jane's plea to forget the past?
answer: She says their conduct has been such that nobody, including Jane and herself, can ever forget it.
evidence: as neither you, nor I, nor any body, can ever forget

quote_text: Just as you please.
question: Why does Mr. Bennet answer his daughters so carelessly?
answer: He is busy writing and indifferent to how the news is passed on, so he lets them do as they please.
evidence: He was writing, and, without raising his head, coolly replied

quote_text: May we take my uncle's letter to read to her?
question: Why does Elizabeth want to take her uncle's letter upstairs?
answer: So the good news can be read aloud once to her mother, Mary and Kitty all together.
evidence: One communication would, therefore, do for all.

quote_text: Take whatever you like, and get away.
question: What does Mr. Bennet's impatient answer show about his feelings?
answer: He wants to be left alone with his writing and cares nothing for how the news is announced.
evidence: Take whatever you like, and get away.

quote_text:
My dear, dear Lydia! This is delightful indeed!--She will
be married!--I shall see her again!--She will be married at sixteen!--My
good, kind brother!--I knew how it would be--I knew he would manage
every thing. How I long to see her! and to see dear Wickham too! But the
clothes, the wedding clothes! I will write to my sister Gardiner about
them directly. Lizzy, my dear, run down to your father, and ask him how
much he will give her. Stay, stay, I will go myself. Ring the bell,
Kitty, for Hill. I will put on my things in a moment. My dear, dear
Lydia!--How merry we shall be together when we meet!
question: What is most striking about Mrs. Bennet's joy at the news?
answer: She thinks only of the wedding and of Lydia being married at sixteen, with no shame over the elopement.
evidence: She will be married at sixteen!

quote_text:
For we must attribute this happy conclusion, in a great
measure, to his kindness. We are persuaded that he has pledged himself
to assist Mr. Wickham with money.
question: What is Jane trying to do by reminding her mother of Mr. Gardiner?
answer: She tries to temper her mother's transports by pointing to the great kindness and expense of her uncle.
evidence: leading her thoughts to the obligations which Mr. Gardiner's behaviour laid them all under

quote_text:
Well, it is all very right; who should do it but
her own uncle? If he had not had a family of his own, I and my children
must have had all his money you know, and it is the first time we have
ever had any thing from him, except a few presents. Well! I am so happy.
In a short time, I shall have a daughter married. Mrs. Wickham! How well
it sounds. And she was only sixteen last June. My dear Jane, I am in
such a flutter, that I am sure I can't write; so I will dictate, and you
write for me. We will settle with your father about the money
afterwards; but the things should be ordered immediately.
question: What does Mrs. Bennet's reply reveal about her sense of gratitude?
answer: She brushes duty aside, saying her brother should do it and that his money would have come to her family anyway.
evidence: who should do it but her own uncle?

quote_text:
I will go to Meryton, as soon as I am dressed, and tell the
good, good news to my sister Philips. And as I come back, I can call on
Lady Lucas and Mrs. Long. Kitty, run down and order the carriage. An
airing would do me a great deal of good, I am sure. Girls, can I do any
thing for you in Meryton? Oh! here comes Hill. My dear Hill, have you
heard the good news? Miss Lydia is going to be married; and you shall
all have a bowl of punch, to make merry at her wedding.
question: Why is Mrs. Bennet so eager to go to Meryton?
answer: She wants to be the first to spread the news of Lydia's marriage to her sister Philips and the neighbours.
evidence: tell the good, good news to my sister Philips

quote_text:
Haye-Park might do, if the Gouldings would quit it, or the
great house at Stoke, if the drawing-room were larger; but Ashworth is
too far off! I could not bear to have her ten miles from me; and as for
Purvis Lodge, the attics are dreadful.
question: What does Mrs. Bennet's house-hunting show about her judgement?
answer: She sizes up houses for Lydia without any thought of the couple's income, rejecting any that lack size and importance.
evidence: without knowing or considering what their income might be, rejected many as deficient in size and importance.

quote_text:
Mrs.
Bennet, before you take any, or all of these houses, for your son and
daughter, let us come to a right understanding. Into _one_ house in this
neighbourhood, they shall never have admittance. I will not encourage
the impudence of either, by receiving them at Longbourn.
question: What firm rule does Mr. Bennet lay down about the Wickhams?
answer: He declares they shall never be received at Longbourn, whatever houses his wife picks for them.
evidence: Into _one_ house in this neighbourhood, they shall never have admittance.

quote_text:
She is so fond of Mrs. Forster, it will be quite shocking
to send her away! And there are several of the young men, too, that she
likes very much. The officers may not be so pleasant in General ----'s
regiment.
question: Why does Mrs. Bennet object to Wickham's removal from the militia?
answer: She laments that Lydia will be carried far north, away from Mrs. Forster and the officers she is fond of.
evidence: it will be quite shocking to send her away!

quote_text:
Only think of its being three months, since I went away;
it seems but a fortnight I declare; and yet there have been things
enough happened in the time. Good gracious! when I went away, I am sure
I had no more idea of being married till I came back again! though I
thought it would be very good fun if I was.
question: How does Lydia behave on returning home as a married woman?
answer: She is unabashed and merry, treating the whole affair as a joke and quite unaware that she has done anything wrong.
evidence: I had no more idea of being married till I came back again! though I thought it would be very good fun if I was.

quote_text:
Oh! mamma, do the
people here abouts know I am married to-day? I was afraid they might
not; and we overtook William Goulding in his curricle, so I was
determined he should know it, and so I let down the side glass next to
him, and took off my glove, and let my hand just rest upon the window
frame, so that he might see the ring, and then I bowed and smiled like
any thing.
question: Why does Lydia make a show of her ring to William Goulding?
answer: She is determined that everyone in the neighbourhood shall know she is married.
evidence: so that he might see the ring, and then I bowed and smiled

quote_text:
Ah! Jane, I take your place now, and you must go
lower, because I am a married woman.
question: What does Lydia's remark at the dinner table show about her?
answer: She vulgarly glories in her married status, claiming precedence over her elder sister.
evidence: I take your place now, and you must go lower, because I am a married woman.

quote_text:
Well, mamma, and what do you think of my husband? Is not he a charming man? I
am sure my sisters must all envy me. I only hope they may have half my
good luck. They must all go to Brighton. That is the place to get
husbands. What a pity it is, mamma, we did not all go.
question: What does Lydia want her mother to say about her husband?
answer: She wants her mother to admire Wickham and agree that her sisters must all envy her good luck.
evidence: Is not he a charming man? I am sure my sisters must all envy me.

quote_text:
Very true; and if I had my will, we should. But my dear Lydia, I don't
at all like your going such a way off. Must it be so?
question: What does Mrs. Bennet admit in the midst of her delight?
answer: She says she would keep Lydia near if she could and dislikes her going so far off to Newcastle.
evidence: I don't at all like your going such a way off.

quote_text:
Oh, lord! yes;--there is nothing in that. I shall like it of all
things. You and papa, and my sisters, must come down and see us. We
shall be at Newcastle all the winter, and I dare say there will be some
balls, and I will take care to get good partners for them all.
question: How does Lydia feel about the move to Newcastle?
answer: She is delighted by it and eagerly plans for the family to visit her and for winter balls.
evidence: there is nothing in that. I shall like it of all things.

quote_text: I should like it beyond any thing!
question: What does Mrs. Bennet's exclamation reveal about her?
answer: She shares Lydia's shallow eagerness for the society and amusements of Newcastle.
evidence: I should like it beyond any thing!

quote_text:
And then when you go away, you may leave one or two of my sisters
behind you; and I dare say I shall get husbands for them before the
winter is over.
question: What does Lydia promise to do for her sisters in Newcastle?
answer: She says that when they visit she will find husbands for them before the winter is over.
evidence: I dare say I shall get husbands for them before the winter is over.

quote_text:
I thank you for my share of the favour, but I do not
particularly like your way of getting husbands.
question: Why does Elizabeth answer Lydia so drily?
answer: She is disgusted by Lydia's vulgar way of hunting husbands for her sisters.
evidence: but I do not particularly like your way of getting husbands.

quote_text:
Lizzy, I never gave _you_ an account of my wedding, I believe. You were
not by, when I told mamma, and the others, all about it. Are not you
curious to hear how it was managed?
question: Why does Lydia want to describe her wedding in detail?
answer: She assumes Elizabeth must be curious and wants to show off how the wedding was managed.
evidence: Are not you curious to hear how it was managed?

quote_text:
No really, I think there cannot be too little said
on the subject.
question: Why does Elizabeth refuse to hear the account?
answer: She thinks the less said about the wedding the better.
evidence: I think there cannot be too little said on the subject.

quote_text:
La! You are so strange! But I must tell you how it went off. We were
married, you know, at St. Clement's, because Wickham's lodgings were in
that parish. And it was settled that we should all be there by eleven
o'clock. My uncle and aunt and I were to go together; and the others
were to meet us at the church. Well, Monday morning came, and I was in
such a fuss! I was so afraid you know that something would happen to put
it off, and then I should have gone quite distracted. And there was my
aunt, all the time I was dressing, preaching and talking away just as if
she was reading a sermon. However, I did not hear above one word in ten,
for I was thinking, you may suppose, of my dear Wickham. I longed to
know whether he would be married in his blue coat.
question: What was Lydia's state of mind on the wedding morning?
answer: She was in a great fuss, terrified that something would happen to postpone the ceremony.
evidence: I was so afraid you know that something would happen to put it off

quote_text:
Well, and so we breakfasted at ten as usual; I thought it would never
be over; for, by the bye, you are to understand, that my uncle and aunt
were horrid unpleasant all the time I was with them. If you'll believe
me, I did not once put my foot out of doors, though I was there a
fortnight. Not one party, or scheme, or any thing. To be sure London was
rather thin, but however the little Theatre was open. Well, and so just
as the carriage came to the door, my uncle was called away upon business
to that horrid man Mr. Stone. And then, you know, when once they get
together, there is no end of it. Well, I was so frightened I did not
know what to do, for my uncle was to give me away; and if we were beyond
the hour, we could not be married all day. But, luckily, he came back
again in ten minutes time, and then we all set out. However, I
recollected afterwards, that if he _had_ been prevented going, the
wedding need not be put off, for Mr. Darcy might have done as well.
question: What secret does Lydia accidentally let slip while telling her story?
answer: That Mr. Darcy was expected at the church with Wickham, which she had promised to keep quiet.
evidence: for Mr. Darcy might have done as well.

quote_text: Mr. Darcy!
question: Why is Elizabeth so astonished by Lydia's mention of Mr. Darcy?
answer: She had no idea Mr. Darcy had been at her sister's wedding, so the name comes as a complete shock.
evidence: he was to come there with Wickham, you know.

quote_text:
Oh, yes!--he was to come there with Wickham, you know. But gracious me!
I quite forgot! I ought not to have said a word about it. I promised
them so faithfully! What will Wickham say? It was to be such a secret!
question: What does Lydia accidentally reveal about Mr. Darcy's involvement in her wedding, and how does she react to her own slip?
answer: She lets slip that Darcy was to come to the wedding with Wickham, then regrets breaking the secrecy she promised.
evidence: I ought not to have said a word about it. I promised them so faithfully!

quote_text:
If it was to be secret, say not another word on the
subject. You may depend upon my seeking no further.
question: How does Jane respond when Lydia admits she was not supposed to reveal Darcy's presence at the wedding?
answer: Jane tells her to say no more and promises not to pry further.
evidence: say not another word on the subject. You may depend upon my seeking no further.

quote_text:
Oh! certainly, we will
ask you no questions.
question: What does Elizabeth's reply show about her feelings while agreeing not to question Lydia?
answer: She agrees to ask no questions even though she is burning with curiosity.
evidence: though burning with curiosity

quote_text:
Thank you, for if you did, I should certainly tell you
all, and then Wickham would be angry.
question: What does Lydia admit about her ability to keep the wedding secret if questioned?
answer: She says she would certainly tell everything and then Wickham would be angry.
evidence: if you did, I should certainly tell you all, and then Wickham would be angry.

quote_text:
Not that I _shall_ though, and my dear aunt, if you do not tell me in an honourable
manner, I shall certainly be reduced to tricks and stratagems to find it
out.
question: What private resolve does Elizabeth make after agreeing not to question Lydia about Darcy's role?
answer: She privately decides she will use tricks or stratagems to learn the truth if her aunt will not tell her honorably.
evidence: I shall certainly be reduced to tricks and stratagems to find it out.

quote_text: I am afraid I interrupt your solitary ramble, my dear sister?
question: How does Wickham address Elizabeth when he finds her alone after she has read Mrs. Gardiner's letter?
answer: He familiarly calls her his dear sister because he has married Lydia.
evidence: my dear sister

quote_text:
You certainly do, but it does not follow
that the interruption must be unwelcome.
question: How does Elizabeth respond to Wickham's apology for interrupting her solitary walk?
answer: She admits he interrupts her but says the interruption need not be unwelcome.
evidence: but it does not follow that the interruption must be unwelcome.

quote_text:
I should be sorry indeed, if it were. _We_ were always good friends;
and now we are better.
question: What does Wickham mean by saying that he and Elizabeth are now better friends than before?
answer: He means their connection is closer because his marriage to Lydia makes them brother and sister.
evidence: We were always good friends; and now we are better.

quote_text: True. Are the others coming out?
question: What does Elizabeth's question about the others suggest about her wish at that moment?
answer: She wants to avoid being alone with Wickham and turns the conversation toward other company.
evidence: Are the others coming out?

quote_text:
I do not know. Mrs. Bennet and Lydia are going in the carriage to
Meryton. And so, my dear sister, I find from our uncle and aunt, that
you have actually seen Pemberley.
question: How does Wickham know that Elizabeth has visited Pemberley?
answer: He says he learned it from her uncle and aunt, the Gardiners.
evidence: I find from our uncle and aunt, that you have actually seen Pemberley.

quote_text:
I almost envy you the pleasure, and yet I believe it would be too much
for me, or else I could take it in my way to Newcastle. And you saw the
old housekeeper, I suppose? Poor Reynolds, she was always very fond of
me. But of course she did not mention my name to you.
question: Why does Wickham say he could not himself visit Pemberley?
answer: He says seeing it would be too much for him emotionally, though he might pass near Newcastle.
evidence: I almost envy you the pleasure, and yet I believe it would be too much for me

quote_text: Yes, she did.
question: What assumption of Wickham's does Elizabeth correct when she says the housekeeper did mention his name?
answer: Wickham assumed Mrs. Reynolds had not mentioned him, but Elizabeth says she did.
evidence: But of course she did not mention my name to you.

quote_text: And what did she say?
question: Why is Wickham anxious to hear what Mrs. Reynolds said about him?
answer: He wants to know whether the housekeeper repeated anything damaging about his reputation.
evidence: And what did she say?

quote_text:
That you were gone into the army, and she was afraid had--not turned
out well. At such a distance as _that_, you know, things are strangely
misrepresented.
question: What does Elizabeth report that Mrs. Reynolds said about Wickham's present life?
answer: She says Mrs. Reynolds reported that he had gone into the army and feared he had not turned out well.
evidence: she was afraid had--not turned out well.

quote_text: Certainly,
question: How does Wickham react when Elizabeth suggests reports from a distance may be misrepresented?
answer: He agrees while biting his lips, showing suppressed annoyance.
evidence: he replied, biting his lips

quote_text:
I was surprised to see Darcy in town last month. We passed each other
several times. I wonder what he can be doing there.
question: Why does Wickham bring up seeing Darcy in London last month?
answer: He is probing whether Elizabeth knows what Darcy was doing there, especially regarding the Lydia affair.
evidence: I wonder what he can be doing there.

quote_text:
Perhaps preparing for his marriage with Miss de Bourgh, It must be something particular, to take him there at this
time of year.
question: What explanation does Elizabeth give for Darcy's presence in London, and why is it ironic?
answer: She suggests he may be preparing to marry Miss de Bourgh, though he was actually in London helping Lydia.
evidence: Perhaps preparing for his marriage with Miss de Bourgh

quote_text:
Undoubtedly. Did you see him while you were at Lambton? I thought I
understood from the Gardiners that you had.
question: How does Wickham turn the conversation back toward Darcy after Elizabeth mentions Miss de Bourgh?
answer: He asks whether she saw Darcy while she was at Lambton, saying the Gardiners implied she had.
evidence: Did you see him while you were at Lambton?

quote_text: Yes; he introduced us to his sister.
question: What does Elizabeth reveal about what happened when she saw Darcy at Lambton?
answer: She says Darcy introduced her party to his sister.
evidence: he introduced us to his sister.

quote_text: And do you like her?
question: Whom does Wickham ask Elizabeth about after she mentions Darcy's sister?
answer: He asks whether Elizabeth likes Miss Darcy.
evidence: And do you like her?

quote_text: Very much.
question: How does Elizabeth's answer about Miss Darcy contradict Wickham's earlier account of her?
answer: She says she likes Miss Darcy very much, contradicting Wickham's claim that Miss Darcy was very proud.
evidence: Very much.

quote_text:
I have heard, indeed, that she is uncommonly improved within this year
or two. When I last saw her, she was not very promising. I am very glad
you liked her. I hope she will turn out well.
question: What does Wickham claim about Miss Darcy's improvement and his former opinion of her?
answer: He says he has heard she improved greatly, though she was not promising when he last saw her.
evidence: When I last saw her, she was not very promising.

quote_text: I dare say she will; she has got over the most trying age.
question: What does Elizabeth imply by saying Miss Darcy has got over the most trying age?
answer: She wryly suggests Miss Darcy is past the awkwardness of youth and that Wickham's old judgment is outdated.
evidence: she has got over the most trying age.

quote_text: Did you go by the village of Kympton?
question: Where does Wickham ask whether Elizabeth's party traveled during their Derbyshire tour?
answer: He asks whether they went by the village of Kympton.
evidence: Did you go by the village of Kympton?

quote_text: I do not recollect that we did.
question: How does Elizabeth answer Wickham's question about Kympton?
answer: She says she does not remember going that way.
evidence: I do not recollect that we did.

quote_text:
I mention it, because it is the living which I ought to have had. A
most delightful place!--Excellent Parsonage House! It would have suited
me in every respect.
question: Why does Wickham say he mentioned Kympton?
answer: He claims it was the clerical living he ought to have had and would have suited him perfectly.
evidence: it is the living which I ought to have had.

quote_text: How should you have liked making sermons?
question: What does Elizabeth's question about sermon-making suggest about Wickham's claim to the living?
answer: She skeptically tests whether he would really have suited clerical duties.
evidence: How should you have liked making sermons?

quote_text:
Exceedingly well. I should have considered it as part of my duty, and
the exertion would soon have been nothing. One ought not to
repine;--but, to be sure, it would have been such a thing for me! The
quiet, the retirement of such a life, would have answered all my ideas
of happiness! But it was not to be. Did you ever hear Darcy mention the
circumstance, when you were in Kent?
question: How does Wickham describe the life he says he lost at Kympton?
answer: He claims its quiet retirement would have answered all his ideas of happiness.
evidence: The quiet, the retirement of such a life, would have answered all my ideas of happiness!

quote_text:
I _have_ heard from authority, which I thought _as good_, that it was
left you conditionally only, and at the will of the present patron.
question: What does Elizabeth say she has heard about the terms of the living left to Wickham?
answer: She says she heard it was left to him only conditionally and at the patron's will.
evidence: it was left you conditionally only, and at the will of the present patron.

quote_text:
You have. Yes, there was something in _that_; I told you so from the
first, you may remember.
question: How does Wickham respond to Elizabeth's correction about the living being conditional?
answer: He concedes there was something in that and claims he told her so from the first.
evidence: I told you so from the first, you may remember.

quote_text:
I _did_ hear, too, that there was a time, when sermon-making was not so
palatable to you as it seems to be at present; that you actually
declared your resolution of never taking orders, and that the business
had been compromised accordingly.
question: What does Elizabeth reveal she knows about Wickham's past declaration regarding taking orders?
answer: She says he once declared he would never take orders, so the matter was compromised.
evidence: you actually declared your resolution of never taking orders

quote_text:
You did! and it was not wholly without foundation. You may remember
what I told you on that point, when first we talked of it.
question: How does Wickham react when Elizabeth says he once refused to take orders?
answer: He admits it was not wholly without foundation and refers to their earlier conversation.
evidence: it was not wholly without foundation.

quote_text:
Come, Mr. Wickham, we are brother and sister, you know. Do not let us
quarrel about the past. In future, I hope we shall be always of one
mind.
question: Why does Elizabeth end her conversation with Wickham by calling for peace between them?
answer: She wants to stop quarreling about the past and keep their new family relationship civil.
evidence: Do not let us quarrel about the past.

quote_text: Oh! my dear Lydia, when shall we meet again?
question: Why is Mrs. Bennet distressed when she asks Lydia when they shall meet again?
answer: Lydia is departing for Newcastle with Wickham, and Mrs. Bennet fears a long separation.
evidence: The day of his and Lydia's departure soon came

quote_text: Oh, lord! I don't know. Not these two or three years perhaps.
question: What does Lydia's answer reveal about her feelings on leaving her mother?
answer: She is casual and unconcerned, saying it may be two or three years before they meet.
evidence: Not these two or three years perhaps.

quote_text: Write to me very often, my dear.
question: What does Mrs. Bennet ask Lydia to do as they say goodbye?
answer: She asks Lydia to write to her very often.
evidence: Write to me very often, my dear.

quote_text:
As often as I can. But you know married women have never much time for
writing. My sisters may write to _me_. They will have nothing else to
do.
question: How does Lydia justify not writing often, and what does it show about her character?
answer: She says married women have little time for writing and suggests her sisters have nothing else to do, showing her selfishness.
evidence: married women have never much time for writing.

quote_text:
He is as fine a fellow, as ever I saw. He simpers, and smirks, and makes love to us
all. I am prodigiously proud of him. I defy even Sir William Lucas
himself, to produce a more valuable son-in-law.
question: What is Mr. Bennet's tone toward Wickham after the couple leaves Longbourn?
answer: He is sarcastic, mock-praising Wickham's smirking and calling him a valuable son-in-law.
evidence: He simpers, and smirks, and makes love to us all.

quote_text:
I often think, that there is nothing so bad as parting with
one's friends. One seems so forlorn without them.
question: Why does Mrs. Bennet lament that parting with friends is so bad?
answer: She is feeling forlorn after Lydia's departure and misses her daughter.
evidence: The loss of her daughter made Mrs. Bennet very dull

quote_text:
This is the consequence you see, Madam, of marrying a daughter, It must make you better satisfied that your other four are
single.
question: How does Elizabeth teasingly console her mother after Lydia's departure?
answer: She says marrying a daughter causes such partings and should make Mrs. Bennet glad her other four are single.
evidence: It must make you better satisfied that your other four are single.

quote_text:
Go, my dear, and shew her ladyship about the
