different walks. I think she will be pleased with the hermitage.
question: Why does Mrs. Bennet urge Elizabeth to go with Lady Catherine?
answer: Lady Catherine has asked Elizabeth to walk with her in the little wilderness, and Mrs. Bennet eagerly tells Elizabeth to show her ladyship the walks.
evidence: I should be glad to take a turn in it, if you will favour me with your company.

quote_text: How could I ever think her like her nephew?
question: What prompts Elizabeth to wonder how she ever thought Lady Catherine resembled her nephew?
answer: Walking with Lady Catherine, Elizabeth finds her more than usually insolent and disagreeable, which makes the contrast with Darcy strike her.
evidence: a woman, who was now more than usually insolent and disagreeable.

quote_text:
You can be at no loss, Miss Bennet, to understand the reason of my
journey hither. Your own heart, your own conscience, must tell you why I
come.
question: What does Lady Catherine presume about Elizabeth in her opening speech?
answer: She presumes Elizabeth already knows why she has come and that Elizabeth's own heart and conscience can explain the visit.
evidence: Your own heart, your own conscience, must tell you why I come.

quote_text:
Indeed, you are mistaken, Madam. I have not been at all able to account
for the honour of seeing you here.
question: How does Elizabeth respond to Lady Catherine's assumption that she knows the reason for the visit?
answer: Elizabeth denies it and says she has truly been unable to account for the honor of Lady Catherine's presence.
evidence: I have not been at all able to account for the honour of seeing you here.

quote_text:
Miss Bennet, you ought to
know, that I am not to be trifled with. But however insincere _you_ may
choose to be, you shall not find _me_ so. My character has ever been
celebrated for its sincerity and frankness, and in a cause of such
moment as this, I shall certainly not depart from it. A report of a most
alarming nature, reached me two days ago. I was told, that not only your
sister was on the point of being most advantageously married, but that
_you_, that Miss Elizabeth Bennet, would, in all likelihood, be soon
afterwards united to my nephew, my own nephew, Mr. Darcy. Though I
_know_ it must be a scandalous falsehood; though I would not injure him
so much as to suppose the truth of it possible, I instantly resolved on
setting off for this place, that I might make my sentiments known to
you.
question: What report has brought Lady Catherine to Longbourn?
answer: She has heard that Jane is about to marry advantageously and that Elizabeth will soon afterward be united to Darcy.
evidence: A report of a most alarming nature, reached me two days ago.

quote_text:
If you believed it impossible to be true, I wonder you took the trouble of coming
so far. What could your ladyship propose by it?
question: What contradiction does Elizabeth point out in Lady Catherine's journey?
answer: If Lady Catherine thinks the reported engagement impossible, Elizabeth wonders why she took the trouble to come so far and what she hopes to accomplish.
evidence: If you believed it impossible to be true,

quote_text: At once to insist upon having such a report universally contradicted.
question: What does Lady Catherine say her purpose is?
answer: She says she has come to insist that the report of Elizabeth's engagement to Darcy be universally contradicted.
evidence: At once to insist upon having such a report universally contradicted.

quote_text:
Your coming to Longbourn, to see me and my family, will be rather a confirmation of it; if, indeed, such a report
is in existence.
question: How does Elizabeth turn Lady Catherine's visit against her?
answer: She says Lady Catherine's coming to Longbourn to see her family would actually confirm the report rather than disprove it.
evidence: will be rather a confirmation of it; if, indeed, such a report is in existence.

quote_text:
If! do you then pretend to be ignorant of it? Has it not been
industriously circulated by yourselves? Do you not know that such a
report is spread abroad?
question: What does Lady Catherine accuse Elizabeth and her family of doing?
answer: She accuses them of industriously circulating the report of the engagement themselves while pretending ignorance of it.
evidence: Has it not been industriously circulated by yourselves?

quote_text: I never heard that it was.
question: What effect does Elizabeth's brief reply have on Lady Catherine's accusation?
answer: Elizabeth calmly denies ever having heard the report, refusing to accept Lady Catherine's charge that her family spread it.
evidence: I never heard that it was.

quote_text: And can you likewise declare, that there is no _foundation_ for it?
question: What is Lady Catherine trying to force Elizabeth to admit?
answer: She wants Elizabeth to declare whether there is any truth at all to the report of an engagement with Darcy.
evidence: And can you likewise declare, that there is no _foundation_ for it?

quote_text:
I do not pretend to possess equal frankness with your ladyship. _You_
may ask questions, which _I_ shall not choose to answer.
question: Why does Elizabeth refuse to answer Lady Catherine's question?
answer: She says she does not claim Lady Catherine's kind of frankness and will not answer intrusive questions she chooses not to answer.
evidence: You may ask questions, which _I_ shall not choose to answer.

quote_text:
This is not to be borne. Miss Bennet, I insist on being satisfied. Has
he, has my nephew, made you an offer of marriage?
question: What direct question does Lady Catherine finally demand answered?
answer: She insists on knowing whether Darcy has actually made Elizabeth an offer of marriage.
evidence: Has he, has my nephew, made you an offer of marriage?

quote_text: Your ladyship has declared it to be impossible.
question: How does Elizabeth use Lady Catherine's own words to deflect the question?
answer: She points out that Lady Catherine herself has already declared such an offer impossible, so she throws that back instead of answering directly.
evidence: Your ladyship has declared it to be impossible.

quote_text:
It ought to be so; it must be so, while he retains the use of his
reason. But _your_ arts and allurements may, in a moment of infatuation,
have made him forget what he owes to himself and to all his family. You
may have drawn him in.
question: What does Lady Catherine suggest about how Elizabeth might have influenced Darcy?
answer: She claims Elizabeth's arts and allurements may have made Darcy forget his duty in a moment of infatuation.
evidence: But _your_ arts and allurements may, in a moment of infatuation, have made him forget what he owes to himself and to all his family.

quote_text: If I have, I shall be the last person to confess it.
question: What does Elizabeth's retort imply about satisfying Lady Catherine?
answer: She refuses to confess any such influence and will not give Lady Catherine the admission she wants.
evidence: If I have, I shall be the last person to confess it.

quote_text:
Miss Bennet, do you know who I am? I have not been accustomed to such
language as this. I am almost the nearest relation he has in the world,
and am entitled to know all his dearest concerns.
question: Why does Lady Catherine invoke her rank and relationship to Darcy here?
answer: She is offended by Elizabeth's defiance and tries to assert her authority as Darcy's near relation, who is entitled to know his concerns.
evidence: I am almost the nearest relation he has in the world, and am entitled to know all his dearest concerns.

quote_text:
But you are not entitled to know _mine_; nor will such behaviour as
this, ever induce me to be explicit.
question: What boundary does Elizabeth draw with Lady Catherine?
answer: She says Lady Catherine has no right to know her private concerns and that such behavior will never make her explicit.
evidence: But you are not entitled to know _mine_; nor will such behaviour as this, ever induce me to be explicit.

quote_text:
Let me be rightly understood. This match, to which you have the
presumption to aspire, can never take place. No, never. Mr. Darcy is
engaged to _my daughter_. Now what have you to say?
question: What claim does Lady Catherine make to block the match?
answer: She insists that Darcy is engaged to her daughter and that Elizabeth's presumptuous match can never take place.
evidence: Mr. Darcy is engaged to _my daughter_.

quote_text:
Only this; that if he is so, you can have no reason to suppose he will
make an offer to me.
question: How does Elizabeth counter Lady Catherine's claim that Darcy is engaged to Miss de Bourgh?
answer: She says that if Darcy is truly engaged, Lady Catherine has no reason to fear he will make Elizabeth an offer.
evidence: if he is so, you can have no reason to suppose he will make an offer to me.

quote_text:
The engagement between them is of a peculiar kind. From their infancy,
they have been intended for each other. It was the favourite wish of
_his_ mother, as well as of her's. While in their cradles, we planned
the union: and now, at the moment when the wishes of both sisters would
be accomplished, in their marriage, to be prevented by a young woman of
inferior birth, of no importance in the world, and wholly unallied to
the family! Do you pay no regard to the wishes of his friends? To his
tacit engagement with Miss De Bourgh? Are you lost to every feeling of
propriety and delicacy? Have you not heard me say, that from his
earliest hours he was destined for his cousin?
question: How does Lady Catherine describe the supposed engagement between Darcy and Miss de Bourgh?
answer: She says it was planned from their infancy by both mothers and that Darcy was destined for his cousin from his earliest hours.
evidence: From their infancy, they have been intended for each other.

quote_text:
Yes, and I had heard it before. But what is that to me? If there is no
other objection to my marrying your nephew, I shall certainly not be
kept from it, by knowing that his mother and aunt wished him to marry
Miss De Bourgh. You both did as much as you could, in planning the
marriage. Its completion depended on others. If Mr. Darcy is neither by
honour nor inclination confined to his cousin, why is not he to make
another choice? And if I am that choice, why may not I accept him?
question: Why does Elizabeth dismiss the family plan for Darcy and Miss de Bourgh?
answer: She says the mothers' wishes do not bind Darcy; if he is not confined by honor or inclination to his cousin, he may choose someone else.
evidence: If Mr. Darcy is neither by honour nor inclination confined to his cousin, why is not he to make another choice?

quote_text:
Because honour, decorum, prudence, nay, interest, forbid it. Yes, Miss
Bennet, interest; for do not expect to be noticed by his family or
friends, if you wilfully act against the inclinations of all. You will
be censured, slighted, and despised, by every one connected with him.
Your alliance will be a disgrace; your name will never even be mentioned
by any of us.
question: What consequences does Lady Catherine threaten if Elizabeth marries Darcy?
answer: She warns that Elizabeth will be censured, slighted, and despised by everyone connected with Darcy, and that the alliance will be a disgrace.
evidence: You will be censured, slighted, and despised, by every one connected with him.

quote_text:
These are heavy misfortunes, But the wife of Mr.
Darcy must have such extraordinary sources of happiness necessarily
attached to her situation, that she could, upon the whole, have no cause
to repine.
question: What does Elizabeth's reply reveal about her attitude toward Lady Catherine's threats?
answer: She remains unshaken and ironically says that being Darcy's wife would bring enough happiness to outweigh such misfortunes.
evidence: the wife of Mr. Darcy must have such extraordinary sources of happiness necessarily attached to her situation, that she could, upon the whole, have no cause to repine.

quote_text:
Obstinate, headstrong girl! I am ashamed of you! Is this your gratitude
for my attentions to you last spring? Is nothing due to me on that
score?
question: Why does Lady Catherine accuse Elizabeth of ingratitude?
answer: She feels Elizabeth is repaying her former attentions at Rosings with defiance rather than compliance.
evidence: Is this your gratitude for my attentions to you last spring?

quote_text:
Let us sit down. You are to understand, Miss Bennet, that I came here
with the determined resolution of carrying my purpose; nor will I be
dissuaded from it. I have not been used to submit to any person's whims.
I have not been in the habit of brooking disappointment.
question: What does Lady Catherine reveal about her resolve in coming to Longbourn?
answer: She says she came determined to carry her purpose and is not used to submitting to anyone's whims or brooking disappointment.
evidence: I came here with the determined resolution of carrying my purpose; nor will I be dissuaded from it.

quote_text:
_That_ will make your ladyship's situation at present more pitiable;
but it will have no effect on _me_.
question: How does Elizabeth respond to Lady Catherine's claim that she never brooks disappointment?
answer: She says that makes Lady Catherine's present situation more pitiable but will have no effect on Elizabeth herself.
evidence: _That_ will make your ladyship's situation at present more pitiable; but it will have no effect on _me_.

quote_text:
I will not be interrupted. Hear me in silence. My daughter and my
nephew are formed for each other. They are descended on the maternal
side, from the same noble line; and, on the father's, from respectable,
honourable, and ancient, though untitled families. Their fortune on both
sides is splendid. They are destined for each other by the voice of
every member of their respective houses; and what is to divide them? The
upstart pretensions of a young woman without family, connections, or
fortune. Is this to be endured! But it must not, shall not be. If you
were sensible of your own good, you would not wish to quit the sphere,
in which you have been brought up.
question: What arguments does Lady Catherine give for Darcy and Miss de Bourgh being suited?
answer: She says they share noble maternal lineage, respectable paternal families, splendid fortunes, and were destined for each other by both houses.
evidence: They are descended on the maternal side, from the same noble line; and, on the father's, from respectable, honourable, and ancient, though untitled families.

quote_text:
In marrying your nephew, I should not consider myself as quitting that
sphere. He is a gentleman; I am a gentleman's daughter; so far we are
equal.
question: How does Elizabeth answer Lady Catherine's claim that she would quit her sphere by marrying Darcy?
answer: She says Darcy is a gentleman and she is a gentleman's daughter, so in that respect they are equal.
evidence: He is a gentleman; I am a gentleman's daughter; so far we are equal.

quote_text:
True. You _are_ a gentleman's daughter. But who was your mother? Who
are your uncles and aunts? Do not imagine me ignorant of their
condition.
question: What does Lady Catherine shift to after conceding that Elizabeth is a gentleman's daughter?
answer: She attacks Elizabeth's mother and uncles and aunts, implying that her maternal connections are inferior and well known to Lady Catherine.
evidence: But who was your mother? Who are your uncles and aunts?

quote_text:
Whatever my connections may be, if your nephew does
not object to them, they can be nothing to _you_.
question: How does Elizabeth rebut Lady Catherine's attack on her relations?
answer: She says that whatever her connections are, they can mean nothing to Lady Catherine if Darcy himself does not object to them.
evidence: if your nephew does not object to them, they can be nothing to _you_.

quote_text: Tell me once for all, are you engaged to him?
question: What does Lady Catherine demand at this point?
answer: She demands a direct, final answer about whether Elizabeth is engaged to Darcy.
evidence: Tell me once for all, are you engaged to him?

quote_text: I am not.
question: Why does Elizabeth answer this question despite not wishing to oblige Lady Catherine?
answer: After a moment's deliberation, she decides she cannot avoid stating the plain truth that she is not engaged.
evidence: she could not but say, after a moment's deliberation,

quote_text: And will you promise me, never to enter into such an engagement?
question: What does Lady Catherine ask for after learning that Elizabeth is not engaged?
answer: She asks Elizabeth to promise never to enter into an engagement with Darcy.
evidence: And will you promise me, never to enter into such an engagement?

quote_text: I will make no promise of the kind.
question: How does Elizabeth respond to the request for such a promise?
answer: She flatly refuses to make any promise of that kind.
evidence: I will make no promise of the kind.

quote_text:
Miss Bennet I am shocked and astonished. I expected to find a more
reasonable young woman. But do not deceive yourself into a belief that I
will ever recede. I shall not go away, till you have given me the
assurance I require.
question: What does Lady Catherine threaten after Elizabeth refuses the promise?
answer: She says she will not leave until Elizabeth gives the assurance and warns her not to believe Lady Catherine will recede.
evidence: I shall not go away, till you have given me the assurance I require.

quote_text:
And I certainly _never_ shall give it. I am not to be intimidated into
anything so wholly unreasonable. Your ladyship wants Mr. Darcy to marry
your daughter; but would my giving you the wished-for promise, make
_their_ marriage at all more probable? Supposing him to be attached to
me, would _my_ refusing to accept his hand, make him wish to bestow it
on his cousin? Allow me to say, Lady Catherine, that the arguments with
which you have supported this extraordinary application, have been as
frivolous as the application was ill-judged. You have widely mistaken my
character, if you think I can be worked on by such persuasions as these.
How far your nephew might approve of your interference in _his_ affairs,
I cannot tell; but you have certainly no right to concern yourself in
mine. I must beg, therefore, to be importuned no farther on the
subject.
question: What logical point does Elizabeth make against Lady Catherine's demand?
answer: Even if Elizabeth promised not to marry Darcy, that would not make Darcy marry Miss de Bourgh.
evidence: would my giving you the wished-for promise, make _their_ marriage at all more probable?

quote_text:
Not so hasty, if you please. I have by no means done. To all the
objections I have already urged, I have still another to add. I am no
stranger to the particulars of your youngest sister's infamous
elopement. I know it all; that the young man's marrying her, was a
patched-up business, at the expence of your father and uncles. And is
_such_ a girl to be my nephew's sister? Is _her_ husband, is the son of
his late father's steward, to be his brother? Heaven and earth!--of what
are you thinking? Are the shades of Pemberley to be thus polluted?
question: What new objection does Lady Catherine add to the match?
answer: She cites Lydia's infamous elopement and marriage to Wickham as a disgrace that would pollute Pemberley and make Elizabeth's family unfit.
evidence: Are the shades of Pemberley to be thus polluted?

quote_text:
You can _now_ have nothing farther to say, You have insulted me, in every possible method. I must beg to return to
the house.
question: Why does Elizabeth end the conversation after Lady Catherine's mention of Lydia?
answer: She considers Lady Catherine's attack on her family an insult and refuses to hear more, asking to return to the house.
evidence: You have insulted me, in every possible method. I must beg to return to the house.

quote_text:
You have no regard, then, for the honour and credit of my nephew!
Unfeeling, selfish girl! Do you not consider that a connection with you,
must disgrace him in the eyes of everybody?
question: What does Lady Catherine accuse Elizabeth of disregarding?
answer: She accuses Elizabeth of not caring about Darcy's honor and credit and of being willing to disgrace him by the connection.
evidence: You have no regard, then, for the honour and credit of my nephew!

quote_text: How hard it is in some cases to be believed!
question: Why does Jane complain that it is hard to be believed?
answer: Elizabeth keeps smiling and teasing that Jane is in danger of making Bingley love her again, so Jane protests that her indifference is sincere.
evidence: you will not let me smile, and are provoking me to it every moment

quote_text: And how impossible in others!
question: What does Elizabeth mean by saying belief is impossible in other cases?
answer: She wittily turns Jane's complaint around, suggesting that in some cases—such as Jane's denial of feeling—it is impossible to believe what is said.
evidence: I think you are in great danger of making him as much in love with you as ever

quote_text:
But why should you wish to persuade me that I feel more than I
acknowledge?
question: Why does Jane ask Elizabeth why she wants to persuade her she feels more than she acknowledges?
answer: Elizabeth has been teasing Jane about still being in love with Bingley, so Jane challenges her motive for insisting on it.
evidence: you will not let me smile, and are provoking me to it every moment

quote_text:
That is a question which I hardly know how to answer. We all love to
instruct, though we can teach only what is not worth knowing. Forgive
me; and if you persist in indifference, do not make _me_ your
confidante.
question: How does Elizabeth answer Jane's demand for an explanation?
answer: She admits the question is hard to answer, jokes that people love to instruct even when teaching worthless things, and asks Jane not to make her a confidante if she persists in indifference.
evidence: We all love to instruct, though we can teach only what is not worth knowing

quote_text: Next time you call, I hope we shall be more lucky.
question: What does Mrs. Bennet hope for after Bingley declines her dinner invitation?
answer: She hopes that the next time he calls they will be luckier, meaning she wants another chance to entertain him and further his acquaintance with Jane.
evidence: with many expressions of concern, he confessed himself engaged elsewhere

quote_text: Can you come to-morrow?
question: Why does Mrs. Bennet press Bingley about coming tomorrow?
answer: She wants him to visit again soon so he can be with Jane, and he eagerly accepts because he has no engagement.
evidence: Yes, he had no engagement at all for to-morrow; and her invitation was accepted with alacrity

quote_text:
My dear Jane, make haste and hurry down. He is come--Mr. Bingley is
come.--He is, indeed. Make haste, make haste. Here, Sarah, come to Miss
Bennet this moment, and help her on with her gown. Never mind Miss
Lizzy's hair.
question: What does Mrs. Bennet's urgency reveal about her purpose?

Lucas's last week; and even Mr. Darcy acknowledged, that the partridges
were remarkably well done; and I suppose he has two or three French
cooks at least. And, my dear Jane, I never saw you look in greater
beauty. Mrs. Long said so too, for I asked her whether you did not. And
what do you think she said besides? She did indeed. I do think Mrs. Long is as good
a creature as ever lived--and her nieces are very pretty behaved girls,
and not at all handsome: I like them prodigiously.
question: Why is Mrs. Bennet so convinced that the dinner party went well?
answer: She saw Bingley's attentions to Jane and repeats Mrs. Long's prediction that Jane will be at Netherfield at last.
evidence: we shall have her at Netherfield at last

quote_text:
It has been a very agreeable day, The
party seemed so well selected, so suitable one with the other. I hope we
may often meet again.
question: What does Jane's wish to meet the party often again suggest despite her claimed indifference?
answer: It suggests she still takes pleasure in Bingley's society and hopes for more meetings.
evidence: I hope we may often meet again.

quote_text:
Lizzy, you must not do so. You must not suspect me. It mortifies me. I
assure you that I have now learnt to enjoy his conversation as an
agreeable and sensible young man, without having a wish beyond it. I am
perfectly satisfied from what his manners now are, that he never had any
design of engaging my affection. It is only that he is blessed with
greater sweetness of address, and a stronger desire of generally
pleasing than any other man.
question: Why is Jane mortified by Elizabeth's smile after the dinner party?
answer: She thinks Elizabeth suspects her of still caring for Bingley, which Jane denies.
evidence: You must not suspect me. It mortifies me.

quote_text:
You are very cruel, you will not let me smile, and
are provoking me to it every moment.
question: Why does Elizabeth accuse Jane of being cruel?
answer: Jane forbids her to smile while saying things that provoke her to smile even more.
evidence: you will not let me smile, and are provoking me to it every moment.

quote_text:
Or in other words, you are determined to have him. He is rich, to be
sure, and you may have more fine clothes and fine carriages than Jane.
But will they make you happy?
question: Why does Mr. Bennet assume Elizabeth is accepting Darcy only because he is rich?
answer: He remembers that Elizabeth has always hated Darcy, so wealth seems to him the only explanation for her sudden acceptance.
evidence: Have not you always hated him?

quote_text:
Have you any other objection, than your belief of my
indifference?
question: Why does Elizabeth ask her father whether he has any other objection to Darcy?
answer: She wants to show that his disapproval rests only on believing she is indifferent, which she can then correct.
evidence: than your belief of my indifference?

quote_text:
None at all. We all know him to be a proud, unpleasant sort of man; but
this would be nothing if you really liked him.
question: What is Mr. Bennet's view of Darcy in this reply?
answer: He has no other objection and thinks Darcy proud and unpleasant, but says that would not matter if Elizabeth truly liked him.
evidence: but this would be nothing if you really liked him

quote_text:
I do, I do like him, I love him.
Indeed he has no improper pride. He is perfectly amiable. You do not
know what he really is; then pray do not pain me by speaking of him in
such terms.
question: How does Elizabeth answer her father's doubt about her feelings for Darcy?
answer: She earnestly affirms that she loves Darcy and defends him, saying he has no improper pride and is perfectly amiable.
evidence: I love him. Indeed he has no improper pride. He is perfectly amiable.

quote_text:
Lizzy, I have given him my consent. He is the kind
of man, indeed, to whom I should never dare refuse any thing, which he
condescended to ask. I now give it to _you_, if you are resolved on
having him. But let me advise you to think better of it. I know your
disposition, Lizzy. I know that you could be neither happy nor
respectable, unless you truly esteemed your husband; unless you looked
up to him as a superior. Your lively talents would place you in the
greatest danger in an unequal marriage. You could scarcely escape
discredit and misery. My child, let me not have the grief of seeing
_you_ unable to respect your partner in life. You know not what you are
about.
question: What warning does Mr. Bennet give Elizabeth along with his consent?
answer: He warns that she cannot be happy or respectable unless she truly esteems her husband and looks up to him.
evidence: unless you truly esteemed your husband; unless you looked up to him as a superior

quote_text:
Well, my dear, I have no more to
say. If this be the case, he deserves you. I could not have parted with
you, my Lizzy, to any one less worthy.
question: What makes Mr. Bennet finally accept Elizabeth's engagement to Darcy?
answer: Elizabeth's earnest explanation of her changed feelings and Darcy's good qualities convinces him, and he says Darcy deserves her.
evidence: If this be the case, he deserves you.

quote_text:
This is an evening of wonders, indeed! And so, Darcy did every thing;
made up the match, gave the money, paid the fellow's debts, and got him
his commission! So much the better. It will save me a world of trouble
and economy. Had it been your uncle's doing, I must and _would_ have
paid him; but these violent young lovers carry every thing their own
way. I shall offer to pay him to-morrow; he will rant and storm about
his love for you, and there will be an end of the matter.
question: Why does Mr. Bennet call this an evening of wonders?
answer: Elizabeth has just told him that Darcy secretly arranged Lydia's marriage and paid Wickham's debts, astonishing him.
evidence: Darcy did every thing; made up the match, gave the money, paid the fellow's debts

quote_text:
If any young men come
for Mary or Kitty, send them in, for I am quite at leisure.
question: What humorous attitude does Mr. Bennet show as Elizabeth leaves the library?
answer: Relieved and amused, he jokes that he is at leisure to receive suitors for Mary or Kitty too.
evidence: If any young men come for Mary or Kitty, send them in, for I am quite at leisure.

quote_text:
Good gracious! Lord bless me! only think! dear me! Mr. Darcy! Who would
have thought it! And is it really true? Oh! my sweetest Lizzy! how rich
and how great you will be! What pin-money, what jewels, what carriages
you will have! Jane's is nothing to it--nothing at all. I am so
pleased--so happy. Such a charming man!--so handsome! so tall!--Oh, my
dear Lizzy! pray apologise for my having disliked him so much before. I
hope he will overlook it. Dear, dear Lizzy. A house in town! Every thing
that is charming! Three daughters married! Ten thousand a year! Oh,
Lord! What will become of me. I shall go distracted.
question: How does Mrs. Bennet react to the news of Elizabeth's engagement to Darcy?
answer: She is astonished and overwhelmed with joy, immediately imagining Elizabeth's wealth, jewels, and carriages.
evidence: how rich and how great you will be! What pin-money, what jewels, what carriages

quote_text:
My dearest child, I can think of nothing else! Ten
thousand a year, and very likely more! 'Tis as good as a Lord! And a
special licence. You must and shall be married by a special licence. But
my dearest love, tell me what dish Mr. Darcy is particularly fond of,
that I may have it to-morrow.
question: What does Mrs. Bennet's follow-up question reveal about her priorities?
answer: She is preoccupied with Darcy's fortune and wants to know his favorite dish so she can please him.
evidence: tell me what dish Mr. Darcy is particularly fond of

quote_text:
I admire all my three sons-in-law highly, Wickham, perhaps,
is my favourite; but I think I shall like _your_ husband quite as well
as Jane's.
question: What does Mr. Bennet's joke about his sons-in-law reveal about his view of the marriages?
answer: He ironically calls Wickham his favorite, then says he expects to like Darcy as well as Bingley.
evidence: Wickham, perhaps, is my favourite; but I think I shall like your husband quite as well as Jane's.

quote_text:
How could
you begin? I can comprehend your going on charmingly, when
you had once made a beginning; but what could set you off in the first
place?
question: What is Elizabeth asking Darcy to explain about his love?
answer: She understands how his love continued once begun, but wants to know what first set it off.
evidence: what could set you off in the first place?

quote_text:
I cannot fix on the hour, or the spot, or the look, or the words, which
laid the foundation. It is too long ago. I was in the middle before I
knew that I _had_ begun.
question: How does Darcy describe the beginning of his love for Elizabeth?
answer: He says he cannot pinpoint when it began and only realized he was in love after he was already in the middle of it.
evidence: I was in the middle before I knew that I had begun.

quote_text:
My beauty you had early withstood, and as for my manners--my behaviour
to _you_ was at least always bordering on the uncivil, and I never spoke
to you without rather wishing to give you pain than not. Now be sincere;
did you admire me for my impertinence?
question: What does Elizabeth suggest Darcy admired in her if not her beauty or manners?
answer: She teasingly implies that her impertinence or lively mind attracted him.
evidence: did you admire me for my impertinence?

quote_text: For the liveliness of your mind, I did.
question: What quality does Darcy admit first attracted him to Elizabeth?
answer: He says he admired the liveliness of her mind.
evidence: For the liveliness of your mind, I did.

quote_text:
You may as well call it impertinence at once. It was very little less.
The fact is, that you were sick of civility, of deference, of officious
attention. You were disgusted with the women who were always speaking
and looking, and thinking for _your_ approbation alone. I roused, and
interested you, because I was so unlike _them_. Had you not been really
amiable you would have hated me for it; but in spite of the pains you
took to disguise yourself, your feelings were always noble and just; and
in your heart, you thoroughly despised the persons who so assiduously
courted you. There--I have saved you the trouble of accounting for it;
and really, all things considered, I begin to think it perfectly
reasonable. To be sure, you knew no actual good of me--but nobody thinks
of _that_ when they fall in love.
question: What explanation does Elizabeth give for why Darcy was attracted to her?
answer: She says he was tired of women courting his approval and that her unlike manner roused and interested him.
evidence: I roused, and interested you, because I was so unlike them.

quote_text:
Was there no good in your affectionate behaviour to Jane, while she was
ill at Netherfield?
question: Why does Darcy mention Elizabeth's care for Jane at Netherfield?
answer: He offers it as an example of her goodness, countering her claim that he knew no actual good of her.
evidence: Was there no good in your affectionate behaviour to Jane, while she was ill at Netherfield?

quote_text:
Dearest Jane! who could have done less for her? But make a virtue of it
by all means. My good qualities are under your protection, and you are
to exaggerate them as much as possible; and, in return, it belongs to me
to find occasions for teazing and quarrelling with you as often as may
be; and I shall begin directly by asking you what made you so unwilling
to come to the point at last. What made you so shy of me, when you first
called, and afterwards dined here? Why, especially, when you called, did
you look as if you did not care about me?
question: How does Elizabeth respond to Darcy's praise of her nursing Jane?
answer: She modestly says anyone would have done as much, while teasingly letting him exaggerate her virtues.
evidence: who could have done less for her?

quote_text: Because you were grave and silent, and gave me no encouragement.
question: Why does Elizabeth say she seemed shy when Darcy first called and dined at Longbourn?
answer: She says Darcy was grave and silent and gave her no encouragement.
evidence: Because you were grave and silent, and gave me no encouragement.

quote_text: But I was embarrassed.
question: What reason does Darcy give for his grave silence during his early visits?
answer: He says he was embarrassed.
evidence: But I was embarrassed.

quote_text: And so was I.
question: What does Elizabeth admit after Darcy says he was embarrassed?
answer: She admits that she was embarrassed too.
evidence: And so was I.

quote_text: You might have talked to me more when you came to dinner.
question: What does Elizabeth reproach Darcy for during his dinner visit?
answer: She says he might have talked to her more when he came to dinner.
evidence: You might have talked to me more when you came to dinner.

quote_text: A man who had felt less, might.
question: What does Darcy mean when he says a man who had felt less might have talked more?
answer: He means his strong feelings made him awkward and silent; a man less in love could have chatted easily.
evidence: A man who had felt less, might.

quote_text:
How unlucky that you should have a reasonable answer to give, and that
I should be so reasonable as to admit it! But I wonder how long you
_would_ have gone on, if you had been left to yourself. I wonder when
you _would_ have spoken, if I had not asked you! My resolution of
thanking you for your kindness to Lydia had certainly great effect. _Too
much_, I am afraid; for what becomes of the moral, if our comfort
springs from a breach of promise, for I ought not to have mentioned the
subject? This will never do.
question: What is Elizabeth teasing Darcy about in this speech?
answer: She jokes that his reasonable answer spoils her argument and that her thanks for Lydia had too much effect in prompting him.
evidence: My resolution of thanking you for your kindness to Lydia had certainly great effect.

quote_text:
You need not distress yourself. The moral will be perfectly fair. Lady
Catherine's unjustifiable endeavours to separate us, were the means of
removing all my doubts. I am not indebted for my present happiness to
your eager desire of expressing your gratitude. I was not in a humour to
wait for any opening of your's. My aunt's intelligence had given me
hope, and I was determined at once to know every thing.
question: What does Darcy say actually prompted him to propose to Elizabeth?
answer: He says Lady Catherine's attempt to separate them gave him hope and made him determined to learn Elizabeth's feelings.
evidence: Lady Catherine's unjustifiable endeavours to separate us, were the means of removing all my doubts.

quote_text:
Lady Catherine has been of infinite use, which ought to make her happy,
for she loves to be of use. But tell me, what did you come down to
Netherfield for? Was it merely to ride to Longbourn and be embarrassed?
or had you intended any more serious consequence?
question: Why does Elizabeth say Lady Catherine has been of infinite use?
answer: She means Lady Catherine's interference inadvertently brought Elizabeth and Darcy together.
evidence: Lady Catherine has been of infinite use

quote_text:
My real purpose was to see _you_, and to judge, if I could, whether I
might ever hope to make you love me. My avowed one, or what I avowed to
myself, was to see whether your sister were still partial to Bingley,
and if she were, to make the confession to him which I have since made.
question: What does Darcy reveal was his real purpose in coming to Netherfield?
answer: He came to see Elizabeth and judge whether he might hope to win her love; his stated purpose was to observe Jane and Bingley.
evidence: My real purpose was to see _you_, and to judge, if I could, whether I might ever hope to make you love me.

quote_text:
Shall you ever have courage to announce to Lady Catherine, what is to
befall her?
question: What is Elizabeth asking Darcy about Lady Catherine?
answer: She asks whether he will have the courage to tell his aunt about their engagement.
evidence: Shall you ever have courage to announce to Lady Catherine, what is to befall her?

quote_text:
I am more likely to want time than courage, Elizabeth. But it ought to
be done, and if you will give me a sheet of paper, it shall be done
directly.
question: How does Darcy respond to Elizabeth's question about telling Lady Catherine?
answer: He says he may lack time rather than courage, and will write to his aunt immediately if given paper.
evidence: if you will give me a sheet of paper, it shall be done directly.

quote_text:
And if I had not a letter to write myself, I might sit by you, and
admire the evenness of your writing, as another young lady once did. But
I have an aunt, too, who must not be longer neglected.
question: What joke does Elizabeth make about Miss Bingley's former behavior?
answer: She alludes to Miss Bingley's habit of sitting by Darcy and admiring his writing, saying she might do the same.
evidence: as another young lady once did

quote_text: Lady Catherine, I have nothing farther to say. You know my sentiments.
question: Why does Elizabeth end her conversation with Lady Catherine at this point?
answer: Lady Catherine has insulted Elizabeth by dragging in Lydia's elopement and the shame of a connection with her family, so Elizabeth refuses to continue.
evidence: You have insulted me, in every possible method. I must beg to return to the house.

quote_text: You are then resolved to have him?
question: What does Lady Catherine infer from Elizabeth's refusal to promise never to marry Mr. Darcy?
answer: She concludes that Elizabeth is resolved to have him.
evidence: I will make no promise of the kind.

quote_text:
I have said no such thing. I am only resolved to act in that manner,
which will, in my own opinion, constitute my happiness, without
reference to _you_, or to any person so wholly unconnected with me.
question: How does Elizabeth answer Lady Catherine's charge that she is determined to marry Darcy?
answer: She denies having said so and says she will act as she thinks will make her happy, regardless of Lady Catherine.
evidence: I am only resolved to act in that manner, which will, in my own opinion, constitute my happiness

quote_text:
It is well. You refuse, then, to oblige me. You refuse to obey the
claims of duty, honour, and gratitude. You are determined to ruin him in
the opinion of all his friends, and make him the contempt of the world.
question: What does Lady Catherine claim Elizabeth's refusal to promise will accomplish?
answer: She says Elizabeth is determined to ruin Darcy in the opinion of his friends and make him contemptible.
evidence: You are determined to ruin him in the opinion of all his friends, and make him the contempt of the world.

quote_text:
Neither duty, nor honour, nor gratitude, have any
possible claim on me, in the present instance. No principle of either,
would be violated by my marriage with Mr. Darcy. And with regard to the
resentment of his family, or the indignation of the world, if the former
_were_ excited by his marrying me, it would not give me one moment's
concern--and the world in general would have too much sense to join in
the scorn.
question: Why does Elizabeth say duty, honour, and gratitude have no claim on her in this matter?
answer: Because she believes marrying Darcy would violate no principle, and she owes Lady Catherine no obedience in choosing a husband.
evidence: No principle of either, would be violated by my marriage with Mr. Darcy.

quote_text:
And this is your real opinion! This is your final resolve! Very well. I
shall now know how to act. Do not imagine, Miss Bennet, that your
ambition will ever be gratified. I came to try you. I hoped to find you
reasonable; but depend upon it I will carry my point.
question: What does Lady Catherine threaten after hearing Elizabeth's final resolve?
answer: She says she came to test Elizabeth and will now act to carry her point, implying she will try to prevent the marriage.
evidence: I came to try you. I hoped to find you reasonable; but depend upon it I will carry my point.

quote_text:
I take no leave of you, Miss Bennet. I send no compliments to your
mother. You deserve no such attention. I am most seriously displeased.
question: How does Lady Catherine end her visit after failing to extract a promise from Elizabeth?
answer: She refuses to take leave or send compliments to Mrs. Bennet, declaring herself most seriously displeased.
evidence: I take no leave of you, Miss Bennet. I send no compliments to your mother.

quote_text: She did not choose it, she would go.
question: How does Elizabeth explain Lady Catherine's failure to come back into the house?
answer: She says Lady Catherine chose not to stay and simply went on her way.
evidence: She did not choose it,

quote_text:
She is a very fine-looking woman! and her calling here was prodigiously
civil! for she only came, I suppose, to tell us the Collinses were well.
She is on her road somewhere, I dare say, and so passing through
Meryton, thought she might as well call on you. I suppose she had
nothing particular to say to you, Lizzy?
question: What does Mrs. Bennet mistakenly believe was Lady Catherine's reason for visiting Longbourn?
answer: She thinks Lady Catherine was merely passing through and called to bring news of the Collinses.
evidence: she only came, I suppose, to tell us the Collinses were well.

quote_text:
If, therefore, an excuse for not keeping his promise, should come to
his friend within a few days, I shall know how to
understand it. I shall then give over every expectation, every wish of
his constancy. If he is satisfied with only regretting me, when he might
have obtained my affections and hand, I shall soon cease to regret him
at all.
question: What does Elizabeth expect to conclude if Mr. Darcy sends an excuse for not returning to Netherfield?
answer: She will take it as proof that Lady Catherine succeeded and will give up all hope of his constancy.
evidence: I shall then give over every expectation, every wish of his constancy.

quote_text: Lizzy, I was going to look for you; come into my room.
question: What prompts Mr. Bennet to seek Elizabeth out and call her into his room?
answer: He has received a letter in his library and wants to discuss it with her.
evidence: who came out of his library with a letter in his hand.

quote_text:
I have received a letter this morning that has astonished me
exceedingly. As it principally concerns yourself, you ought to know its
contents. I did not know before, that I had _two_ daughters on the brink
of matrimony. Let me congratulate you, on a very important conquest.
question: What news does Mr. Bennet believe the letter contains about Elizabeth?
answer: He thinks she is on the brink of matrimony and congratulates her on a conquest.
evidence: I did not know before, that I had _two_ daughters on the brink of matrimony.

quote_text:
You look conscious. Young ladies have great penetration in such matters
as these; but I think I may defy even _your_ sagacity, to discover the
name of your admirer. This letter is from Mr. Collins.
question: What does Mr. Bennet assume about Elizabeth's ability to guess the letter writer?
answer: He assumes she cannot guess it, though he teasingly notes she looks conscious.
evidence: I think I may defy even _your_ sagacity, to discover the name of your admirer.

quote_text: From Mr. Collins! and what can _he_ have to say?
question: Why is Elizabeth surprised that the letter is from Mr. Collins?
answer: She had suspected it might be from Lady Catherine about the report of her and Darcy.
evidence: It suddenly struck her that it might be from lady Catherine

quote_text:
Something very much to the purpose of course. He begins with
congratulations on the approaching nuptials of my eldest daughter, of
which it seems he has been told, by some of the good-natured, gossiping
Lucases. I shall not sport with your impatience, by reading what he says
on that point. What relates to yourself, is as follows.
question: What does Mr. Collins's letter first discuss before turning to Elizabeth?
answer: It congratulates the family on Jane's approaching marriage to Mr. Bingley.
evidence: He begins with congratulations on the approaching nuptials of my eldest daughter

quote_text: Can you possibly guess, Lizzy, who is meant by this?
question: What does Mr. Bennet want Elizabeth to guess from the passage he quotes?
answer: He wants her to identify the illustrious gentleman Mr. Collins says she will marry.
evidence: who is meant by this?

quote_text: Have you any idea, Lizzy, who this gentleman is? But now it comes out.
question: How does Mr. Bennet build suspense about the gentleman named in Collins's letter?
answer: He withholds the name while quoting Collins's warning about the match.
evidence: Have you any idea, Lizzy, who this gentleman is? But now it comes out.

quote_text:
_Mr. Darcy_, you see, is the man! Now, Lizzy, I think I _have_
surprised you. Could he, or the Lucases, have pitched on any man, within
the circle of our acquaintance, whose name would have given the lie more
effectually to what they related? Mr. Darcy, who never looks at any
woman but to see a blemish, and who probably never looked at _you_ in
his life! It is admirable!
question: Why does Mr. Bennet find the idea of Darcy as Elizabeth's admirer so absurd?
answer: Because he believes Darcy never looks at a woman except to find a blemish and probably never looked at Elizabeth.
evidence: Mr. Darcy, who never looks at any woman but to see a blemish

quote_text: Are you not diverted?
question: Why does Mr. Bennet ask whether Elizabeth is diverted?
answer: He expects her to enjoy the absurdity of the report, since Darcy's name seems the least likely match for her.
evidence: whose name would have given the lie more effectually to what they related?

quote_text: Oh! yes. Pray read on.
question: How does Elizabeth hide her real feelings about her father's jokes?
answer: She forces a reluctant smile and pretends to be amused, asking him to continue reading.
evidence: she could only force one most reluctant smile.

quote_text:
Mr.
Collins moreover adds,
question: What does Mr. Collins add about Lydia's marriage in his letter?
answer: He says he is glad it was hushed up but condemns the couple being received at Longbourn.
evidence: I am truly rejoiced that my cousin Lydia's sad business has been so well hushed up

quote_text:
_That_ is his notion of christian
forgiveness! The rest of his letter is only about his dear Charlotte's
situation, and his expectation of a young olive-branch. But, Lizzy, you
look as if you did not enjoy it. You are not going to be _Missish_, I
hope, and pretend to be affronted at an idle report. For what do we
live, but to make sport for our neighbours, and laugh at them in our
turn?"
question: Why does Mr. Bennet call Mr. Collins's notion of Christian forgiveness hypocritical?
answer: Because Collins says Lydia should be forgiven but never admitted or mentioned again.
evidence: You ought certainly to forgive them as a christian, but never to admit them in your sight

quote_text:
Oh! I am excessively diverted. But it is so
strange!
question: Why does Elizabeth call the report strange despite pretending to be amused?
answer: She is privately hurt, because her father assumes Darcy is indifferent to her and she is only feigning diversion.
evidence: Never had his wit been directed in a manner so little agreeable to her.

quote_text:
Yes--_that_ is what makes it amusing. Had they fixed on any other man
it would have been nothing; but _his_ perfect indifference, and _your_
pointed dislike, make it so delightfully absurd! Much as I abominate
writing, I would not give up Mr. Collins's correspondence for any
consideration. Nay, when I read a letter of his, I cannot help giving
him the preference even over Wickham, much as I value the impudence and
hypocrisy of my son-in-law. And pray, Lizzy, what said Lady Catherine
about this report? Did she call to refuse her consent?
question: Why does Mr. Bennet find the supposed match so delightfully absurd?
answer: Because Darcy is perfectly indifferent and Elizabeth has shown pointed dislike, making the report ridiculous.
evidence: _his_ perfect indifference, and _your_ pointed dislike, make it so delightfully absurd!

quote_text:
Mr. Darcy, I am a very selfish creature; and, for the sake of giving
relief to my own feelings, care not how much I may be wounding your's. I
can no longer help thanking you for your unexampled kindness to my poor
sister. Ever since I have known it, I have been most anxious to
acknowledge to you how gratefully I feel it. Were it known to the rest
of my family, I should not have merely my own gratitude to express.
question: Why does Elizabeth thank Mr. Darcy during their walk?
answer: She has learned he rescued Lydia and arranged her marriage, and she wants to acknowledge her gratitude.
evidence: I can no longer help thanking you for your unexampled kindness to my poor sister.

quote_text:
I am sorry, exceedingly sorry, that you have ever been informed of what may, in a
mistaken light, have given you uneasiness. I did not think Mrs.
Gardiner was so little to be trusted.
question: Why is Darcy sorry that Elizabeth learned of his role in Lydia's affair?
answer: He thinks the knowledge may have given her uneasiness and had wished it kept private.
evidence: that you have ever been informed of what may, in a mistaken light, have given you uneasiness.

quote_text:
You must not blame my aunt. Lydia's thoughtlessness first betrayed to
me that you had been concerned in the matter; and, of course, I could
not rest till I knew the particulars. Let me thank you again and again,
in the name of all my family, for that generous compassion which induced
you to take so much trouble, and bear so many mortifications, for the
sake of discovering them.
question: How did Elizabeth learn that Darcy was involved in Lydia's marriage?
answer: Lydia let slip that Darcy attended the wedding, prompting Elizabeth to write to Mrs. Gardiner for details.
evidence: Lydia's thoughtlessness first betrayed to me that you had been concerned in the matter

quote_text:
If you _will_ thank me, let it be for yourself alone.
That the wish of giving happiness to you, might add force to the other
inducements which led me on, I shall not attempt to deny. But your
_family_ owe me nothing. Much as I respect them, I believe, I thought
only of _you_.
question: What does Darcy reveal as his main motive for helping Lydia?
answer: His wish to give happiness to Elizabeth; he says he thought only of her.
evidence: I believe, I thought only of _you_.

quote_text:
You are too generous to trifle with me. If your
feelings are still what they were last April, tell me so at once. _My_
affections and wishes are unchanged, but one word from you will silence
me on this subject for ever.
question: What does Darcy ask Elizabeth to tell him after her thanks?
answer: Whether her feelings are still as they were last April, or whether she now returns his affection.
evidence: If your feelings are still what they were last April, tell me so at once.

quote_text:
It taught me to hope, as I had scarcely ever allowed myself
to hope before. I knew enough of your disposition to be certain, that,
had you been absolutely, irrevocably decided against me, you would have
acknowledged it to Lady Catherine, frankly and openly.
question: Why did Lady Catherine's interference actually encourage Darcy?
answer: Her report of Elizabeth's refusal to promise never to marry him made him hope Elizabeth might accept him.
evidence: its effect had been exactly contrariwise

quote_text:
Yes, you know enough of
my _frankness_ to believe me capable of _that_. After abusing you so
abominably to your face, I could have no scruple in abusing you to all
your relations.
question: What does Elizabeth admit about how she spoke of Darcy to Lady Catherine?
answer: She admits she abused him to his relations as freely as she had to his face.
evidence: After abusing you so abominably to your face, I could have no scruple in abusing you to all your relations.

quote_text:
What did you say of me, that I did not deserve? For, though your
accusations were ill-founded, formed on mistaken premises, my behaviour
to you at the time, had merited the severest reproof. It was
unpardonable. I cannot think of it without abhorrence.
question: How does Darcy respond to Elizabeth's joke about abusing him to his relatives?
answer: He says his behavior at the time deserved her reproof and cannot be thought of without abhorrence.
evidence: my behaviour to you at the time, had merited the severest reproof. It was unpardonable.

quote_text:
We will not quarrel for the greater share of blame annexed to that
evening, The conduct of neither, if strictly examined,
will be irreproachable; but since then, we have both, I hope, improved
in civility.
question: What does Elizabeth propose instead of arguing over who was more to blame for their past quarrel?
answer: She says neither was blameless and that they have both improved in civility since.
evidence: The conduct of neither, if strictly examined, will be irreproachable

quote_text:
I cannot be so easily reconciled to myself. The recollection of what I
then said, of my conduct, my manners, my expressions during the whole of
it, is now, and has been many months, inexpressibly painful to me. Your
reproof, so well applied, I shall never forget:
question: Why does Darcy say he cannot be easily reconciled to himself?
answer: He is pained by remembering his own proud, rude conduct and expressions when he first proposed.
evidence: The recollection of what I then said, of my conduct, my manners, my expressions

quote_text:
Those were your words. You know not, you
can scarcely conceive, how they have tortured me;--though it was some
time, I confess, before I was reasonable enough to allow their justice.
question: Which reproof of Elizabeth's has haunted Darcy?
answer: Her charge that he had not behaved in a gentleman-like manner.
evidence: had you behaved in a more gentleman-like manner.

quote_text:
I was certainly very far from expecting them to make so strong an
impression. I had not the smallest idea of their being ever felt in such
a way.
question: Why is Elizabeth surprised by Darcy's reaction to her old reproof?
answer: She had no idea her words had affected him so deeply.
evidence: I had not the smallest idea of their being ever felt in such a way.

quote_text:
I can easily believe it. You thought me then devoid of every proper
feeling, I am sure you did. The turn of your countenance I shall never
forget, as you said that I could not have addressed you in any possible
way, that would induce you to accept me.
question: What does Darcy remember about Elizabeth's manner when she rejected him?
answer: He remembers her expression as she said nothing could induce her to accept him.
evidence: The turn of your countenance I shall never forget, as you said that I could not have addressed you

quote_text:
Oh! do not repeat what I then said. These recollections will not do at
all. I assure you, that I have long been most heartily ashamed of it.
question: How does Elizabeth react to Darcy's recollection of her harsh words?
answer: She is ashamed and begs him not to repeat them.
evidence: I have long been most heartily ashamed of it.

quote_text:
Did it, did it _soon_ make you
think better of me? Did you, on reading it, give any credit to its
contents? I knew, that what I wrote must give you pain, but it was
necessary. I hope you have destroyed the letter. There was one part
especially, the opening of it, which I should dread your having the
power of reading again. I can remember some expressions which might
justly make you hate me.
question: What does Darcy want to know about the effect of his letter?
answer: Whether it soon improved her opinion of him and whether she believed its contents.
evidence: did it _soon_ make you think better of me? Did you, on reading it, give any credit to its contents?

quote_text:
The letter shall certainly be burnt, if you believe it essential to the
preservation of my regard; but, though we have both reason to think my
opinions not entirely unalterable, they are not, I hope, quite so easily
changed as that implies.
question: Why does Elizabeth offer to burn Darcy's letter?
answer: He dreads her rereading its bitter opening, so she jokes she will burn it if he thinks it essential.
evidence: The letter shall certainly be burnt, if you believe it essential to the preservation of my regard

quote_text:
When I wrote that letter, I believed myself perfectly
calm and cool, but I am since convinced that it was written in a
dreadful bitterness of spirit.
question: Why does Darcy bring up the letter after Elizabeth offers to burn it?
answer: He admits that although he thought he was calm when writing it, he now believes it was written with bitter feeling.
evidence: I believed myself perfectly calm and cool, but I am since convinced that it was written in a dreadful bitterness of spirit.

quote_text:
The letter, perhaps, began in bitterness, but it did not end so. The
adieu is charity itself. But think no more of the letter. The feelings
of the person who wrote, and the person who received it, are now so
widely different from what they were then, that every unpleasant
circumstance attending it, ought to be forgotten. You must learn some
of my philosophy. Think only of the past as its remembrance gives you
pleasure.
question: How does Elizabeth soften Darcy's self-criticism about his letter?
answer: She says the letter may have begun bitterly but ended charitably, and urges him to stop dwelling on it.
evidence: The adieu is charity itself. But think no more of the letter.

quote_text:
I cannot give you credit for any philosophy of the kind. _Your_
retrospections must be so totally void of reproach, that the contentment
arising from them, is not of philosophy, but what is much better, of
ignorance. But with _me_, it is not so. Painful recollections will
intrude, which cannot, which ought not to be repelled. I have been a
selfish being all my life, in practice, though not in principle. As a
child I was taught what was _right_, but I was not taught to correct my
temper. I was given good principles, but left to follow them in pride
and conceit. Unfortunately an only son, (for many years an only _child_)
I was spoilt by my parents, who though good themselves, (my father
particularly, all that was benevolent and amiable,) allowed, encouraged,
almost taught me to be selfish and overbearing, to care for none beyond
my own family circle, to think meanly of all the rest of the world, to
_wish_ at least to think meanly of their sense and worth compared with
my own. Such I was, from eight to eight and twenty; and such I might
still have been but for you, dearest, loveliest Elizabeth! What do I not
owe you! You taught me a lesson, hard indeed at first, but most
advantageous. By you, I was properly humbled. I came to you without a
doubt of my reception. You shewed me how insufficient were all my
pretensions to please a woman worthy of being pleased.
question: Why does Darcy reject Elizabeth's advice to remember only pleasant parts of the past?
answer: He says her past is free from reproach, so her contentment is ignorance rather than philosophy; his own painful memories intrude.
evidence: Painful recollections will intrude, which cannot, which ought not to be repelled.

quote_text: Had you then persuaded yourself that I should?
question: What does Elizabeth's question reveal about her reaction to Darcy's confession?
answer: She is surprised and amused that he had been confident she would accept him despite her earlier rejection.
evidence: I came to you without a doubt of my reception.

quote_text:
Indeed I had. What will you think of my vanity? I believed you to be
wishing, expecting my addresses.
question: What does Darcy admit about his expectations when he proposed?
answer: He admits his vanity: he had believed Elizabeth was wishing for and expecting his addresses.
evidence: I believed you to be wishing, expecting my addresses.

quote_text:
My manners must have been in fault, but not intentionally I assure you.
I never meant to deceive you, but my spirits might often lead me wrong.
How you must have hated me after _that_ evening?
question: Why does Elizabeth blame her manners in this conversation?
answer: She explains that she never meant to deceive him, but her lively spirits may have misled him unintentionally.
evidence: I never meant to deceive you, but my spirits might often lead me wrong.

quote_text:
Hate you! I was angry perhaps at first, but my anger soon began to take
a proper direction.
question: What does Darcy mean by saying his anger took a proper direction?
answer: He did not hate Elizabeth; his first anger soon turned into a more appropriate self-reproach.
evidence: my anger soon began to take a proper direction.

quote_text:
I am almost afraid of asking what you thought of me; when we met at
Pemberley. You blamed me for coming?
question: What does Elizabeth want to know about the Pemberley meeting?
answer: She asks whether Darcy thought badly of her for coming to Pemberley.
evidence: You blamed me for coming?

quote_text: No indeed; I felt nothing but surprise.
question: How did Darcy react to Elizabeth's unexpected arrival at Pemberley?
answer: He says he felt only surprise, not blame.
evidence: I felt nothing but surprise.

quote_text:
Your surprise could not be greater than _mine_ in being noticed by you.
My conscience told me that I deserved no extraordinary politeness, and I
confess that I did not expect to receive _more_ than my due.
question: Why was Elizabeth surprised by Darcy's politeness at Pemberley?
answer: Her conscience told her she deserved no extraordinary politeness after her past treatment of him.
evidence: I did not expect to receive _more_ than my due.

quote_text:
My object _then_, was to shew you, by every civility
in my power, that I was not so mean as to resent the past; and I hoped
to obtain your forgiveness, to lessen your ill opinion, by letting you
see that your reproofs had been attended to. How soon any other wishes
introduced themselves I can hardly tell, but I believe in about half an
hour after I had seen you.
question: What did Darcy intend by being civil to Elizabeth at Pemberley?
answer: He wanted to show he did not resent the past and hoped to obtain her forgiveness.
evidence: that I was not so mean as to resent the past; and I hoped to obtain your forgiveness

quote_text: I must ask whether you were surprised?
question: What is Elizabeth asking Darcy to reveal about Bingley and Jane's engagement?
answer: She asks whether Darcy was surprised by their engagement.
evidence: Darcy was delighted with their engagement; his friend had given him the earliest information of it.

quote_text: Not at all. When I went away, I felt that it would soon happen.
question: Why was Darcy not surprised by Bingley's engagement?
answer: He says he had felt when leaving that it would soon happen.
evidence: When I went away, I felt that it would soon happen.

quote_text: That is to say, you had given your permission. I guessed as much.
question: What does Elizabeth teasingly imply about Darcy's role in Bingley's engagement?
answer: She implies that Darcy had given his permission or approval, as she had guessed.
evidence: you had given your permission. I guessed as much.

quote_text:
On the evening before my going to London, I made a confession
to him, which I believe I ought to have made long ago. I told him of
all that had occurred to make my former interference in his affairs,
absurd and impertinent. His surprise was great. He had never had the
slightest suspicion. I told him, moreover, that I believed myself
mistaken in supposing, as I had done, that your sister was indifferent
to him; and as I could easily perceive that his attachment to her was
unabated, I felt no doubt of their happiness together.
question: What confession did Darcy make to Bingley before leaving for London?
answer: He admitted that his former interference in Bingley's affairs had been absurd and impertinent.
evidence: I told him of all that had occurred to make my former interference in his affairs, absurd and impertinent.

quote_text:
Did you speak from your own observation, when you told him
that my sister loved him, or merely from my information last spring?
question: What does Elizabeth want to know about Darcy's assurance to Bingley concerning Jane?
answer: She asks whether he spoke from his own observation or only from her earlier information.
evidence: Did you speak from your own observation, when you told him that my sister loved him

quote_text:
From the former. I had narrowly observed her during the two visits
which I had lately made her here; and I was convinced of her affection.
question: How did Darcy become convinced Jane loved Bingley?
answer: He says he had closely observed her during his two recent visits and was convinced of her affection.
evidence: I had narrowly observed her during the two visits which I had lately made her here

quote_text:
And your assurance of it, I suppose, carried immediate conviction to
him.
question: What does Elizabeth suppose about Bingley's reaction to Darcy's assurance?
answer: She supposes Darcy's assurance immediately convinced Bingley of Jane's affection.
evidence: It did. Bingley is most unaffectedly modest.

quote_text:
It did. Bingley is most unaffectedly modest. His diffidence had
prevented his depending on his own judgment in so anxious a case, but
his reliance on mine, made every thing easy. I was obliged to confess
one thing, which for a time, and not unjustly, offended him. I could not
allow myself to conceal that your sister had been in town three months
last winter, that I had known it, and purposely kept it from him. He was
angry. But his anger, I am persuaded, lasted no longer than he remained
in any doubt of your sister's sentiments. He has heartily forgiven me
now.
question: Why was Bingley so easily convinced by Darcy about Jane?
answer: Bingley was modest and diffident, so his reliance on Darcy's judgment made everything easy.
evidence: his reliance on mine, made every thing easy.

quote_text: My dear Lizzy, where can you have been walking to?
question: Why does Jane ask where Elizabeth has been?
answer: Elizabeth and Darcy have returned late after wandering without direction, and Jane asks innocently.
evidence: they had wandered about, till she was beyond her own knowledge.

quote_text:
You are joking, Lizzy. This cannot be!--engaged to Mr. Darcy! No, no,
you shall not deceive me. I know it to be impossible.
question: Why does Jane refuse to believe Elizabeth's news?
answer: She thinks an engagement to Mr. Darcy is impossible and suspects Elizabeth is joking.
evidence: engaged to Mr. Darcy! No, no, you shall not deceive me. I know it to be impossible.

quote_text:
This is a wretched beginning indeed! My sole dependence was on you; and
I am sure nobody else will believe me, if you do not. Yet, indeed, I am
in earnest. I speak nothing but the truth. He still loves me, and we are
engaged.
question: Why does Elizabeth call this a wretched beginning?
answer: Jane is her sole confidante, so Elizabeth fears nobody else will believe the engagement if Jane doubts it.
evidence: nobody else will believe me, if you do not.

quote_text:
Oh, Lizzy! it cannot be. I know how much
you dislike him.
question: What reason does Jane give for doubting Elizabeth's engagement to Darcy?
answer: She says she knows how much Elizabeth has disliked Darcy.
evidence: I know how much you dislike him.

quote_text:
You know nothing of the matter. _That_ is all to be forgot. Perhaps I
did not always love him so well as I do now. But in such cases as these,
a good memory is unpardonable. This is the last time I shall ever
remember it myself.
question: How does Elizabeth explain her changed feelings toward Darcy?
answer: She says her past dislike should be forgotten and that she may not always have loved him as she does now.
evidence: Perhaps I did not always love him so well as I do now.

quote_text:
Good Heaven! can it be really so! Yet now I must believe you, My dear, dear Lizzy, I would--I do congratulate you--but are you
certain? forgive the question--are you quite certain that you can be
happy with him?
question: What concern does Jane express even after accepting the engagement?
answer: She asks whether Elizabeth is quite certain she can be happy with Darcy.
evidence: are you quite certain that you can be happy with him?

quote_text:
There can be no doubt of that. It is settled between us already, that
we are to be the happiest couple in the world. But are you pleased,
Jane? Shall you like to have such a brother?
question: What reassurance does Elizabeth seek from Jane after assuring her of her happiness?
answer: She asks whether Jane is pleased and would like Darcy as a brother.
evidence: But are you pleased, Jane? Shall you like to have such a brother?

quote_text:
Very, very much. Nothing could give either Bingley or myself more
delight. But we considered it, we talked of it as impossible. And do you
really love him quite well enough? Oh, Lizzy! do any thing rather than
marry without affection. Are you quite sure that you feel what you ought
to do?
question: Why does Jane still question Elizabeth despite expressing delight?
answer: She wants Elizabeth to marry only with real affection and not without love.
evidence: do any thing rather than marry without affection.

quote_text:
Oh, yes! You will only think I feel _more_ than I ought to do, when I
tell you all.
question: What does Elizabeth mean by saying Jane will think she feels more than she ought?
answer: She is teasing that her feelings for Darcy are stronger than Jane expects, and promises to explain.
evidence: You will only think I feel _more_ than I ought to do

quote_text: What do you mean?
question: Why does Jane ask what Elizabeth means?
answer: Elizabeth's cryptic remark about feeling more than she ought prompts Jane to demand an explanation.
evidence: You will only think I feel _more_ than I ought to do, when I tell you all.

quote_text:
Why, I must confess, that I love him better than I do Bingley. I am
afraid you will be angry.
question: What teasing confession does Elizabeth make to Jane?
answer: She jokingly confesses that she loves Darcy better than she loves Bingley, fearing Jane will be angry.
evidence: I love him better than I do Bingley. I am afraid you will be angry.

quote_text:
My dearest sister, now _be_ be serious. I want to talk very seriously.
Let me know every thing that I am to know, without delay. Will you tell
me how long you have loved him?
question: What does Jane want Elizabeth to do after her joking?
answer: She asks Elizabeth to be serious and tell her how long Elizabeth has loved Darcy.
evidence: Will you tell me how long you have loved him?

quote_text:
It has been coming on so gradually, that I hardly know when it began.
But I believe I must date it from my first seeing his beautiful grounds
at Pemberley.
question: What does Elizabeth jokingly identify as the start of her love for Darcy?
answer: She says it came gradually but dates it from first seeing the beautiful grounds at Pemberley.
evidence: I must date it from my first seeing his beautiful grounds at Pemberley.

quote_text:
Now I am quite happy, for you will be as happy as myself. I
always had a value for him. Were it for nothing but his love of you, I
must always have esteemed him; but now, as Bingley's friend and your
husband, there can be only Bingley and yourself more dear to me. But
Lizzy, you have been very sly, very reserved with me. How little did you
tell me of what passed at Pemberley and Lambton! I owe all that I know
of it, to another, not to you.
question: Why is Jane now happy about Elizabeth's engagement?
answer: She is convinced Elizabeth will be as happy as she is and values Darcy for his love of Elizabeth.
evidence: for you will be as happy as myself.

quote_text:
Good gracious! if that disagreeable Mr. Darcy is not coming here again with
our dear Bingley! What can he mean by being so tiresome as to be always
coming here? I had no notion but he would go a shooting, or something or
other, and not disturb us with his company. What shall we do with him?
Lizzy, you must walk out with him again, that he may not be in Bingley's
way.
question: Why is Mrs. Bennet annoyed by Darcy's arrival?
answer: She still dislikes Darcy and thinks he is tiresomely always coming with Bingley.
evidence: What can he mean by being so tiresome as to be always coming here?

quote_text:
Mr. Bennet, have you no more lanes
hereabouts in which Lizzy may lose her way again to-day?
question: What does Bingley's teasing question reveal that he knows?
answer: He knows about Elizabeth and Darcy's engagement and teases about her losing her way again.
evidence: left no doubt of his good information

quote_text:
I advise Mr. Darcy, and Lizzy, and Kitty, to walk
to Oakham Mount this morning. It is a nice long walk, and Mr. Darcy has
never seen the view.
question: Why does Mrs. Bennet propose the walk to Oakham Mount?
answer: She wants Darcy kept occupied away from Bingley so Bingley can be alone with Jane.
evidence: that he may not be in Bingley's way.

quote_text:
It may do very well for the others, but I am
sure it will be too much for Kitty. Wont it, Kitty?
question: Why does Bingley object to Kitty joining the walk?
answer: He pretends the walk is too much for Kitty so Darcy and Elizabeth can go together.
evidence: but I am sure it will be too much for Kitty.

quote_text:
I am quite sorry, Lizzy, that you should be forced to have that
disagreeable man all to yourself. But I hope you will not mind it: it is
all for Jane's sake, you know; and there is no occasion for talking to
him, except just now and then. So, do not put yourself to
inconvenience.
question: Why does Mrs. Bennet pity Elizabeth about walking with Darcy?
answer: She thinks Darcy is disagreeable and believes Elizabeth is entertaining him only to help Jane.
evidence: it is all for Jane's sake, you know

quote_text:
Go to your father, he
wants you in the library.
question: Why does Darcy send Elizabeth to the library?
answer: He has just asked Mr. Bennet for consent, and Mr. Bennet now wants to speak with Elizabeth.
evidence: she saw Mr. Darcy rise also and follow him

quote_text:
Lizzy, what are you doing? Are you out of your senses, to be
accepting this man? Have not you always hated him?
question: Why is Mr. Bennet alarmed by Elizabeth's engagement?
answer: He remembers that Elizabeth always hated Darcy and fears she is accepting a man she cannot respect.
evidence: Have not you always hated him?
